This summary of the meaning of the *Gītā*: This world, consisting of an expansive and shimmering cycle of various phenomena,
which possesses mutual distinctions and becomes an object of experience— by virtue of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of it as being one with [the Self]...
Victorious is that Śambhu, the destroyer of inauspiciousness, who is the treasury of the lights of awakening and whose nature is non-dual;
for in this scripture consisting of one hundred thousand verses composed by the sage Dvaipāyana, liberation is the primary fruit.
It is proclaimed that other factors such as dharma and so forth are taught in order to nourish that [faith]. || 1-2 ||

And liberation (mokṣa), in brief, is absorption into the Lord, the Sovereign, who is eternally manifest, devoid of all desire, whose nature is auspicious— consisting of omniscience, the capacity for all actions, and so forth— and whose form is entirely undivided. || 1-3 ||
Although liberation is mentioned here in connection with other topics, nevertheless, the Bhagavad Gītā perfectly bestows the attainment of that very liberation. 1-4.
Although many commentaries have been composed on these by others in the past, my present effort is nevertheless justified as it illuminates their hidden meaning. (1.5)
Having long discerned the tradition through his intellect from Bhaṭṭendurāja, this *Gītārthasaṃgraha* has been composed by Abhinavagupta. (1.6)
Now begins the first chapter:
the introduction to the first chapter, intended to demonstrate that the two— knowledge and ignorance— are characterized by the relationship of the subduer and the subdued.

For one who has not yet produced even a trace of knowledge is not a fit vessel for instruction, nor is one for whom the entire proliferation of ignorance has been uprooted; this is because it is impossible to cause one who has come to rest in that single extreme to fall away from it. However, the state of being a candidate for instruction belongs to those who are ignorant and those who are deluded.

That which is stated occurs only in certain instances; thus, when an object must be taught as being such-and-such, there is indeed doubt. For this very reason, instruction consists precisely in the removal of doubt;
therefore, doubt is said to consist of the conjunction of the limbs of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Since the creation of the gods and asuras consists of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), the very commencement of that narrative is an instruction on the path to liberation. Furthermore, since knowledge is primary and actions are to be relinquished, even when actions are performed with a focus on knowledge, they [are subsumed under it].
The point is this: knowledge is primary because it possesses the nature of being non-binding, whereas action is merely its necessary concomitant;
the intention is not that knowledge and action are to be combined as equals on the same footing. And such indeed is the Sage’s intention at the appropriate place.
Since we shall establish [the truth], what is the use of other webs of words whose only fruit is to create obstacles to the vision of reality?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of dharma, at Kurukṣetra, where all the kṣatriyas had assembled, what did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do, O Sañjaya?

Regarding this, some state various interpretations: that which is the field (*kṣetra*) of the Kurus— that is, of the instruments (*karaṇas*)— is the very field of all worldly phenomena (*saṃsārika-dharmas*), because it is the cause of their arising.

"This is that supreme dharma, which is the perception of the Self through yoga" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti); and the field for this dharma is the body qualified for it, which serves as a protection by securing liberation through the exhaustion of all [other] dharmas.

In that place where there is a gathering of all fields— since the root *kṣi* has the meaning of "injury"— namely, passion and dispassion, anger and forbearance, and so forth, which exist in a state of mutual slayer and slain.

Those who are "mine" (*māmakāḥ*) are the volitions (*saṅkalpāḥ*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyāmaya*), appropriate for the person of ignorance (*avidyāpuruṣa*). The Pāṇḍavas, however, are those whose nature is knowledge (*vidyātman*), appropriate for the person of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyāpuruṣa*).
What did they do? That is to say, by whom were which [beings] conquered? [The word] *mama* signifies that which extends itself (*kāyati*).
My person is the man of ignorance; he is pale and pure. || 1 ||
Sañjaya said:
Having seen the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana then approached the Teacher and spoke these words.
Behold, O Teacher, this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up in battle array by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple.
Here are heroes, great archers equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great car-warrior.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic King of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaivya, the bull among men. 1-5 ||
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas, as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī— all of them were indeed great car-warriors (mahārathas).
But as for those who are distinguished among us, listen to them, O best of the twice-born;
I shall name them to you for the sake of identifying the leaders of my army.
All those who are leaders in this great army and esteemed as heroes— you, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Jayadratha, Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and the valiant son of Somadatta— [are here]. (1–8)
Moreover, there are many other heroes who have renounced their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and there is none among them who is not skilled in diverse modes of warfare.
What is the use of this detailed calculation? He states that this is the actual state of affairs:
"That army of ours, protected by Bhīma, is insufficient; however, this army of theirs, protected by Bhīṣma, is sufficient. (1.10)

The Pāṇḍava army, protected by Bhīmasena, is "insufficient" for us—meaning it is impossible to conquer; or, "insufficient" means that it is merely a small fraction compared to our own force. But this...
"Our army, protected by Bhīṣma, is sufficient to conquer these Pāṇḍavas; or rather, it is so vast that they cannot be defeated by them in battle. (1-10)
And in all the flanks, stationed each according to his allotted place,
may you all indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.
Producing joy for him, the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus, let out a loud lion’s roar and blew his conch shell. 1.12.
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded; that noise became tumultuous.
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava blew their divine conchs.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta,
and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [possessed] the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva [had] the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
And Kāśya, the supreme archer; Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki. || 1.17 ||
And the great archer Pāñcālya, the five sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, each blew their conchs separately.
That tumultuous roar, making both heaven and earth resound, rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stationed in their positions, the Pāṇḍava whose banner bears the monkey, raised his bow as the clash of weapons was about to begin.
Then, O lord of the earth, Arjuna spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies. (1.21)
As long as I observe these who stand ready, desiring to fight, with whom must I contend in this undertaking of war? (1.22)
I shall behold those who have gathered here,
desiring to fight, wishing to do what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies, [said]: 1-24.
In front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth, he said, "O Pārtha,
behold these Kurus assembled here."
There, Pārtha beheld his fathers and grandfathers stationed,
as well as his teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
As well as their fathers-in-law and friends, belonging to both armies.
Beholding all those kinsmen standing there, that son of Kuntī, overcome by supreme compassion and sinking down, spoke this: || 1.28 ||
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here desirous of fighting,
my limbs fail me and my mouth is parched.
Trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end; the Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand and my skin is burning all over.
And I am unable to remain steady; my mind seems to reel, O Keśava! And I behold portents that are adverse.
Nor do I foresee any good from killing my own kinsmen in battle. O Kṛṣṇa! I do not desire victory, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
Of what use is sovereignty to us, O Govinda! Of what use are enjoyments or even life itself, for the sake of which we desired sovereignty, enjoyments, and pleasures?
These are standing here in battle, having renounced both their lives and their wealth: teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers.
O Madhusūdana! I do not wish to kill these—maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—even though they are killing me. (1.35)
Even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds—how much more so for the sake of the earth?

These [beings], such as the teachers and others, when brought to mind with the specific thought "these are the teachers," etc., and designated as the objects of the act of killing, will necessarily bring about sin. Likewise:

The intention of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that if one engages in battle with the thought, "This war is being waged for the sake of visible ends such as wealth and pleasure," then acts such as killing those who should not be killed in battles will necessarily constitute a sin. For this very reason, [it is said] solely by way of it being one's own duty (svadharma).
"Perform actions without a sense of distinction"—this will be the answer given. || 35 ||
"O Janārdana, what joy would there be for us even after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?"
"By slaying these aggressors, we would only take upon ourselves sin; therefore, it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen. (1.37)
Regarding the word "having slain": in the killing of those who act as aggressors (*ātatāyin*), the evil itself is the agent. Therefore, this is the meaning:
first, these enemies of ours have been slain—that is, rendered subject to another—by evil;
and having slain them, that very evil shall take refuge even in us. Here, "evil" refers to the power of greed.
The failure to perceive the faults such as the destruction of one's family. || 1-36 ||
For this very reason, Arjuna introduces the matters of the destruction of the family and so forth with the words, "How indeed [can I slay my own kin]," and so on:
"O Mādhava! How indeed, having slain our own kin, shall we be happy? Even though these [are not...]"
Those whose minds are afflicted by greed do not see [this]. || 1.38 ||
How could we not recognize the fault caused by the destruction of the family and the sin of betraying friends, so as to turn away from this evil? (1.39)
O Janārdana, clearly perceiving the evil resulting from the destruction of a lineage, [we see that] upon the destruction of a lineage, the eternal family traditions perish. (1.40)
When dharma is destroyed, indeed, adharma overcomes the entire family;
and from the prevalence of adharma, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupt. (1.41)
O Vārṣṇeya! When women are corrupt, a confusion of castes arises; this intermixture leads to hell for both the destroyers of the lineage and the lineage itself.
For their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water, due to these faults of the destroyers of the lineage who cause the intermixture of castes.
The eternal laws of caste and the laws of family are destroyed;
O Janārdana, for those men whose family laws have been destroyed, [the sins of the world fall upon them]. (1.44)

"We have heard that residence in hell is certain; for killing with the notion of a specific reward, or with the notion of a specific [victim] such as one who ought to be killed, constitutes a mortal sin (mahāpātaka). To state this very point in brief:
To indicate the intensity of his anguish, Arjuna spoke these words to himself:
"Alas! What a great sin we have resolved to commit, that out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty, we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen. (1.45)
"We" means all [of us] without exception, divided into the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas. || 1-45 ||

Thus, while all these others are undiscriminating, what is appropriate for me, who possess discrimination? First, it is appropriate to desist from battle; indeed, this is even more appropriate, as he says:
"If these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, [should attack] me, who am unarmed and offer no resistance..."
If they should slay me in battle, that would be more secure for me. || 1.46 ||
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows,
his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Regarding this, there is a summary verse:
Rendered helpless by the collision of the destruction of both knowledge and ignorance, the sage, having abandoned both through skillful means, becomes free from discrimination. (1.1)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara tradition. May there be auspiciousness.
Then begins the second chapter.
Sañjaya said:
To him who was thus overcome with compassion, his eyes clouded and filled with tears—
To him who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
The Blessed One said:
"O Arjuna, whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis? It is un-Aryan, not leading to heaven, and causing infamy."

At the outset, the Blessed One instructs Arjuna by relying solely on worldly convention, thinking that he will subsequently attain true knowledge; therefore, He says, "practiced by the ignoble" (2.2),
thereby censuring him for his unmanliness and other traits as being contrary to dharma.
He shows this through the words "This is merely an overestimation of righteousness," and so forth:
"Do not yield to unmanliness, O son of Kuntī; this does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (2.3)
Arjuna said: O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of worship?
"Indeed, by not slaying my high-souled gurus, it would be better for me to live on alms in this world;
but I would not, desiring wealth, slay my gurus and then enjoy pleasures stained with blood"—
by such statements as "Bhīṣma and Droṇa," and by the phrase "I would enjoy pleasures."
It indicates, as a point to be rejected in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), the pursuit of specific types of karma and the pursuit of specific types of fruits. || 5 ||
We do not know which is better for us: whether we should conquer them or they should conquer us.
Even by slaying whom we would not wish to live, those very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand arrayed before us. (2.6)
By the phrase "you do not know this," he refers to the pursuit of specific types of action;
for indeed, action without a motive is not possible, nor does one engage in battle intending defeat, since even victory in this case is nothing but a calamity.
Therefore it was said: "It is better even to live on alms than to slay our elders.
And this is impossible to determine: do we desire victory or defeat?
For even victory [is undesirable] because of the destruction of our kinsmen.
My nature overcome by the defect of miserliness, my mind bewildered regarding dharma, I ask you: tell me decisively what would be for my highest good;
I am your disciple, instruct me who have taken refuge in you. (2.7)
"I do not indeed see anyone who could dispel this grief of mine that withers the senses— not even by attaining unrivaled, prosperous sovereignty over the earth, or even lordship over the gods.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent.
O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of both armies.

By the phrase "in the midst of both armies," he indicates this: Arjuna, being overwhelmed by doubt, did not withdraw from battle out of partiality for one side alone; for this reason he said, "Instruct me, who have sought refuge in you. (2.10)
Therefore, standing between both knowledge and ignorance, the Blessed Lord instructs him;
the Blessed Lord said:
"Your inner self is afflicted by human frailty, and you have lost your composure due to being overwhelmed by despondency and delusion."
Seized by compassion, he gazed upon his kinsmen who had fallen into the very jaws of Death.
Humanity is the human state; what objection do you have that these have entered the mouth of Death themselves? 11.
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, and you speak as one lacking wisdom; the wise do not mourn for the dead or for the living. (2.12)

You grieve for the body, which is impossible to grieve for because it is eternally perishable, and you grieve for the Self, which is not worthy of grief. Neither one whose life-force has departed—the dead—nor one whose life-force has not departed—the living—is worthy of grief. For instance, the Self is indeed indestructible across various bodies.

There is nothing to be pitied in his migrating; nor is there anything to be pitied merely in the transition to another body, for if that were so, there would likewise be cause for pity even at the onset of youth and other such stages.
Thus he has stated two points:
"Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men; nor indeed shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter. (2.13)
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this. 2.14
For I did not indeed not exist, but rather I existed; so too did you and these kings.
(13) If there were cause for grief when there is a change in outward form, then why is one not grieved when attaining youth from childhood? He who is steadfast does not grieve, and steadfastness is—
It is easy for one who has no attachment even to this body; therefore, you should seek fortitude. (2-14)

But the undiscerning also grieve over those impermanent states— cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and so forth— which are produced by the contacts (*sparśa*) formed through the sense organs between the self and the objects denoted by the term "elements" (*mātrā*); they do not [grieve for the eternal].
To this he said:
"But, O son of Kuntī, the contacts of the senses with their objects, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata! (2.15)

Alternatively, those whose contact is through the "measures"—that is, the senses—and not directly with the Supreme Self: *āgama* means origination; *apāya* means destruction. Endure—that is, bear—the occurrence of these. 15.
For that steadfast man, O bull among men, whom these do not perturb, who is equal in pleasure and pain—he is fit for immortality. (2.16)
But surely, it may be argued, these various states are to be lamented precisely because they are subject to coming and going?
Not so. For instance, what is this so-called "coming" (āgama)? If you say it is "origination," then what is that?
To say it is "the acquisition of self-nature by the non-existent" is incorrect; for [if it were so], it would entail the nature of being non-existent.

Lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is selflessness (*nirātmatā*). And how can that which is selfless and lacks intrinsic nature be made to possess intrinsic nature? For it is impossible to turn what is not blue into blue, because it would entail the fault of becoming a different intrinsic nature. Thus, the treatise says:

"For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities does not depart, just as heat does not depart from fire. Thus, if origination (*utpatti*) is simply the acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*) by that which already exists, then since such a thing—having already acquired its self—can never be non-existent, it is eternal; what cause for lamentation is there in the scriptures? Likewise, disappearance (*apāya*) also applies to both the existent and the non-existent.

Or [if you say it is] non-existent, then it is simply non-existent. How can that which has the nature of existence possess the nature of non-existence? If you argue that it possesses the nature of non-existence in the second moment, then it would be so in the first moment as well;
thus, no entity whatsoever would exist because its own nature would never be abandoned. Now, if [you claim it is destroyed] by a hammer or the like—

Destruction is brought about. If it [destruction] were distinct from the entity, what would have happened to that entity? If you say, "It is simply not seen," then let the entity indeed not be seen; however, it has not become something else, as if it were covered by a cloth. But it has already been stated that destruction is not non-distinct [from the entity]. He states this very point in summary:
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being; the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality. (2.17)

And yet, according to worldly convention, he says this: there is no existence of the non-existent body—that is, that which is subject to constant destruction—because it is perpetually transformed through various states;
nor is there [non-existence] of the eternally existent Supreme Self.
Sometimes there is destruction because [the world] has the nature of non-transformation; and thus says the Veda:
"Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī, for it is of a nature that does not perish" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).
The foundation within these two—the existent and the non-existent—is that wherein both find their rest. 17
Anticipating the doubt as to whether that which is perceived by the seers of reality is indeed eternal or non-eternal, he says:
"But know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded. No one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable. (2.18)
The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of "ca" (and). And the self is indestructible. || 18 || The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of "ca" (and). And the self is indestructible. || 18 ||
These bodies of the eternal, imperishable, and immeasurable embodied self are said to have an end; therefore, fight, O Bhārata! (2.19)

At the time of its becoming indefinable, because that [state] would otherwise be impossible, the entity is subject to destruction; thus, it undergoes a different state at every moment. As it has been said: "Having observed its antiquity at the end, the loss of its newness at every moment is inferred."

Thus it is said: "The Sage has also declared that the differentiation of the various constituent parts occurs moment by moment in all entities; however, because of their extreme subtlety, they are not perceived."
Thus: "of those with distinct purposes" means, in other words, because they perform distinct purposeful actions.

Bodies are finite and perishable; the Self, however, is eternal, because it is immeasurable. It is the measurable, which is insentient, that is subject to transformation, but not that which is non-insentient and consists solely of consciousness.

Because it is impossible for there to be another intrinsic nature [to the body], bodies are thus eternally finite and cannot be mourned. The self is eternal and indestructible; therefore, it is not worthy of grief.
By means of a *tantra* (elliptical expression), the Sage has shown that the suffix *-tavya* (denoting obligation) applies to both meanings simultaneously.
"Those who are not to be grieved for," [so it is said]. || 19 ||
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. (2.20)
He who perceives this Self and the body as the slayer and the slain possesses ignorance;
for that very reason, he is bound. || 20 ||
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (2.21)

He clarifies this very point with the words "not having been...": this Self, having once come into being, will not cease to be; rather, having come into being, it simply continues to exist. Therefore, it is not born. Nor does it die, because having come into being, it will not cease to be, but will indeed continue to exist. (21)
How can that person, O Pārtha, who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable, be slain or how can he slay? (2.22)
He who, through awakening, knows this Self as "he neither kills nor is he killed"—how can there be bondage for him? || 22 ||
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out clothes, takes up others that are new,
so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones;
just as one who is clothed is not [considered naked] when his clothes are destroyed because he is covered by another appropriate garment.
In this way, the self perishes, enveloped by another body. || 23 ||
Weapons do not cut this, fire does not burn it; water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (2.24)
This Self is indeed uncuttable, unburnable, undissoluble, and likewise undryable; it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. (2.25)
This Self is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable; therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.

No cause of destruction, such as a weapon or the like, can affect this [consciousness], for it is of the singular nature of consciousness, unconditioned, independent, partless, and autonomous; [destruction] occurs through the manifestation of another nature, the destruction of the substratum, or the disjunction of parts— none of which apply here.

Because it is impossible to destroy [the self] through the sequence beginning with [birth]; nor is its transition to another body something unprecedented. Even while possessed of a body, it constantly goes to another body; the meaning is that it becomes connected with it, [this being] the nature of the body.
Because it does not remain stable for even a single moment; having understood the self to be of such a nature, you ought not to grieve.
Or even if you consider this one to be constantly born or constantly dying, even so, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for him. (2.27)

Moreover, even if you consider this body to be "constantly born" because its stream is never destroyed, there is still no cause for grief; or if it is "perpetually perishing" through its momentary process, even then what cause for grief is there? Thus, [it is the same] whether it concerns the self or the conjunctions and disjunctions of that body.
Whether you consider [the self] to be eternally born or eternally dead, in either case, lamentation is entirely improper for those who follow authoritative principles. (27)
Nor is this alternative—that there is both permanence and impermanence—logically tenable;
for it is certain that death awaits what is born, and birth awaits what has died.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve over this inevitable matter. (2.28)

Since birth is immediately followed by destruction, and destruction is immediately followed by birth, this cycle of birth and death proceeds like a wheel; what, then, is its limit that it should be lamented? || 28 ||
Moreover, O Bhārata, beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, and unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (2.29)

Whether things are eternal or non-eternal, that which causes grief regarding them is itself unmanifest at the beginning and unmanifest at the end; its manifest state in the middle is merely a modification (*vikāra*). Thus, one should grieve over the modification rather than the inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore:

Whatever that fundamental cause may be conceived to be, it alone is eternal, manifesting within its own self the various wonders of infinite creation, maintenance, and withdrawal in their respective order through its manifold nature.
Even if its nature were such, what cause for lamentation would there be? || 29 ||
Someone beholds such a one as a marvel; likewise, another speaks of him as a marvel;
and another hears of him as a marvel; yet even having heard, no one at all truly knows him.

Now, if this Self is indeed indestructible in this way, why is it not perceived by everyone as such? For it is like a marvel that only someone rare perceives it; even after hearing about it, no one truly knows or realizes it.
This embodied being in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible, O Bhārata; therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings.
Therefore, the self is eternally indestructible. || 31 ||
Moreover, considering your own duty as well, you ought not to waver; for there exists nothing better for a Kshatriya than a righteous war. (2.32)
And because one's own duty (*svadharma*) cannot be abandoned, trembling regarding battle is not appropriate.
O Pārtha, such a battle as this—arrived by chance and with the gates of heaven flung open—is obtained by Kṣatriyas through their meritorious deeds. (2.32–33)
The purport is that even other Kṣatriyas who are driven by desire should not abandon such a battle because it leads to heaven,
let alone one for whom such knowledge has been taught; however, it does not culminate merely in heaven.
Verse 33.
"That very thing from which you fear and would therefore withdraw from battle will fall upon you with a hundred branches," he said:
"Now, if you do not engage in this righteous battle... and so forth.
Having abandoned your own duty and your reputation, you will incur sin.
Moreover, people will speak of your undying infamy; and for one who has been honored, ill repute is worse than death. (2.35)
The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will now incur contempt.
Your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, reviling your prowess;
what indeed could be more painful than that? (2.37)
Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth;
therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle.
Having accepted these five verses as a form of debate, it is said: "Even if you abide by worldly convention, nevertheless this must necessarily be practiced. (38)
Having made pleasure and pain the same, as well as gain and loss, victory and defeat, then engage in battle; thus you shall not incur sin. (2.39)
But for you, performing actions through your own inherent nature alone, there shall never be any connection with sin.
This wisdom has been declared to you from the perspective of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, endowed with which you shall cast off the bondage of action. (2.40)
And this intellect (*buddhi*) of yours, characterized by certainty, has been described in the context of *sāṃkhya*—that is, right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Now listen to how this very same [intellect] is to be applied to *yoga*—that is, to skill in action (*karma-kausala*), so that by means of that intellect you shall abandon the binding nature of actions; for actions do not bind of their own accord.
Because of its insentience, it binds; therefore, the self itself binds itself by means of karmas consisting of latent impressions (vāsanās). || 40 ||
In this [path], there is no loss through transgression, nor is any obstacle found; even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear. (2.41)

In this state of mind, there is no destruction through transgression, offense, or negligence, because of the absence of negligence. And just as a cauldron of oil, though blazing with fire, is instantly cooled by even a small amount of sandalwood paste, so too by this [state of mind].
Even by a very slight application of the intellect to yoga, the great terror that is the nature of saṃsāra is destroyed.
(41) Nor is this intellect something brought forth from before;
rather, O descendant of Kuru, the intellect characterized by resolute determination is one alone, whereas those with many branches are indeed infinite.
The intellects of those lacking resolve [are thus]. || 2-42 ||
The intellect of everyone is essentially one and innate, consisting of the nature of determination; however, it attains multiplicity according to the objects to be determined. (42)
And so it is said:
"O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who delight in the mere recitation of the Vedas and who assert that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech. (2.43)
Those whose nature is desire, who look toward heaven, who long for the fruits of birth and action, are intent upon various specific rites directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power. (2.44)
For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [attachment], the resolute intellect is not established in meditative concentration. (2.45)

Those who desire sense-objects themselves speak these words consisting of the Vedas as "flowering"—that is, covered with the fruit of a future heaven. For this very reason, those of little intelligence desire only action as the fruit of birth; and they—

The purport of these three verses is as follows: those whose minds are carried away by the very words of the Veda imagined by themselves—though they may possess a resolute intellect—are not fit for *samādhi*, because their focus is fixed upon the results [of ritual action]. (2.45)
And for this very reason:

"The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna! Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, beyond acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self. (2.46)

The Vedas bind—that is, they fetter—by means of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as their instrument; however, they are not themselves the bond. Since Vedic rituals, when performed with a mind characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion, become causes of bondage, therefore the three qualities—which take the form of desire—must be abandoned. If...

If this [text] were intended primarily as a critique of the Vedas, then the present context of engaging in battle would have been inconsistent—since there is nothing other than the Veda that can determine one's own duty (*svadharma*). However, for those whose desire for fruits has dissolved, the Vedas are not binding. (46)

Since the Vedas are for the sake of their correct knowledge, he therefore says: "As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir when there is water overflowing everywhere, so much is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses discernment. (2.47)

For whomsoever there is a preeminence in the knowledge of their own specific duty (svadharma) alone, even that which is derived from a limited portion of what is spoken in the Vedas, [that is the path to be followed]. || 47 ||
Therefore, let your entitlement be to action alone, never to its fruits; do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. (2.48)
Be engaged in action alone, but not in the fruits of action. [Objection:

Is it not the case that when an action is performed, the fruit necessarily follows as an invariable consequence? [Reply: Not so. For in that regard, if you are permeated by the impurity of desire for the fruit, then the fruit of actions [accrues].
The cause [of bondage] is as follows: that fruit which is not sought after is knowledge.

Since that [fruit] does not belong to one who lacks desire for it, the attachment that arises through the absence of action is itself of the nature of intense grasping and is essentially false knowledge; therefore, it must indeed be abandoned. (2.48)
What then?
Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions having abandoned attachment;
becoming the same in success and failure—this equanimity is called yoga. (2.49)
Established in yoga, perform your actions; and yoga is equanimity. 49.
He whose every undertaking here is free from the bonds of desire, and for whom everything is offered as a sacrifice in renunciation—he is a true renouncer and he is wise. (2.50)
He whose every activity is not joined with the bond of aspiration—for desire is indeed a fetter. || 50 ||
For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya; seek refuge in wisdom. Miserable are those whose motive is the fruit of action.
Indeed, through the yoga of wisdom, as a result, inferior action—which yields wicked fruit and is empty—is cast far away.
Therefore, seek refuge—that is, pray—for such wisdom, so that it may be attained. 51.
One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds in this very world; therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in actions. (2.52)
The word "both" indicates their mutual variability. Therefore, the sense is that just as good and evil deeds perish, so too non-action alone is the supreme skill. || 52 ||
For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action, are liberated from the bond of birth and attain the state that is free from all suffering. (2.53)
Those endowed with the intellect of yoga, having renounced the fruit of actions, cast off the bond of birth and attain the reality of Brahman. || 53 ||
When your intellect has passed beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what remains to be heard and what has already been heard. 2.54
When your intellect, which has been perplexed by the various scriptural teachings, stands firm and unwavering in meditative concentration, then you shall attain yoga. (2.55)
And at that moment of attaining the intellect of yoga, this very higher knowledge (*abhijñāna*) becomes manifest:
that both types of scripture—that which has been heard and that which is desired to be heard—are characterized by a state of world-weariness (*nirveda*). By this—

And this has been said: "This is the power of the delusion produced by the impressions from hearing the scriptures that favor the knower who has fallen into the state of ignorance—that you perceive defects such as the destruction of the family in an inappropriate place; for that occurs when reverence for the teaching has thus dissolved."
"It will perish," [he said]. || 55 ||
Arjuna said:
What is the description, O Keśava, of one whose wisdom is steady and who is established in samādhi? How does the man of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move? (2.56)

By the statement "when the intellect shall stand firm," that word *sthita-prajña* (one of steady wisdom) which was declared as the designator for the yogi established in samādhi— what is its *bhāṣā*, what is its *pravṛtti-nimitta* (the ground for its application), by means of which [ground] it is expressed through words, considering that words denote an object?
One question is whether the term *sthitaprajña* denotes the yogin by convention (*rūḍhi*) or by its etymological meaning (*anvarthatā*). Although there is no doubt regarding its conventional usage,
nevertheless, even though its etymological meaning has been established, it must be defined through the determination of its essential characteristics and causes.

This question is raised in order to clarify the matter. Regarding the term *sthiradhīḥ* (one of steady intellect), which functions as both a word-meaning (*śabdapadārtha*) and a referential meaning (*arthapadārtha*), does the word *sthiradhīḥ* denote only the meaning characterized by its usage (*prayogalakṣaṇa*), or does it also denote the ascetic (*tapasvin*)? The second [alternative] is the case.
The question: What does that yogi of steady intellect do—what should he practice, where would his steadiness be established? This is the third [question]. And what would he attain by practicing?
This is the fourth. || 56 ||
This very set of four questions is resolved in sequence by the Blessed Lord. The Blessed Lord said:
"O Pārtha, when one abandons all desires of the mind and, by the self alone, rests in the Self..."

Then he is called one whose wisdom is established (sthitaprajña), being content. One whose wisdom (prajñā) is established (sthitā)—that is, firmly rooted (rūḍhā). And this rooting occurs because, while remaining eternally established in the nature of the Self, the delusion in the form of desire—which causes distraction toward sense objects—has ceased for that yogin.
The term *sthitaprajña* (one of steady wisdom) is etymologically significant, and since he is endowed with these qualities, the first question has been resolved. || 57 ||
One whose mind is unperturbed amidst sufferings, who is free from longing amidst pleasures, and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed—he is called a sage of steady intellect. (2.58)
He whose mental state regarding pleasure and pain is free from attachment and aversion is indeed a sage of steady wisdom, and no other. || 58 ||
And this is appropriate, because:
"He who is everywhere without attachment, and having encountered whatever is auspicious or inauspicious, neither rejoices nor feels aversion—his wisdom is firmly established. (2.59)
Upon the attainment of the auspicious or the inauspicious, he experiences neither joy nor distress. || 59 ||
And when he withdraws these senses from the objects of the senses in every way, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, then he is said to be one of steady wisdom. (2.60)

Nor does this term possess the nature of both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍhi*), like the word "cook" (*pācaka*). For whenever he withdraws his senses into himself alone, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs,
having warded off the objects from the sense-faculties, at those times he is one of steady wisdom.
Alternatively, from the objects of the senses onwards, he withdraws the senses into the self—he brings everything, including the objects and the senses, under the mastery of the self. (2.60)
But surely, why is the term "one of steady wisdom" (*sthiraprajña*) not applied even to an ascetic? It is said:
Objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food, except for their taste; yet even that taste turns away from him upon seeing the Supreme. (2.59)

Although he has no connection with external objects such as forms and the like that are brought forth by desire, nevertheless, those objects cease for him only after leaving behind the "taste" (rasa) characterized as a coloring (uparāga) residing within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Therefore, he is not one of steady wisdom. But as for the yogi—
Upon seeing the Supreme Lord, no further defilement occurs; however, for other ascetics, that [defilement] does not cease. || 61 ||
For even of that wise man, O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind. (2.62)
Because even the mind of that ascetic is carried away by the senses— or rather,
because it is so even for him despite his effort— it has been determined as the second [point] that the mind alone must be conquered by the yogi. || 62 ||
Restraining these [senses] with the mind, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me; for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. (2.63)

He alone who thus restrains the senses by means of the mind, and not by mere inactivity, is one of steady wisdom; and he should dwell with me alone—meaning he should practice toward me, the Supreme Lord, the conscious Self. 63.
In a person who dwells upon sense objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment, desire is born; and from desire, anger is produced. (2.64)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the destruction of intellect; and from the destruction of intellect, one perishes. (2.65)

For ascetics, the very renunciation of sense objects results in their grasping at those same objects; for they are abandoned only after being meditated upon, and it is precisely at the time of meditation that attachment and the like arise—thus, the renunciation of sense objects is no means for one of steady wisdom. 65.
But one who moves among sense objects with senses freed from passion and hatred, being self-controlled and having a disciplined mind, attains serenity. (2.66)
When there is serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him; for the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established. (2.67)

For one who is undisciplined, there is no wisdom; for the undisciplined, there is no meditative cultivation. For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness? (2.68)
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters. (2.69)
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established. (2.70)

But he who is the controller of the mind, even while experiencing sense objects, is not overwhelmed by the waves of anger and the like; this is the intended meaning—that such a person alone is the yogi of steady wisdom. || 70 ||
And by the Supreme Lord, who defines that even while performing all worldly transactions the yogi remains transcendent, the nature of this [yoga] is stated in brief:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake; that wherein..."
That which is night for the world is the day for the sage who perceives. || 2.71 ||

That illusion which is the night of delusion for all beings— in that [illusion], the sage remains awake, considering, "How may this be abandoned? And that state in which the world remains awake, performing various activities, is the night of the sage, because he [perceives it as such].

He is unawakened with respect to conventional usage. This is what is meant: this which is indeed *māyā* has the nature of deluding, as well as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the appearance of independence from bliss. In that regard, the world, without even reflecting upon its primary nature, [perceives] only in its second form.

The one established in mindfulness remains thus; the yogi, however, being the opposite of that, perceives its delusive nature in order to uproot it, and does not heed its state of being dependent on pleasure. Seeing correctly, the possessor of right knowledge disregards dependence on pleasure because of the destruction of false knowledge.

It is a marvel that this night passes even as he watches! It is also a marvel that the yogi applies his attention to that which is knowledge (*vidyā*), where everyone else is utterly deluded; yet he remains unawakened to that which is ignorance (*avidyā*), where ordinary people are fully awakened. (71)
Therefore,
just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains unmoved and established in its steadiness,
so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the seeker of desires.

The yogi does not run outward for the sake of desire, but rather by the very nature of his senses; objects entering him do not cause him to waver, just as the currents of a river do not disturb the ocean. Thus, the third [case] is determined. 72.
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing, without the sense of "mine," and without egoism, attains peace. (2.73)
That yogi, because of his renunciation of all desires, attains liberation in the form of peace. || 73 ||
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding in this even at the time of death, one attains the liberation of Brahman. (2.74)

This is that very being of Brahman, by abiding in which—even for a mere moment—and attaining stability therein, one reaches the supreme Brahman upon the dissolution of the body; thus the four questions have been resolved. May there be auspiciousness. || 74 ||
On this point, there is a summary verse:
"Oh, how wondrous is the course of the mind! For by means of renunciation, it indeed ascends to objects, yet while relying upon them, it must abandon them. (2)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītārtha-saṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
Now begins the third chapter:
"If you consider intelligence to be superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava? (3.1)
With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my intellect. Therefore, tell me with certainty that one thing by which I may attain the highest good. (3.2)

Action and knowledge have been mentioned. In that regard, it is not logical for both to be primary; rather, knowledge is primary. Since actions are to be destroyed by its power—according to the principle of "one endowed with wisdom abandons these"—what purpose would action serve at the root level?
The intention behind the question. || 2 ||

The Blessed Lord replied: "O sinless one, in this world, a twofold path of steadfastness was declared by Me in the past: the path of knowledge for the followers of Sāṅkhya, and the path of action for the practitioners of Yoga. (3.3)

In the world, this twofold path is well known: knowledge is primary for the Sāṃkhyas, and action for the Yogins. But by me, that [path] has been declared to be one alone, because the principle of consciousness consists of both knowledge and action; such is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
For it is thus:
"A person does not attain freedom from action by abstaining from the commencement of actions, nor does he achieve perfection merely through renunciation. (3.4)
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature. (3.5)
Knowledge is never devoid of action, and action endowed with skill is never devoid of knowledge; thus, knowledge and action are but a single reality. And so it has been said:
Knowledge is not devoid of action, nor is action devoid of knowledge;
the teacher, perfected in both knowledge and action, is the destroyer of the fetters of bound souls.
Thus, because action exists within knowledge, it is unavoidable; for, being dependent on others due to its nature as the movement of body, speech, and mind, one necessarily performs some action.
"He who sits restraining the organs of action, yet continues to dwell upon objects with the mind..."
One whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called a person of deluded conduct. (3.6)
If he does not act with the organs of action, he necessarily acts with the mind; indeed, such is the conduct of a fool, because mental actions are absolutely unavoidable. (6)
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind, engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached—he is preeminent. (3.7)
While actions are being performed, there is no loss of knowledge, because the action is carried out like a mechanical man when the mind is not engaged. || 7 ||
Therefore,
perform action with resolve, for action is indeed superior to inaction; even the maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction.
Perform obligatory duties prescribed by the scriptures, since even the mere maintenance of the body is dependent upon action. || 8 ||
For this world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice; therefore,
O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
Other actions than those performed for the sake of sacrifice—which must necessarily be done—are binding.
An obligatory duty, when performed without attachment to its fruit, does not yield fruit.
In the beginning, having created mankind together with sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures said: "By this..."
Procreate; may this [cow] be for you a granter of desired boons.

Prajāpati, the Supreme Self, created living beings together with their actions. And it has been said by him that the birth and continuity of beings arise from actions alone; these very actions will grant either worldly existence or liberation. From attachment comes worldly existence.
Liberation [arises] from being free from attachment. || 10 ||
It is said that those for whom liberation is the primary goal should indeed enjoy sense objects:
"By nourishing these gods with this [offering], may those gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you shall attain the supreme good. (3.11)

The *devas*—the deities presiding over the senses, whose nature is to sport (*krīḍanaśīla*), who exercise sovereignty over the instruments [of perception], and who are well-known from the secret scriptures (*rahasyaśāstra*)—satisfy them by means of this action; that is to say, let them consume their objects as far as possible. And being satisfied...
May they truly contemplate you— those whose liberation is appropriate solely to their own essential nature—

as being fit for abiding in their own self. Thus, within the continuous succession of the states of emergence and absorption, there occurs the gratification of the senses and their identification with that [Self].
When there is mutual cultivation of these characteristics, you will very quickly attain Brahman, which is characterized by the dissolution of mutual distinctions and is the supreme good. || 11 ||
"This path is not only for liberation, but even for the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhis)"; thus he says:
"For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will grant you your desired objects.
He who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief. (3.12)
For the senses, when satiated by sacrifice, become fixed upon whatever object of meditation or the like they encounter. Therefore, when their activity occurs,
the objects— the various states— of those sense-objects are indeed presented by the senses themselves through memory, volition, meditation, and so forth.

If these [means] are not given for their very enjoyment, then there would be the state of a thief—that is, theft—due to practicing deception. For it was stated previously by the Blessed One: "He is called one of deluded conduct. Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence: he who [attains] success—the means to happiness and liberation—...
Or, one who desires [pleasure] should enjoy objects as they happen to come, since their fruit is merely the cessation of curiosity regarding the senses. || 12 ||
The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are freed from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake alone, they truly eat sin.

Those who enjoy the objects of enjoyment—which have come to them by virtue of the majesty of the teaching that consists in what must necessarily be done—do so merely as an intermediate operation; and for this very reason, because they lack a separate fruit, [these objects] constitute auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Now...

Those who eat the *vighasa*— characterized by the bliss of abiding in the inner essence of the Self— which remains from the sacrifice characterized by the gratification of the hosts of deities consisting of the senses, they become established therein; for that [eating] serves as a means to be adopted.
Those who desire the enjoyment of sense objects are liberated from all taints, both auspicious and inauspicious.

But those who, under the influence of ignorance (*avidyā*), thinking "this is for our own sake," perform actions while regarding gross sense enjoyment itself as the supreme goal, act [only for themselves]. Ta...
In this very way, they obtain misfortune consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. || 13 ||
Beings arise from food; the production of food comes from rain; rain comes from sacrifice; and sacrifice originates from action. (3.14)
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (akṣara). Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice. (3.15)

From *anna*— which is by nature an object of enjoyment inseparable [from the subject] and which has various synonyms such as *māyā*, *avidyā*, and *kāla*— the diverse elements (*bhūta*) come into being. And that *anna* arises from *parjanya*, which is the Self whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness.
Because the state of being an object of enjoyment (bhogyatā) arises from the very nature of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), that enjoyer is the rain-cloud;

for the status of being an enjoyer depends upon the act of enjoyment, which in turn depends upon ritual action (yajña). And the act of enjoyment proceeds from karma, by virtue of the power of the autonomy of the power of action (kriyā-śakti-svātantrya). And that...
This autonomy, though uninterrupted,

[is so] by virtue of contact with the Supreme Self, Brahman, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is the surging fullness of unlimited and infinite autonomy; and that [autonomy] is a surging sovereignty that is neither veiled nor unveiled.
From the imperishable Brahman, which consists of pure consciousness and from which all waves of sovereignty have subsided—
thus well-established is this sacrifice, driving the six-spoked wheel toward liberation through the union of the three spokes.
Through the non-binding of the three spokes, it sets forth the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Thus, Brahman—beautiful with the waves of the manifestation of knowledge and ignorance—is established in sacrifice alone.
Others, however, [hold that] food is the cause of the elements through the sequence of semen and blood; and food...
Through rain, [it comes] from Parjanya; he too [comes] from sacrifice; sacrifice [comes] from ritual action;

and that [action] is preceded by knowledge; knowledge [comes] from the Imperishable. Others, however, [interpret it as]: "Food" refers to the five objects of the senses being consumed, depending upon which the elements and the sense organs [subsist].

And objects are of the nature of the Self’s own manifestation; therefore, it is the Self alone that is nourished by the enjoyment of objects. Consequently, the all-pervading Brahman is established in action, because it consists of that [action]. 15.
He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion, O Pārtha, lives in vain—he whose life is sinful and who delights in the objects of the senses. 3.16
But he who does not accept this is composed of evil; for he delights only in the senses, not in the Self.
For that person who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is contented in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed. (3.17)
For him there is no purpose whatsoever served by action here, nor any by inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object.

But for one who delights in the Self, while performing actions solely through the operation of the organs of action, there is equanimity regarding both doing and not doing; therefore, he does not exercise restraint or favor toward beings with any personal motive, but acts merely on the thought, "This is what ought to be done. (18)
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone; you should likewise perform action, having regard for the maintenance of the world.
Therefore, even for those who perform this [practice], Janaka and others are seen as examples of its successful accomplishment. || 19 ||
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. (3.20)
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me; nor is there anything unattained to be attained, yet I engage in action nonetheless.
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly at any time, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
These worlds would perish if I did not perform action; I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings. (3.23)
Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment; for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme. (3.24)
Just as the ignorant act with attachment to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world. 3.25

Even for one who has attained what was to be attained and whose mind is fully perfected, the purpose for engaging in action is the welfare of the world; in this regard, the Blessed Lord makes Himself the very example. Therefore, one should perform the duty to be done while remaining entirely unattached.

Furthermore, one who has known what is to be known— if he should abandon ritual action— then for the world it becomes truly difficult to break away from that very well-known position, characterized by a lack of firm rooting due to the loosening of the bonds of conviction. This is because people are unable to relinquish the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ritual action.
And they are unable to rely upon the stream of knowledge; moreover, they become slack. || 25 ||

Since they have not been purified by right knowledge, the distraction or agitation of their intellects would be their supreme misfortune; therefore, for the sake of favoring them, one should not disturb their minds. Thus he says:
"One should not create a disturbance of the intellect in those who are ignorant and attached to action; rather, one should encourage them."
Performing all actions with discipline, the wise man remains ever-yoked. || 3-26 ||
Understanding it thus for himself, he should perform his duties and should not unsettle the minds of the people. || 26 ||

It has been stated that this is ignorance; now it demonstrates that state of ignorance: "Actions performed in their various parts by the qualities of Prakṛti, one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer. (3.27)
Indeed, actions are performed by the qualities—such as *sattva* and the rest—which are related to *prakṛti*.
Yet the fool, determining falsely that "I am the doer," binds himself. (27)

But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the divisions of the qualities and their functions, does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities that operate among the qualities. (3.28)
But one who knows the truth regarding the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and actions liberates himself [from the thought]: "Prakṛti acts; what has come to me? || 28 ||
It was said, "of those attached to action"; he now demonstrates that state of attachment to action:

"Those who are deluded by the qualities of nature become attached to the qualities and their actions. One who knows the Whole should not unsettle those dull-witted people who do not know the Whole. (3.29)

Fools become attached to actions performed through the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which are related to *prakṛti*, due to the power of those very qualities like *sattva*. Therefore, it has been said that one should engage in actions while being disciplined (*yukta*). || 29 ||
In this regard, he clarifies how it is so:
"Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Self, become free from desire and free from the sense of 'mine,' and fight, devoid of feverish anxiety. (3.30)
Having renounced all actions with the thought, "I am not the doer," and having resolved that the independent Supreme Lord alone is the doer of everything and that you yourself are nothing at all,
perform the worldly conduct consisting of battle, desiring to show favor to the world. 30.
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and free from cavil, are liberated from all karmic bonds. (3.31)
And whatever anyone does while relying upon this view, that does not bind him.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—know them to be deluded in all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of discernment. (3.32)
But those who have no faith in this knowledge are ruined, because they are constantly permeated by the fear of birth, death, and so forth. || 32 ||
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature; all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish? (3.33)
Furthermore, even for the wise man, there is no error whatsoever in worldly activity such as eating and the like;

rather, he too acts only in accordance with what is appropriate for beings [composed of] the *guṇas*. Knowing this to be exactly so, because the dissolution of the elements—earth and the others—occurs within their own nature (*prakṛti*), and the Self is a non-agent (*akartṛ*).
If [the self] is eternally liberated, for whom is there the cessation of birth and so forth? || 33 ||
How, then, does bondage occur? It is explained as follows:
"Lust and hatred are established toward the objects of each respective sense-faculty; one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries. (3.34)
One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed; death in one's own duty is better than success in the duty of another. (3.35)
Furthermore, the transmigrating being (saṃsārī) grasps attachment and aversion toward each respective object;

because of his delusion, he falsely imagines that actions have himself as their agent. Thus, even though the knower and the transmigrating being perform identical activities such as eating and so forth, there exists this distinction between them.

This is our established conclusion: for one who has completely abandoned attachment and follows his own dharma, there is no bondage consisting of merit or demerit; for one's own dharma does not depart from the heart, being firmly rooted in its very essence, and by it, no one is ever rendered empty.
The notion that "a living being is born" must not be abandoned. || 35 ||
Arjuna said:
Now, by what impelled does this man commit sin, even against his will, as if constrained by force? (3.36)
The question is: "Even though a person knows evil to be evil, how does he engage in it?
The underlying intention in raising this question is: if one's own duty (*svadharma*) is not to be abandoned because it never departs from one's own heart, then how...
"In that case, there would be the practice of unrighteousness by them. To this it is said: "What is this so-called 'one's own duty' (svadharma) by which a living being is not destitute? || 36 ||

To this, the Blessed One spoke with the following intention: "Even though one's own true nature (svadharma) remains present within the heart, this delusion is caused by adventitious obscurations, and not caused by the absence of that [nature]."
This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas; it is a great devourer and a great sinner—know this to be the enemy here in this world.
By these two words, their absolute dissimilarity is indicated;
furthermore, since these two—desire and anger—exist in a state of constant connection through mutual inseparability, he explains them as having a single nature. And this [is] the greatness—
Anger alone bestows evil, for it is the cause of great sin and acts as a consumer that devours happiness;
therefore, a wise person should recognize this enemy. 37.
Now, with the intention that an object whose nature is known—and which causes harm to one's goals and so forth—might be easily abandoned, Arjuna said:
"How does this arise, O Kṛṣṇa, and how does it increase? What is its essence?"
Tell me, who am asking you, what is his conduct?

Regarding this [faith], the questions are: what is the cause of its arising, what is the reason for its growth, what is its essential nature, and once it has arisen and become firm, what does it practice—what does it do? || 38 ||
To this, the Blessed One replied:
"This subtle, supreme enemy of embodied beings, together with the senses, is dependent upon pleasure."
Seated as it were, O Pārtha, it remains deluding [the world]. || 3.39 ||

This [pleasure] is subtle—unperceivable by the senses at the moment of its arising. Existing in this manner, it arises as if to extend happiness; yet in reality, it consists of suffering and delusion because of its nature as *tamas*. For this very reason, it deludes. (39)
Consisting of desire and anger, terrible, arising from arrogance and joy, egoism is characterized by self-conceit; it is difficult to cross for those of evil deeds.

Arrogance (*stambha*) is the conceit regarding one's family and so forth; the joy produced by that is the thought, "I am such a person. For this very reason, it is called *ahaṃkāra* (egoism). || 40 ||
This [mind], repeatedly deluding him, turns away his joy, bestows sorrow upon him, and causes him fear. (3.41)
And for this very reason, pride increases from arrogance, and it arises in the form of a cognition of pleasure; thus, the three questions have been answered. || 41 ||
This very one, O Dhanañjaya, is turbid, base, seeking out flaws, driven by passion, deluded in nature, and a source of affliction for human beings. (3.42)
Thinking "this is he," he looks for vulnerabilities, [thinking]: "Through this vulnerability, I shall destroy his worlds in this life and the next. And so it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*:
Arjuna said—

Whatever one who is angry sacrifices, whatever he gives, whatever austerity he performs, or whatever oblation he offers—all that Vaivasvata seizes from him; the exertion of the angry man becomes fruitless.
Thus; the meaning is that he is one whose nature is tamas, though impelled by rajas. || 42 ||
As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so is this [Self] covered by that [unmanifest]. (3.43)
By means of these three similes, its inescapability, its incapacity for action, and its being an object of loathing have been stated. "This" refers to the self (ātman). 43.
Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise, O son of Kuntī— by desire in the form of fire, which is impossible to satiate.
It is called *kāmarūpa* because it moves according to its will; and it is like fire (*anala*), for it is impossible to fill it, as it burns away both the seen and the unseen. || 44 ||
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge. (3.45)

In the beginning, it abides in the sense organs. For example, when an enemy is seen with the eye, one generates anger within oneself precisely in the region of the sense organ. Thence it moves to the mind (*manas*)—in volition;
thence to the intellect (*buddhi*)—in determination. Producing delusion through this gateway, it destroys knowledge.
He states the means for its prevention: "Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses and abandon this evil which destroys knowledge and realization. (3.46)

Therefore, one should first restrain the senses; one should not first allow anger and the like to take hold of the senses. For knowledge—Brahman—and realization destroy the ritual action dedicated to the Lord. Since this is so, abandon sin, which is anger.

Alternatively, having performed the destruction—that is, the warding off—by means of *jñāna*, *manas*, *vijñāna*, and *buddhi* (this being an adverbial modifier of the action), one should not grasp what has arisen in the senses through conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*). The intended meaning is that one should not resolve upon what has been conceptualized. || 46 ||

On this point, he states the reasoning in two verses: "They say that the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses; the intellect is superior to the mind; and that which is even beyond the intellect is He. (3.47)
Thus, having understood that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by means of the self, slay the enemy,
O mighty-armed one, who takes the form of desire and is difficult to overcome.

Since the sense-faculties are distinct from their objects, which are characterized as enemies, and since the mind is distinct from them, it follows that there is a distinction from the intellect (*buddhi*) as well. That whose nature is distinct even from the intellect is the Self (*ātman*). Thus, how could [the Self] be affected by anger produced by the sense-faculties?
The meaning is that one should reflect: "Is this an agitation of the mind, of the intellect, or of the self?

However, the intention of those who know the secret is as follows: that supreme ego which exists beyond the intellect—the non-dual self consisting of the thought "I am everything"—is indeed the ultimate non-duality.
And for this very reason, because there is no fragmentation in that which is complete, anger and the like do not arise.
Therefore, having grasped the supreme ego—the essence of consciousness characterized by supreme enthusiasm—abandon anger, the enemy whose nature is ignorance. May there be auspiciousness! (48)
Regarding this, there is a summary verse:
For one who perceives wealth, wife, and body as something other [than the self], what indeed can the delusions of the mind, such as anger and the like, do? (3)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"In this way, I taught the imperishable Yoga to Vivasvat; Vivasvat declared it to Manu."
Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku. || 4-1 ||
Thus, the royal sages knew this [teaching] as received through tradition; but over a long period of time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga was lost here on earth.

And by stating that this [knowledge], though obtained through the lineage of teachers (*guruparamparā*), has been lost in the present day, the Blessed One demonstrates the rarity and the great value of this wisdom.
"This very same ancient yoga has been declared to you by Me today; for you are My devotee."
And "friend" (sakhā) is indeed this supreme secret. || 4-3 ||
"You are my devotee and my friend," [He says]. You are both My devotee and My supreme friend.

By the word "and" (ca), a secondary conjunction (*anvācaya*) is expressed. Thus, just as in the act of begging for alms, the alms are primary while the fetching of the cow is secondary, so too here is devotion primary toward the Guru.
The intended meaning is that even friendship is not the primary concern. || 3 ||
Arjuna, although knowing the true nature of the Blessed One, asks in order to make it manifest to the world:
Arjuna said:
"Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier; how may I understand this?"
"You spoke [this] at the beginning," thus [it is said]. || 4-4 ||
The Blessed Lord said: Many births of mine have passed away, as well as yours, O Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own power of illusion (māyā).
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata, and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest My own portion. 4.7.
The Blessed Lord, indeed,

because he possesses the sixfold perfections in their entirety, creates a portion of himself out of compassion for the sake of maintaining the world, even though he is devoid of any physical contact with a body.

The meaning is that he assumes a body which is "ātmaṃśam"—that is, a body where the Self possesses the six complete attributes (ṣāḍguṇya), while the "aṃśa" (the partial aspect) is subordinate by virtue of being a helper. || 7 ||
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evil-doers, and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age. (4.8)
He who thus knows in truth My divine birth and action, upon leaving the body, does not take rebirth; he comes to Me, O Arjuna. (4.9)

For this very reason, his birth is divine, since it was initiated by means of his own *māyā*—namely, the power of his own sovereignty consisting of yogic wisdom—and not by *karma*. Even his *karma* is divine, because it is incapable of yielding [ordinary] fruits. And he who knows this reality...
He who understands even his own self in this very way certainly knows the reality of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. || 9 ||
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in Me and taking refuge in Me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state of being. (4.10)
And likewise, knowing this very truth— because they consist of Me (manmaya) and because their desires are fulfilled— they are free from anger and other such passions;
performing actions that are fruitless [in terms of worldly results], many have attained My own nature, for:
In whatever way people approach me, in that same way do I reward them;
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.
p.
111) Whichever specific form of consciousness those who take refuge in me possess, I favor them by assuming that very same nature for their sake. In this very way, my path consists of me.

And all these follow me alone; indeed, there is no other path such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth, for that desire is mine alone. For it will be stated: "The fourfold caste system was created by me. But another says: the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*); as in the case of "one [takes] the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra sacrifice."
"They grasp" means "they might grasp. Likewise here too, [the words] "they follow" and "they would follow" are understood by way of ellipsis. || 11 ||
Desiring the success of their actions, people here worship the deities; for in the world of men, success born of action is quickly attained. (4.12)
Success, characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation, exists only in the human world and not elsewhere. || 12 ||
The fourfold caste system was created by me according to the divisions of qualities and actions;
know me to be its author, yet also its non-author, the immutable.
"Actions do not taint me, nor do I have any desire for their fruits. He who understands me thus is not bound by actions. (4.14)

"How indeed can there be any taint of karma for me, who am like space? My resemblance to space arises from the absence of desire. By means of this mode of knowledge, he who takes refuge in the Blessed One alone—who is a mass of bliss everywhere and at all times—[is not stained].
For one who reflects according to the principle that "there is nothing whatsoever superior to Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Lord," how could there be bondage through actions? || 14 ||
Knowing this, perform action alone—action which was performed even by the ancient seekers of liberation, performed by the ancients before them. (4.15)
Therefore, having been purified by this understanding, you too should perform those actions that must necessarily be done. || 15 ||
