Now, it may be argued that perfection is achieved simply through non-action. That is not so, because even the wise are deluded in this matter as to what is action and what is inaction. Therefore, I shall declare to you that action, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil. (4.16)
For one must understand action, and one must understand improper action; one must also understand inaction—for the way of action is profound. (4.17)

The distinction between action and non-action is difficult to discern. For instance, even within a prescribed rite there exists a wicked act— such as the slaughter of an animal in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice— and likewise,
even within a prohibited act there may be a virtuous one, as for example in the case of killing predatory animals.

There is an absence of affliction for living beings. Furthermore, even in the case of non-performance [of ritual acts], auspicious and inauspicious karma exists, because actions performed by speech and mind necessarily occur;
since these are difficult to avoid without knowledge, even those who are virtuous [must act].
Because of its profundity, action is not understood: "By this auspicious action, something auspicious will happen for us;
and by the non-commencement of this action, liberation will not occur.
Therefore, the fire of consciousness that is about to be described must necessarily [be applied].
The Blessed One’s intention is that [the Tathāgata], being capable of incinerating the fuel of all wholesome and unwholesome karma, should be sought out as a refuge. || 17 ||
To awaken him to this very point, He says:
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction—he among men is wise, and he is called a performer of all actions. (4.18)

Regarding "actions": he who, through tranquility, perceives non-action within his own actions because of his state as a non-doer; and who, by virtue of having fully manifested his true nature, recognizes his own agency even in actions performed by others—he alone among all is wise.

In the state described above, he performs action in its entirety—that is, completely. Therefore, when the question arises, "By which action shall the fruit be given to him?"—in the state of tranquility, however, he cuts away (kṛntati), meaning he severs, all actions entirely. Consequently, he either does everything or nothing at all.
"He acts"—this is the Upaniṣad. || 18 ||
Whose every undertaking is free from desire and purposeful intent—the wise call that man a sage whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. (4.19)

Therefore, actions performed while abandoning attachment to the fruits desired in the realm of sense-objects enter and are consumed by the fire of knowledge, whose nature has been described and will be further described. || 19 ||
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all. (4.20)
Even though he has set out—that is, even though he has proceeded directly toward [his goal]. || 20 ||
With his mind and self free from desire, having renounced all possessions, he who performs action solely for the sake of the body incurs no sin. (4.21)
Bodily action consists of the activity of the senses that is useful for the body, which is not colored by the mind and the intellect in such a manner. (21)
Content with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy—one who remains equanimous in success and failure is not bound, even while acting. (4.22)

This is a construction where the self is both the agent and the object of the action; the meaning is that the self binds itself by taking on the defilement of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the fruits [of actions]. Otherwise, the independence of insentient *karmas* in the act of binding would not be as readily intelligible. || 22 ||
For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who undertakes action for the sake of sacrifice, all action dissolves entirely. (4.23)
The term "yajñāya" uses the singular number to denote a class; "yajñāḥ" refers to sacrifices whose characteristics will be described hereafter.
It was said, "for the sake of sacrifice"; first, He describes its general nature:
"Offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the contemplation of Brahman as action, Brahman alone is to be reached. (4.24)
"Offering in Brahman" means that which has proceeded from Brahman and is again reabsorbed into that very same source. This entire universe, which is the self of all, is the oblation.
It is offered into Brahman, the supreme awakening, the tranquil fire. By means of "Brahman"—that is, by whatever action whatsoever.

That which is offered (*hutam*) is that which is presented for the increase of its own radiance; such an act of Brahman itself is the *samādhi* of that yogi. By him, Brahman alone is to be reached and known, and nothing else, because of the non-existence of anything else. Or rather, by means of that [offering].
The connection is established precisely by implication of the meaning: that which is indeed offered as the oblation of Brahman into the fire of Brahman by the sacrificer who is Brahman in essence—
that is, the offering made to the deity whose nature is Brahman, directed toward Brahman— is of such a character.
That which is the action of Brahman (*brahmakarma*) is itself *samādhi*, because it is the means for attaining the true nature of the Self;
by that *samādhi* of the action of Brahman, no other fruit is obtained, but rather Brahman alone—this has indeed been established in the verse: "In whatever way people take refuge in Me."
It has been stated that those who have made their own self into a sacrifice consisting of limited forms partake of such fruits;
but how is it for those who know the nature of the sacrifice consisting of the unlimited and perfectly full Self?
The intended meaning is that they should become partakers of a desire for only limited fruits. By this verse, as well as by the verses to be spoken hereafter, the supreme secret is set forth;
and that has been [explained] by us, even though our intellects are limited, according to our own understanding and according to the oral tradition of our gurus.

This has been explained. We are not to be censured for this, because without the traditional lineage of oral instruction (*mukhasaṃpradāyakrama*), this [text] does not enter the mind, just like a painting in the sky. Here, the oblation (*havis*), the fire (*agni*), the implements (*karaṇa*) such as the *sruk* ladle and so forth, and the ritual action (*kriyā*) function as qualifiers of Brahman.
What has been said by some should indeed be disregarded, because their secret lineage of transmission remains unimpaired. || 24 ||
Some yogis offer sacrifice to the divine alone; others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman. (4.25)

Others, relying upon the senses whose nature is playfulness, remain engaged in that sacrifice characterized by the grasping of their respective objects; investigating it thoroughly from its very root, they attain the realization of their own Self. Therefore, they—

Because the yogis are constantly engaged in yoga in all states, the possessive suffix here denotes a constant connection (*nityayoga*). And this very sacrifice, which consists of the grasping of objects,
they offer with sacrifice itself— that is, by that very characteristic— into the fire of Brahman, which cannot be filled by others.

Some have explained [the verse] as "they offer oblations. However, because the Sage’s words are free from internal contradiction, we shall clarify the meaning that resides in his heart: certain ones, being engaged in yoga...

The *daiva* [sacrifice] consists of performing a sacrifice consisting of external substances specifically for the sake of deities such as Indra in his various forms; and others, regarding that very sacrifice being performed as "this is what ought to be done," perform it without regard for results, [offering it] to those who are difficult to satisfy.
"Offering into the fire of Brahman"—thus even those who perform sacrifices with material substances go to the Supreme Brahman;
for it will be stated later that "all these are knowers of sacrifice. The Śruti also says: "By sacrifice the gods sacrificed to Sacrifice. (25)
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses. (4.26)
Others, however, offer the senses into the fires of self-restraint (*saṃyama*). Self-restraint is the mind;

its "fires" are the sparks that burn away desire, consisting of the cultivation of the states one has undertaken. Into these they cast the senses. For this very reason, they are performers of the sacrifice of austerity (*tapoyajña*).

Others offer sense-objects into the fires of the senses—which are kindled by knowledge and which burn away their fruits—desiring enjoyments solely for the sake of dispelling the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment; such is the Upaniṣad. And likewise, by me alone, in the *Laghvī*:
It is stated in the *Prakriyā*:
"Indeed, no object of enjoyment is perceived as distinct from you, the enjoyer; for this alone is enjoyment, namely the identity between the enjoyer and the enjoyed."
Thus, even in the Spanda [Kārikās], it is said:
"The enjoyer alone always and everywhere exists in the form of the object of enjoyment" (Spanda-nirṇaya,
verse 4).
Thus [ends the section]. || 26 ||
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge. (4.27)
Others perform sacrifices of material possessions, sacrifices of austerity, and likewise sacrifices of yoga;
and others, ascetics of firm vows, perform sacrifices of Vedic study and sacrifices of knowledge. (4.28)
And all those functions of the senses, whether mental, or consisting of the exit through the mouth and nose, the downward flow of urine and so forth, or pertaining to the vital air (vāyavīya),
[he restrains] properly within the fire of one-pointedness called yoga, which is the cause for the self's mastery over the mind.

They cause [the mind] to be established in that which is to be fulfilled and illuminated by knowledge. The intended meaning is that the Buddhas perceive an object—whether it be being grasped or being conceptualized—with one-pointedness alone, having abandoned all other activities. As it is said in the Śivopaniṣad:
"When the object [of meditation] is not abandoned, consciousness, though restrained, does not go to another object;
then, through that state of being absorbed in it, the supreme contemplation blossoms" (Viśvabhairava, verse 62).
Thus, the sacrifices of yoga have been explained. 27.
Thus, the sacrifice of material objects, the sacrifice of austerity, and the sacrifice of yoga have been described according to their characteristics.
Now, those who perform the sacrifice of self-study and the sacrifice of knowledge are characterized as follows:
"Others offer the out-breath into the in-breath, and likewise the in-breath into the out-breath."
Having restrained the movements of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they are solely devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Others, restricted in their food, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths; all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice.

Offering the rising *prāṇa*—the *nāda* beginning with the *praṇava* and ending at the abode of the *mātrās*—into the *apāna* as it sets, which consists of entering into one's own bliss, is the *svādhyāya* whose nature is the stabilization of the body (*piṇḍasthairya*). Furthermore, some [offerings] are for the sake of leading the disciple’s self to grasp what is right and what is wrong; [others] are for the sake of setting [it] to rest.
Because it bestows liberation by causing the departing [breath] to rest within the rising [breath] through their unification,

those whose minds are established in the sacrifice of self-study— which consists of purification, awakening, entry, and application within the Self and the disciple’s Self, and which is composed of the bliss of oneself and others— therefore, this is the *pūraka* (the filling).

The exhalation (*recaka*) occurs last, having been first released. By the first foot, the turning inward toward the enjoyment of objects is indicated; by the second, the departure for the sake of grasping objects through the sequence of the *mahāvidehadhāraṇā* is intimated.

And therefore, there are sacrifices of knowledge distinct from the sacrifices of Vedic study; these very ones have their desires for themselves and their disciples fulfilled by the force of constant practice regarding the aforementioned activities. Having restrained both of these paths—namely, food and the enjoyment of sense objects—they [attain the goal].

They offer the vital breaths—the arising of all mental fluctuations—into the vital breaths, which are the manifestations of supreme bliss; through the tranquility of *kumbhaka* (retention), they surrender them. All these, from the sacrifice of material objects up to the sacrifice of knowledge, are those who know the true essence of sacrifice.

By that very [path], those whose taints have been exhausted—having uprooted from their very foundations the great delusion consisting of the latent impressions of duality—eating the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice, go to the eternal Brahman. This... [is not].
O best of the Kurus, how could there be any other world for one who does not perform sacrifice? (4.31)

Even while consuming at will the nectar— which is brought forth by sacrifice, which remains as the residue after the satisfaction of one's own organs through sacrifice, which consists of resting in one's own Self, and whose nature is the bliss beyond all bliss— ...
They are united through the state of Brahman;

thus, this [discussion] is concluded, lest there be excessive loquacity in revealing that which is most secret and manifest. And herein, a vast amount of the essence of the secret, though dissolved within, remains.

For those whose constituent elements (dhātus) have been rendered uniform by the great ocean of the tradition obtained from the feet of the Guru— whose feet were propitiated through service with most intense devotion— it becomes an object of relish and the cause for tasting the true meaning. And herein lie other interpretations.

These have been demonstrated by the authors of commentaries, as well as those explained by our own venerable teacher; let the discerning examine them for themselves. Alas, what is the use of further diversion in critiquing the words of commentators? Therefore, we shall proceed with that which has already been commenced.
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices have been spread out at the mouth of Brahman; know them all to be born of action. Knowing this, you shall be liberated.

All these sacrifices are said to be at the mouth—the gateway—of Brahman in the sense of being its means; within them, there is the persistence of ritual action. Knowing this, you too shall attain liberation from bondage. || 32 ||
O scorcher of the foe, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
for all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge. (4.33)

In this regard, however, there is this distinction: a sacrifice illuminated by knowledge is superior to a sacrifice consisting solely of material substances. And its "sole-ness" is indicated by the suffix *-maya*. For all action culminates in knowledge. (33)
Learn that by means of humble prostration, inquiry, and service; the wise who have seen the truth will instruct you in that knowledge. 4.34
And know that knowledge through prostration, devotion, inquiry, reasoning, deliberation, reflection, and so forth, as well as through service and practice;
for these are indeed your own, O knower of truth, who has become such as this.
The specific sense organs, when assisted by specific forms of consciousness, will show—that is, bring one near to—the reality (*tattva*). For it is so that they show reality itself;
thus, they are called "seers of reality" (*tattvadarśinaḥ*). As it has been said:

"Yoga itself is the means for yoga; therein, wisdom is that which bears truth" (Yoga Sūtra 1.48). If it were explained as "other persons who possess knowledge," it would imply that what the Blessed One himself taught was untrue.

And the purpose of stating it thus is to establish a convention so that other people as well may receive knowledge from those who possess it through prostration and the like, and not in an arbitrary manner. || 34 ||
Knowing which, O Pāṇḍava, you will not again fall into such delusion;
by means of which you will see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in me. (4.35)
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is expressed as "in the Self," meaning when the Self has attained my own nature—that is, my essential form.

The word *atha* is used for the purpose of filling the meter. A certain distinction has been stated regarding the equality of the Self and the Lord; however, if there were inequality, the logical alternative (*vikalpa*) would be untenable. || 35 ||

In order to clarify what was stated as "all action without exception," the first verse says that even unrighteousness (*adharma*) perishes; the second verse indicates that "all" [action] means not even a trace of residual impression (*saṃskāraleśa*) remains; and by the word "entirely" (*akhila*), [the same point is further emphasized].
He explains [the passage] beginning with "api cet" and ending with "saṃśayātmanaḥ":
"Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone. (4.36)
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. (4.37)
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
The man of faith, devoted to it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge; having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay. (4.39)
The ignorant man, the faithless one, and the doubting soul perish; for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (4.40)

One should strive in such a way that the fire of knowledge becomes kindled by the bond of firmness born from repeated practice; for there is nothing as purifying as knowledge. It is not out of fear of over-extension that we say the purity of anything else is not real through its growth.
It unfolds; and he will personally come to know its purity upon attaining supreme awakening.

In this regard, faith arises—characterized by trust in the scriptures and total dedication to that [goal]—instantly, provided there is a state of being free from doubt due to one's conviction. Therefore, it is for one who is free from doubt...
One must not exist without the arrival of the Guru, because doubt leads to total ruin.
For one who is full of doubt knows nothing at all, due to a lack of faith. Therefore, the meaning of the statement is that one must remain free from doubt. || 40 ||
The subject matter expanded throughout the entire chapter is summarized in these two verses:
"O Dhananjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge, and who is established in the Self. (4.41)
It has been deliberated, and will further be deliberated, that the renunciation of actions is possible only through yoga and not otherwise. || 41 ||
Since this is so, therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart which has arisen from ignorance, take recourse to yoga; arise, O Bhārata! (4.42)
Having severed doubt, abide in yoga—the skillfulness of action—according to the stated sequence. Then arise and perform your own duty as a mere obligation; may there be auspiciousness. || 42 ||
Here is a summary verse:
Whatever action one performs preceded solely by the will of the senses, by that alone the deities of the instruments become satisfied and partake in auspiciousness. (4)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa! You praise the renunciation of actions, and yet again, you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is superior. || 5.1 ||
"Renunciation is primary, yet yoga is [also] primary"—this is the question of one who has a doubt. (1)
The Blessed Lord said:
Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good; however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action. (5.2)

In this context, neither renunciation nor action alone is prescribed; rather, both combined together bestow the supreme good. Since renunciation is not possible without yoga, this is the specific excellence of yoga. || 2 ||
He who neither hates nor desires should be known as a perpetual renunciant; for, O mighty-armed one, he who is free from the pairs of opposites is easily liberated from bondage. 5.3.
Therefore, he alone is a renunciant for all time who has renounced the desire and aversion of the mind,
since his intellect has emerged from the pairs of opposites— anger, delusion, and the rest; he is liberated happily.
Thus [it is]. || 3 ||
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as distinct;
one who is properly established in even one of them attains the fruit of both. (5.4)
The state which is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is reached by the practitioners of Yoga as well; he who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one truly sees. 5.5.

This is Sāṃkhya and this is Yoga—there is no difference between them. For these two are eternally connected; knowledge does not exist without Yoga, nor does Yoga exist without that [knowledge]. Therefore, there is oneness of these two. || 5 ||
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga; the sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman without delay. (5.6)

The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis and is to be construed out of its natural order. For one devoid of yoga, attaining renunciation is indeed difficult—because, according to the established rule, the renunciation of actions is hard to achieve; however, for yogis, this is easily accomplished, as was stated previously. || 6 ||
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses, whose self has become the self of all beings—even while acting, he is not tainted. 5.7
He who has become the Self of all beings—that is, whose Self is the Self [of all]—is not tainted even while performing everything, because he has ascended beyond the agency [of action]. || 7 ||
The one who knows reality, even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, breathing, or sleeping, should consider himself disciplined, thinking, "I am doing nothing at all. (5.8)
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, and even closing them—
he should maintain the awareness that it is merely the senses operating upon their respective objects.
He who performs actions by dedicating them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (5.10)

Therefore, even while performing acts such as seeing and so forth, he maintains this and resolves through the firmness of his practice: "If the activity of the sense organs, such as the eye, were directed toward their own respective objects..."

"What concern is it of mine? There is no taint for another due to what is done by someone else"—this indeed is the dedication of actions to Brahman. Herein, the sign of this is the absence of attachment. Therefore, the yogi is not tainted by body, mind, intellect, or even by the senses alone; thus do the yogis perform action.
Having abandoned attachment for the sake of self-purification. || 5-11 ||
And yogis perform actions with their body and other instruments that are solitary—meaning free from attachment and independent of one another—because of the absence of attachment. || 11 ||
The disciplined one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains peace that is final; the undisciplined one, impelled by desire and attached to the fruit, becomes bound. (5.12)
Final, from which there is no returning. || 12 ||
Having mentally renounced all actions, the embodied self, having attained mastery, dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done. (5.13)
Just as a man situated inside a house has no connection with the old age and other defects belonging to the house,
so too for me, who am situated within the house of the body adorned with the nine windows of the apertures such as the eyes, there is no connection with those [physical] attributes. 13.
The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is nature that acts. (5.14)

This Self does nothing whatsoever for anyone; its activity, however, is merely its own nature and not out of a desire for a fruit. For instance, this is the case with the Blessed One, whose nature is consciousness, whose ultimate essence is light, bliss, and absolute freedom.

For one whose continuous stream of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal is projected solely by their own nature (*svabhāva*), there is never, even in the slightest degree, any departure from that very nature. Thus, agency is nothing other than the state of being the agent. In the absence of that [state], what actions could there be?
If that [self] exists, to whom would the fruit belong, or what would be the connection between the action and its fruit? Here, "action" (*karman*) refers to activity (*kriyā*).

Furthermore, the fruit of action is simply the fruit of activity. For instance, the activity of turning the staff and the wheel is not one thing, nor is it something other than that. And that [activity]...

Because consciousness is contained within the jar that has been produced, the conscious, independent Supreme Lord alone shines forth in such and such ways; therefore, it is the established conclusion that there is no action, nor its fruit, and so forth, distinct from Him. || 14 ||

Therefore, having stated in one half-verse that in the absence of both action and its fruit, there is no "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) agency whatsoever even for the fruit of an injunction, he speaks in the other half-verse to establish that [point] from the perspective of those still subject to transmigratory existence:
The omnipresent Lord does not take on the sin or even the merit of anyone;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded. (5.15)
Evil deeds and the like were not committed by this [person]; rather, they were done through his own ignorance, like mistaking poison for nectar out of doubt. (15)
Therefore,
for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, just like the sun. (5.16)

But when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, the self-luminosity of knowledge is established by itself, just as that of the sun when darkness has vanished. For once doubt has been removed, the Immortal (Brahman) itself performs its immortal function. || 16 ||
To reveal the intention that this is possible for those whose intellects and minds are fixed on Him and who have abandoned all other activities, he says:
"With their intellects absorbed in That, with Their very selves being That, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal."
Those whose impurities have been washed away by knowledge go to the state from which there is no return. || 5.17 ||
Even while constantly remembering this, even while touching it in their own actions, and even while being attached to it, they do not become stuck, just like the rays of the sun upon the mud. (5.18)
Since it is thus that [the world] proceeds by its own nature, he says that such is the state of those whose ignorance has been destroyed:
"In a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, and even in a dog or an outcaste."
The wise are seers of equality. || 5-19 ||

And likewise, for those yogins, there is no such thought regarding a brahmin as, "By serving him and so forth, I shall become meritorious," and so on; nor [the thought] regarding a cow, such as, "It must be purified," and so on; nor the notion of wealth and the like regarding an elephant; nor [such thoughts] regarding a dog.

There is no certainty regarding [the object] being impure, harmful, and so forth; nor is there the notion that a dog-cooker (śvapāka) is sinful, impure, or the like. For this very reason, they "see all equally," but they do not act [upon those notions]. As it has been said:

"The nature of consciousness (*ciddharma*) exists in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere. Therefore, contemplating everything as consisting of that, one becomes a conqueror of existence. (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā 100).
Here too, by the word "contemplating" (*bhāvayan*), this very stream of knowledge is being described. (19)
Regarding this, he states how such a person should conduct themselves:
"Having obtained what is pleasant, he should not rejoice; having obtained what is unpleasant, he should not be agitated.
Steadfast in intellect and undeluded, the knower of Brahman remains established in Brahman. (5.20)
For this one who possesses equal vision, even the distinction between enemy and friend is merely a matter of conventional usage,
because he is inwardly established in Brahman.
One whose self is unattached to external objects of touch finds that happiness which is within the self; with his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable happiness. 5.21
He who has no attachment to external touch, which consists of sense objects. || 21 ||
For he thinks thus, as it is said:
"Those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering; they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them. (5.22)
For he meditates thus: "All enjoyments born of external objects are of the nature of causes of suffering, and even such things as these are impermanent. (22)
He who is able here, even before liberation from the body, to endure the impulse arising from desire and anger—he is disciplined; he is considered happy. (5.23)
And this is not difficult: if the impulse born of anger and desire is endured for even a moment until the end of the body's life, then there is the attainment of ultimate happiness. || 23 ||
He who finds happiness within, who rejoices within, and who likewise has light only within—he, O Pārtha, having become Brahman, attains the supreme Yoga. (5.24)

Therefore, within that very state, independent of anything external, he rejoices in bliss; and therein lies his manifestation. In worldly transaction, however, it is as if there were dullness. And it has been said: "One whose mind is fixed on non-duality should move about as if insentient" (Pañcārthabhāṣya 71). || 24 ||
The sages, whose taints are exhausted, who have severed all doubts, who are self-controlled, and who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvana.

And this is to be attained by those ascetics who are liberated from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained, and who have known the Self; for them, whose knots in the form of doubt regarding duality are destroyed, the extinction into Brahman exists on every side. (5.26)
For them, the absolute existence of Brahman is present in all respects and in all states; it does not depend upon the time of cessation. || 26 ||
Having withdrawn the external objects of touch and having fixed the eyes between the eyebrows,
one should make the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils.
Having cast aside external tactile objects— that is, having rejected them—
one [should remain] between the two eyebrows, which consist of the left and right gazes and are of the nature of wrath and passion, specifically in that particular place free from those two.
Having established all the sense organs, characterized by the eye [and the rest],

and having placed the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇa and apāna), as well as merit and demerit (dharma and adharma), in a state of equilibrium within the fluctuations of the mind; it does not act with crookedness— that is, with a lack of equilibrium under the influence of anger and so forth— therefore it is called "nāsā" (the nose).
This is the modification of the mind; this very same [process] occurs externally. || 27 ||
The sage whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, who is devoted to liberation, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is indeed always liberated. (5.28)
A yogi of this kind is indeed liberated, even while engaging in all worldly activities. || 28 ||
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the Friend of all beings, one attains peace. (5.29)

He is the enjoyer of the fruits of sacrifice because he has renounced those fruits; likewise regarding austerities. Knowing the reality of the Blessed One in this way, one is liberated even while remaining in whatever state one may be—may there be auspiciousness.
29. Here is a summary verse:
For one who perceives all beings here with equanimity, even conduct that appears inert is conducive solely to liberation. || 5 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and...
And the yogi is neither without fire nor without ritual action. || 6-1 ||
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogi who has not renounced purposeful intention.

Thus, the matter established by the preceding group of chapters is stated in two verses. "Duty" (*kāryam*) refers to that which is prescribed for one's own caste and so forth. "Renunciant" (*saṃnyāsī*) and "yogi" are synonyms; therefore, he says, "that which is called renunciation. Likewise:

Without the conjunction of *ca* (and), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is simply not possible; likewise, without the renunciation of mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), yoga is not tenable. Therefore, yoga and renunciation are constantly connected. By the words "not without the sacred fire" (*na niragniḥ*) and so forth, this meaning is implied: he is not one who is without the sacred fire.
And yet he is not inactive, even though he is a renunciant—this is a marvel! || 2 ||

Although it has been stated by reasoning that gambling, the royal throne, and sovereignty are [worldly attachments], and thus the state of renunciation (saṃnyāsitva) is established for one who is solitary and inactive, nevertheless, for the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for him alone once he has ascended to yoga—
Tranquility is said to be the cause. || 6-3 ||

For the sage—one possessed of knowledge—the "action" (karman) is that which brings about the attainment of the goal; "tranquility" (śama) is the non-cessation [of effort] upon reaching the stage [of realization]. Here, "cause" (kāraṇa) refers to the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa). || 3 ||
This very point is clarified:
"When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga. (6.4)
The objects of the senses are the sense-objects; and the activities for their sake are those such as the acquisition of sense-objects. || 4 ||
And regarding this state of being a Buddha, one must certainly apply oneself; thus he says:
One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. (6.5)
And here, there is no other means; rather, it is the self alone—that is to say, the mind alone—this is the meaning. || 5 ||
The self is the friend of that person by whom the self has been conquered by the self; but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would behave as an enemy toward the state of enmity.
For a conquered mind acts as a friend that delivers one from the most terrible cycle of existence; but an unconquered mind acts as an enemy by casting one into the fierce hells.

In that regard, this is the form of one who has conquered the mind: for one who has mastered the self and is tranquil, there is equanimity toward others and oneself, as well as toward cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise honor and dishonor. (6–7)
Tranquil means free from egoism. Having the cognition of non-difference regarding others and oneself, as well as toward cold, heat, and so forth, means the absence of attachment and aversion. || 7 ||

One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is unchanging and has conquered the senses, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal— he is called a yogi who is disciplined.
Knowledge is unerring cognition; where there is manifold knowledge, that is specific cognition (*vijñāna*), which is the action previously described through reasoning. (8)
One who possesses an even mind toward friends, allies, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen—and likewise toward the virtuous and the wicked—is preeminent. (6.9)

A friend (*suhṛd*) is one whose heart is naturally auspicious toward another without any external cause. Friendship (*mitratva*) is mutual; enmity (*aritva*) is reciprocal. A neutral person (*udāsīna*) is one devoid of both these qualities.
An intermediary (*madhyastha*) is one who is a friend in some respect and an enemy in another. [One who is] worthy of hatred (*dveṣārha*)...
One who is incapable of being hated is "the one to be hated" (dveṣya). A "kinsman" (bandhu) is one related by birth and so forth.
One whose mind is equal toward all these, as well as toward the virtuous and the sinful—he is distinguished in this way:
he crosses over the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra) step by step. || 9 ||
And with such words worthy of being chanted by those whose feet are to be revered:
"In this very world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity; for Brahman is indeed faultless and equal, therefore they are established in Brahman. (6.10)
Even while still connected to a body, in this very state, creation has been conquered because they abide in a state of equilibrium.
For the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is no longer a bondage for them; indeed, they are established in equilibrium, and that equilibrium is Brahman. 10.

Now, an objection may be raised: "It was stated that one must have 'conquered the self'; how, then, is that conquest achieved? Anticipating this doubt, some means for one who desires to ascend—such as equanimity of body and so forth—is taught as a method for the restraint of the mind.
The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline the self. (6.11)
One should yoke—that is, concentrate—the self and the mind; "constantly" means not for a limited time. This practice is appropriate when conditions such as solitude are present, and not otherwise.
(11) Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place, neither too high...
It should not be too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kuśa grass, in that order.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, one should sit upon a seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self. (6.13)
From steadiness in posture comes steadiness in time, and from that, steadiness of mind.
Mental activities consist of volitions and other sensory functions; by which [steadiness], these are restrained—that is, brought under control. || 13 ||
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, steady,
gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around at the quarters.
With a tranquil self, free from fear, established in the vow of celibacy, and having restrained the mind, one should sit disciplined, with the mind fixed on Me, intent on Me as the Supreme.
Holding [his gaze] with effort, he sat looking at the tip of his nose and not looking toward the directions; the meaning is that he remained endowed with devotion to Me as the Supreme. || 15 ||
Thus constantly yoking the self, my devotee with undivided mind attains the peace that culminates in liberation and abides in me. (6.16)
For one who thus disciplines and composes the self, peace arises; in which [peace] lies the yoga of attaining Me, the ultimate limit and final goal. || 16 ||
Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all; it is not for him who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, nor for him who is excessively wakeful, O Arjuna. (6.17)
For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, disciplined in actions, and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness,
yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.

Regarding "foods" (āhāreṣu), it refers to sense objects being brought forward. "Enjoyment" (vihāraḥ) is the engagement [with them] for the sake of experience. And its "propriety" (yuktatvam) consists in neither excessive attachment nor total avoidance. This applies everywhere. The remainder is clear.
"Of one who is awake," and so forth—this is because the Sage is an authority, just as the Veda is. The same applies elsewhere as well.
"When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be 'yoked' (yukta). (6.19)
And the sign of this yogi is that, with his mind fixed on the Self alone, he does not desire anything at all;
as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker—this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices yoga in the Self. (6.20)

Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker, so it is with the yogi; for him, "wavering" consists of the exertions involved in acquiring and maintaining sense objects and the like. (20)
Now, the essential nature of that Brahman, which is one's own true self, is defined through a multitude of qualifiers,
and its distinction from the forms imagined by other philosophical schools is established:
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest; and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction in the Self alone. (6.21)
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—he who knows that, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; || 6.22 ||
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. (6.23)
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as yoga. That yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency. (6.24)

Where the mind, being restrained, comes to rest by itself through the absolute absence of impurity caused by sense objects, there one experiences bliss. This is a gain superior to wealth, wife, sons, and the like; it is yoga attained through disciplined application, unlike any other.
The meaning is that this is the very nature of things: even when the cognition of pleasure ceases,

it is not "shaken"— that is, it is not shaken in a specific way— but rather its movement lasts for only the first moment due to mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), arising from the influence of compassion and so forth, and not out of delusion.
"Alas, I am ruined! What should I do? and so forth.
Since liberation is the separation from the conjunction with suffering, that [liberation] must be pursued by all means—that is, practiced—through *śraddhā* (faith) born of certainty and conviction.
One whose mind is undiscouraged in attaining the goal, or whose mind is firmly disillusioned with saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering. || 24 ||
He states that the means for the renunciation of desires is the renunciation of mental constructs (saṅkalpa):
"Having abandoned all desires without exception, which arise from mental constructs, and having fully restrained the entire collection of senses by the mind alone" (6.25).
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness; having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all. (6.26)
By the mind alone— not by the cessation of activity— having maintained fortitude and gradually attenuated the suffering of desire,
one should not think at all about the abandoning or grasping of sense objects.
As for what has been explained by others—that one should not think of anything at all—that is not pleasing to us, because it would entail the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). || 26 ||
Nor is it said that the mere cessation from sense objects is the goal to be attained; for:
"From whatever cause the mind wanders, restless and unsteady, from that very cause one should restrain it and lead it to peace within the Self alone. (6.27)
From whatever [object] the mind turns away, immediately upon that turning away, one should pacify it within the Self;
otherwise, the unestablished mind will once again take hold of sense objects alone. || 27 ||
For supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint. (6.28)
There, happiness—acting as the agent—approaches the yogin, who has become the object of action, as his mind is stilled within the self. || 28 ||
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi of restrained mind easily attains the ultimate union with Brahman. (6.29)
The essential meaning is that by this very sequence, yogis attain Brahman with ease, and not through arduous yoga or other such means. || 29 ||
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere.

One should meditate upon the Self as entering into all beings by way of being the subject (the grāhaka); and within the Self, one should unify all beings through the cognition of their being objects (the grāhya). From this, the state of equal vision arises, and that is Yoga.

This is the summary of the meaning. The detailed exposition, however, has already been determined by me in the *Devīstotravivaraṇa* within the section on the shattering of the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*) and so forth; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—of him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me. (6.31)

Destruction [of the Self] results from performing what ought not to be done. To explain: for one who does not perceive the all-pervading form of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self has fled—that is, because there is no manifestation of its own nature. And as for this multitude of objects...

That which is thus situated within the Supreme Self, whose nature is the manifestation of that [Self], he who does not perceive is lost from the true nature of the ultimate reality, because there is no manifestation [of it] apart from that. But for him who perceives me as omnipresent, I am not [lost].

"Lost" means not manifesting in its own true nature. And since he perceives those [objects] within Me, when his state as a perceiver—which is the manifestation of those objects—is fully perfected, he is not lost from the Supreme Self. || 31 ||
He who worships me as abiding in all beings, established in the state of oneness—even while acting in every way, that yogi dwells in me. (6.32)
But he who is thus permeated by this knowledge, necessarily perceiving the Blessed One as omnipresent in His oneness, is not tainted even while existing in all conditions. || 32 ||
O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere—whether it be pleasure or pain—that yogi is considered supreme. (6.33)
And he views the happiness and suffering of everyone as equal to his own;
this is merely a restatement of its essential nature, not a novel injunction. || 33 ||
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by you, I do not perceive its steady endurance because of the mind's restlessness. (6.34)
For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (6.35)
This very [Brahman] is thus indicated by the two terms "immediate" (*aparokṣa*) and "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*);

for although Brahman is clearly pointed out as directly perceived through the succession of means taught by the Blessed One immediately following [the initial instruction], it is nevertheless indicated in this manner.

Because of the fickleness and wickedness of the mind, it remains far away and thus appears as if beyond perception. It crushes both the seen and the unseen; it is powerful—meaning capable—and firm—meaning impossible to restrain from its evil activities. || 35 ||
To this, the Blessed One replied:
"Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain; but by practice, O son of Kuntī..."
And it is grasped by means of dispassion. || 6-36 ||

Through dispassion (*vairāgya*), the longing for sense objects is destroyed; through practice (*abhyāsa*), the side of liberation is gradually made the object of focus. Thus, both are mentioned. And it has been said there by the venerable author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*):
"The cessation of the fluctuations of the mind depends upon both. (Yoga Sūtra 1.12). || 36 ||
Yoga is difficult to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my conviction. But by one whose self is subdued and who strives by the proper means, it can be achieved. (6.37)

Therefore, this is the proposition: for one whose self is uncontrolled—that is, for one who lacks dispassion—there is no attainment of yoga by any means whatsoever. "By one whose self is controlled" means by one possessing dispassion; "by one striving" means by one with practice; "means" refers to those prescribed in various scriptures of established tenets and so forth.
Having resorted to [it]. || 37 ||
Arjuna said:
One who is unsteady, though endowed with faith, whose mind has wavered from yoga, and who desires to follow the path of the virtuous,
becomes bewildered on the way to Brahman.
Distraught by many thoughts and fallen under the very sway of delusion, having failed to attain perfection in yoga, what end does he go to, O Kṛṣṇa? (6.39)

If faith does not diminish even when the mind has wavered from its attainment through yoga, [one is secure]; for one whose faith is destroyed makes everything fruitless, even if they have achieved perfection in yoga. As it is said: "When, despite having attained realization, the mind is corrupted by delusion, at that very moment..."
"It perishes quickly like a heap of cotton from fire. || 39 ||
O mighty-armed one, does he not perish like a scattered cloud, deprived of both, falling into instability and meeting with destruction? (6.40)
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely; for indeed, no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt.

The question is: if the yoga has not been perfectly accomplished, does one perish because one has departed from the world yet is not properly merged into Brahman, or does one perish due to the lack of establishment in Brahman, resulting in the obstruction of the next world?
In this regard, the Blessed One gave this definitive conclusion:
"O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him; for one who performs auspicious deeds..."
Does anyone ever go to an evil rebirth? || 6-42 ||
For that one who has fallen from yoga, there is no destruction either in this world or in the next world— the sense being that his faith is not lost.
For him, who is thus indestructible in both worlds, there is indeed auspiciousness.

The Blessed One has established the characteristic of the path; and that [path] is not perishable like the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, for after having dwelt for countless years in the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds, one who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous. (6.43)
The years of Viṣṇu are the Vaiṣṇava years;
"of the pure" refers to those whose minds have been touched by a portion of the Blessed Lord. (43)
Or else, it arises in the family of wise yogis; for such a birth as this is indeed most difficult to obtain in the world. (6.44)

If, however, there must be a gradual progression toward its final liberation, then one is born into the very family of yogis. Thus he says: "For this is indeed more difficult to attain. Indeed, in the homes of the illustrious, obstacles are inevitably present regarding the attainment of perfection in the form of liberation. (44)
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his previous body; from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection.
For by that very same prior practice, one is carried forward even against one's will; even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Indeed, being entirely dependent and lacking self-mastery, he is led by that previous practice alone, as if by force, toward the practice of yoga. And this is not common;
for the transcendence of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma) occurs only through the mere desire to know yoga.
And it transcends—that is, does not accept—the Śabdabrahman consisting of the recitation of mantras and so forth.
But the yogi who strives with assiduity, purified of all taints and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal. (6.47)

Thereafter, following the desire to know, one who is diligent attains the state of Vāsudeva at the end of the body through the process of practice. It should not be thought that he achieves perfection with that very same body;
rather, it should be understood that he practiced this over many births. For this very reason:
It should be understood that he whose devotion to the activities of the Blessed One is characterized by the absence of any other activity is one who has fallen from yoga. || 47 ||
He states the preeminence of yoga:
"The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge;
and the yogi is superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi! (6.48)
His superiority over ascetics has already been indicated.

His superiority over those possessed of knowledge is due to the fact that knowledge is the fruit of yoga. His excellence over those who perform ritual actions is because he alone knows how to perform those very actions. 48.
Nor is it said that mere difficult yoga, devoid of a Lord, bestows perfection:
"Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith—he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. (6.47)

Among all yogis, he who, having placed Me within his heart, is devoted solely to devotion and faith, and who— having received the traditional lineage through service at the feet of the Guru— worships and contemplates none other than Me, is the most disciplined; he is one who is fully permeated by the Supreme Lord.
Thus, it has been stated that knowledge accompanied by the Lord possesses supreme primacy; may there be auspiciousness. || 49 ||
Here is a summary verse:
By the mere attainment of the Blessed One’s name, everything is obtained; just as when a proper rain is merely seen, the rice crops come to fruition. (6)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Maheśvara, the venerable Rājānaka Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Pārtha! With your mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, you shall undoubtedly [attain perfection].
Listen to how you shall know me in my entirety.
I shall declare to you in its entirety this knowledge along with its realization, knowing which nothing further remains to be known. (7.2)
Knowledge and discernment are indeed the activity of knowing; therefore, nothing remains over, because everything that is to be known culminates in the activity of knowing. || 2 ||
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (7.3)
"And no one is unfit for this subject"—by this, he states that because it is difficult to attain, it must be pursued with effort. || 3 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus is my nature divided eightfold. (7.4)
But know, O mighty-armed one, that there is another, higher nature of Mine, distinct from this, which is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained.

"This" refers to that state which, during the period of transmigratory existence, is perceived by everyone through direct perception. And although it is one and the same, it is divided into eight modes; thus, because it is originated from a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the universe is indeed one.

Even in the doctrine of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), non-duality has been demonstrated. That very [nature], having attained the state of the individual soul (*jīvatva*) and the state of the person (*puruṣatva*), is indeed my own supreme [power] and not that of anyone else. She possesses both forms and is variegated by the construction of the manifold world consisting of the object of knowledge and the knower. Precisely for that reason—

The innate nature (*prakṛti*) is that which consists of its own essential being, is eternal and unchanging, and reflects the entire sphere of all phenomena within the surface of the stainless mirror of its own self; this refers to the world, beginning with the earth. (5)
Understand that all beings have this as their source; I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.
"Reflect upon this—bring it close to yourself through the sequence of experience produced by repeated practice. And reflect thus:
'I am Vāsudeva, the source and the dissolution of all'—by means of this [realization] that 'I am'."

It has been demonstrated that there is no doctrine of duality in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, for the Lord, although non-different from primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), and the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), abides as the all-pervading presence in every way. || 6 ||
There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. (7.7)
In the Sūtra it is said that the collection of jewels alone [is the cause]: just as the thread, though its form is not perceived, exists as something internally latent, so do I exist everywhere.
I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the light in the moon and the sun; I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas; I am the sound in space; and I am the virility in men. (7–8)

"In the waters"—in all [elements]—that which is being tasted as a commonality (*sāmānya*) whose distinctions such as sweetness and so forth have not yet emerged, that am I. Likewise, "light" (*prakāśa*) is devoid of qualities such as softness or harshness.
"In the ether" (*khe*) means in space—that which is sound, the essence of every sound whatsoever.
Because it possesses the quality of space (*nabhoguṇatva*), there is here a restriction: that sound which exists solely as a quality of the ether,

devoid of other causal complexes such as conjunction and disjunction, which reaches the depths of the cave of Brahmā for those with attentive hearts, and which is to be experienced by hosts of yogis— this is what is called the "Unstruck" (*anāhata*).

The reality of that Blessed One conforms to the entirety of the collection of scriptures—that supreme human splendor by which the person attains the status of a universal sovereign, thinking "I am the Person. (8)
I am the pure fragrance on the earth, and I am the radiance in the fire; I am the life-force in all beings, and I am the austerity in ascetics. (7.9)

That quality of fragrance which exists in the earth by virtue of its exclusive nature is inherent merit (*svabhāvapuṇya*); however, [qualities] such as putridity and pungency arise from the connection with other elements. And it has been said:
"Due to the predominance of the qualities of the earth, there is solidity; due to the emergence of the qualities of fire, there is foul odor."
Inert due to the abundance of the quality of water... [text missing] ... ||
And so forth. || 9 ||
Know Me, O Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.
Of powers, I am the power of the powerful, devoid of desire and attachment; I am the desire for beings that is not contrary to dharma, O bull among the Bharatas. (7.11)

*Bīja* is the subtle primordial cause. *Bala* is the form of vigor capable of sustaining all things, free from the passion of desire (*kāmarāga*). *Kāma* is the will, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, and which does not exist as distinct entities such as pots, cloths, or other objective phenomena.

There is no contradiction; for desire, everywhere following as the power (*śakti*) of the Lord, is not contradicted by anything, though it is differentiated by adventitious attributes (*dharma*) such as jars and cloths.
Thus, by virtue of being its worshiper, the nature of the knower is that of pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvit*). And it has been said:
In the Śivopaniṣad it is said:
"When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should fix the mind [therein]" (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā, 18).
The meaning is that this occurs precisely when [the state] has arisen, and not when it is directed toward external objects. Such is the explanation.
Those who explain [the text] with the intention that one should pursue the three aims (trivarga) while abandoning mutual injury—
being ignorant of the traditional lineage yet explaining the secret of the Blessed One—
are indeed to be saluted. 11.
Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.

The qualities such as *sattva* and the rest consist of me, yet I do not consist of them; for this very reason, one who is absorbed in the Blessed Lord perceives everything through the state of the Blessed Lord. One does not, however, attain the reality of the Blessed Lord by being intent upon the cognition of various distinct objects.
This sequence is that which wins over the entire mind. With this very intention, it will be stated [in the scripture]:

"Vāsudeva is everything. By means of such knowledge, for those in whom the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*) has arisen immediately following the equilibrium of karma produced through the experiences of many lifetimes—

With his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) thus restrained, he realizes the reality of the Blessed One—that everything is Vāsudeva—and having awakened to this, he becomes a great soul; such a person is indeed rare. For this world, on the contrary, remains unawakened and is deluded by the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest.
One does not perceive at all the reality of Vāsudeva, which transcends the qualities (guṇas). || 13 ||
How indeed do beings, remaining as mere [objects of] the senses, not know the reality of the Blessed One?
To this he says:
"For this divine illusion of mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome. Those who [worship] me alone..."
Those who take refuge in Me transcend Māyā.
"Deva" means one who plays; thus, "daivī krīḍā" (divine play) means "this is my play.

By this, although the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are in reality not distinct from the Supreme Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, there is nevertheless the perception of them as being distinct from that.

That very state of being a quality (*guṇatva*)—namely, the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) consisting in dependence upon the principle of the enjoyer—is a form characterized by duality.

For transmigrating beings, because it cannot be defined [as real], it appears as *māyā* to them. Therefore, for those who possess the illumination of the ultimate Brahman, that [form] is not distinct from it.

"Beholding the universe"—that is, seeing through the nature of Māyā, which is characterized by the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, and whose essence is the manifestation of duality—they transcend it;
this is the intended meaning of the restrictive particle "eva" in the phrase "māmeva" (only me). But as for those who [behold] it as it truly is...
Those who know [reality] as merely the appearance of difference do not transcend māyā; therefore it was rightly said, "But I am not among them. || 14 ||
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me;
their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have resorted to a demonic nature. (7.15)

And those who do not respect me, even though I possess a body endowed with full authority—they are evildoers, the lowest of men, deluded, demonic, and characterized by darkness (tamas). Thus, this is merely the power of my illusory manifestation (māyā-mahima).
O bull among the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people always worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. (7.16)

Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is ever-disciplined, and whose devotion is single-minded, is preeminent; for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me. (7.17)
All these are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge is, in my view, My very Self; for, with a disciplined mind, he is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, realizing that "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled one is very rare. (7.19)

But those who worship me are the virtuous, and they are of four kinds. All of these are noble, for others are of miserable intellect; [others] seek only the removal of suffering or wealth and the like from beings whose hands, feet, bellies, and bodies are equal to their own, or even from those inferior to themselves.
They seek [the goal], yet they are of inferior capacity compared to the Knower (jñānin), because even in that much [of their practice],
there exists a distinction for them due to the clear manifestation of duality in the form of "I desire this from the Blessed One. The Knower, however, takes hold of Me alone as non-dual.

Therefore, I am indeed non-different from Him; and I alone am dear to Him, not the fruit [of action]. For this very reason, his heart has been purified by the firm conviction that "Vāsudeva alone is everything."
Those whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities,
adhering to their respective rules of discipline, constrained by their own innate natures.
"Whichever embodied being a devotee desires to worship with faith in whichever form, I make that very faith of his unwavering. (7.21)
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity]; and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by me as beneficial.
But for those of small intelligence, their fruit is finite; the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, but My devotees come to Me alone. (7.23)

Furthermore, those whose minds are limited by their own various natures of desire— such as for the highest state and so forth— and whose consciousness is carried away by such desires, worship only a particular deity who is an intermediate form of mine, appropriate to those very desires. Therefore, [they receive their fruits] from me alone.

They obtain the fruits of desire; however, those fruits have an end, because they are limited by one’s own very own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For this very reason, those who perform sacrifices and other rites with the intent of becoming Indra and so forth obtain only such a fruit as that. But those whose goal is the attainment of Me [obtain] Me alone.
Now, if the reality of the Blessed One is all-pervading, why is the fruit for those who worship other deities limited? It is said:
"The unintelligent think of me, the unmanifest, as having attained manifestation; [they do not know] the Supreme."
Not knowing my supreme and imperishable nature. || 7-24 ||

Indeed, due to their limited intelligence, they do not recognize my ultimate nature, which is devoid of manifest individuality; rather, [they perceive me] as having the nature of knowledge characterized by forms corresponding to their own desires.
They know it only as having attained manifestation, and not otherwise; for this very reason, there is no grasping at either name or form.
However, this is the established conclusion here: for one who, free from desire, takes recourse in any form of a deity whatsoever, that [deity] appears to him in a state of pure liberation.
It culminates there; conversely, from the opposite [case], the reverse follows. || 24 ||
I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my yoga-māyā; deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable. (7.25)
I know the beings that have passed away and those that are present, O Arjuna, as well as those that will be in the future;
but no one knows Me.
I do not fall within the range of perception of any of them. || 26 ||
Now, one might object: "Do not actions themselves, while being performed, bring about liberation at the time of dissolution?

Otherwise, why would the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) occur? Anticipating this doubt, [the Lord] begins: "O Bhārata, by the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and hatred, all beings fall into utter confusion."
they go forth at the time of creation, O scorcher of the foe.

First, by means of desire, aversion, anger, delusion, and so forth, that very essence of delusion is brought to a state of expansion; whereby the entire universe, existing within the belly of primordial nature (prakṛti), assumes a state of deep sleep, becoming incapable of performing its own functions.

Due to the experience of the latent impression of non-delusion every day at nightfall, as in deep sleep, there is not yet the state of being liberated; for when the experience of delusion ceases, the cycle of transmigratory existence with its various activities is seen once again. || 27 ||
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end, being freed from the delusion of dualities, worship Me with firm resolve. (7.28)
Those who strive for liberation from old age and death by taking refuge in Me, they know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action in its entirety. (7.29)
But those whose darkness has been destroyed, who have made their selves secure through the exhaustion of merit and demerit,

and who have rent asunder the canopy of great delusion— they know Brahman alone, which is inlaid with the rays of the Blessed One and flows from the deep gloom consisting of old age and death. || 29 ||
Those who know Me as being with the elemental beings and the divine powers, and also as being with the sacrifice—
even at the time of departure, they, with disciplined minds, know Me.

The internal, external, celestial, and sacrificial [afflictions] are indeed my own different forms. And at the time of departure, those whose inner faculties have been constantly permeated by the Blessed One know me— those for whom this has occurred even prior to birth.

May they remember the reality of the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, at the time of their end. For those who think, "What is the use of this worldly birth and its pursuits?", silence alone is for them the most auspicious state—may there be peace. || 30 ||
Here is a summary verse:
The *Kalpamañjarī* clearly presents devotion to the Blessed One;
by means of it, one may fulfill every hope according to the practitioner's desire. (7)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Maheśvara, Rājānaka Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Arjuna said:
What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action, O Supreme Person? And what is the elemental (adhibhūta)?
What is declared as the presiding deity (adhidaiva), and what is it called? || 8-1 ||
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana? And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint? (8.2)

He determines that which was proposed by the Blessed One in the passage beginning with "They know That as Brahman," by means of nine questions: "Who is the Adhiyajña here in this body? How does He abide? (2).
The Blessed Lord said: The supreme, imperishable Brahman is called the Self (adhyātma) by its very nature;
the creative emission that brings about the origin of beings is designated as action (karman). || 8.3 ||

Because of its vastness and its capacity to expand, it is the Supreme Brahman; for this very reason, it is denoted by the term *adhyātma*. This is because its essential nature (*bhāva*) is called consciousness (*caitanya*), whose attributes are never-ceasing. And of that which has consciousness as its own nature—
Due to the sovereignty characterized by the power of encompassing the universe— by virtue of Brahman’s external characteristic being undivided— and due to that freedom (svātantrya),
there arises the manifestation of external existence and the manifestation of other external entities.

That emission which, in due order, brings about the emergence of the elements— the subjects beginning with Brahmā— and of insentient objects, manifesting the manifold variety of both the insentient and the sentient;
and likewise [the emission] of the state of being, which is reality itself from which all false proliferation has fallen away.
It brings about arising. || 3 ||
The perishable state is the object of experience (adhibhūta), and the Puruṣa is the presiding deity (adhidaivata);
I alone am the sacrifice (adhiyajña) here in this body, O best among the embodied.

That which perishes—that is, flows away—by virtue of such qualities as transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth, is called the "perishable" (*kṣara*); this refers to the collection of objects such as jars and the like. The "Person" (*puruṣa*) is the Self (*ātman*), and he is the "presiding deity" (*adhidaivata*) because all deities are fully established within him. For this very reason, by virtue of being the enjoyer of all sacrifices, [he is the imperishable].

The Supreme Person who abides presiding over sacrifices and the duties that must necessarily be performed is indeed I myself; and it is I alone who abide within the body—thus, two questions have been resolved with a single effort. || 4 ||
Now, He resolves that remaining question—how You are to be known at the time of departure—with the words:
"And he who, at the time of death, departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone... He who departs...
He attains my own state; there is no doubt about this. || 8.5 ||
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes,
O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state.
Therefore, at all times remember Me and fight;
with your mind and intellect surrendered to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. (8.7)

Not only in the state of health, but even at the time of death, [one should think] "unto me alone"—meaning, one whose every limiting condition (*upādhi*) has been excluded. And how [can this be] in the state of illness, when all activity of the senses has ceased? The Blessed One [says]:
He teaches even the means by which [the Lord] may come within the path of one's memory: for him whose reality as the Blessed One does not depart from his heart even during all worldly conditions,
who has renounced all actions in the Blessed One alone, and who is constantly absorbed in the Blessed One— [for him, the Lord] will certainly [come within the range of his memory].

The reality of the Blessed One itself comes to be the object of memory; and here, the reason is that one’s inner being is constantly permeated by that state. For this very reason it is said: "Whatever object the internal organ has been constantly permeated by, that very thing is remembered at the time of death, and one becomes that very state."

The intended meaning here is that since [the goal] is attained [only through Me], one who desires Me must in every way be intent on Me alone; it does not mean that whatever is meditated upon at the end is the very reality that is reached. For if that were the case, then even for the knower (jñānin) [this would apply].

As long as the mental state is impaired by the defects of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) that persist throughout life, one would reach a state of insentience, following a path like that of the *tāmasa* (darkness). Nor is such an admission logical here, because it contradicts the authoritative scripture (*śruti*). For there exists [the following]:

"Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even one who has lost consciousness, upon casting off the body, is liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge and, with sorrow destroyed, attains absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). (Pañcadaśī, verse).
Therefore, these are injunction and restatement [respectively]. By whomsoever the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been constantly purified...

That very state is attained at the end, immediately after departing; and as for whether that [attainment] is remembered or not, there is no insistence on this point. Moreover, this is a secondary mention (*anvācaya*), as indicated by the word "also" (*api*). The word "or" (*vā*) clarifies the possibility that remembrance may not occur at all. And always—

The Sage himself reveals his intended meaning—that people should be devoted to Me alone in every way—when he says: "Therefore, at all times, remember Me. Thus, the syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: remembering whatever state of being [at the time of death], one abandons the body.

Or else, whether remembering it or not remembering it due to the failure of verbal expression, he goes to that very state because he has always been permeated by that being. Others, however, explain that "at the end" means at the moment of casting off the body, within the range of perception of kinsmen, sons, and others.

In the final moment of existence, characterized by such activities as labored breathing, exhaustion, hiccups, and stammering, when the firm bonds of the body have become attenuated and one is rendered barren of the pleasure, pain, and delusion produced by the body— at that point in time designated by the term "leaving the body"— whatever one remembers, that alone [is what follows].
