His form becomes endowed with the first consciousness; and at such a time, the cause of remembrance is "constant cultivation of that state. The word *tyajati* (he abandons) should be construed as being in the locative case (*saptamī*)—this is the same meaning as before. Now, in this way, what [happens] at the time of death?

What is the purpose served by remembering that [object]? Who says there is a purpose? Rather, it simply arises from the actual state of things at that final moment. But surely, at the final moment, there are [remembrances] of one's children, wife, kinsmen, wealth, or the drinking of cool water and so forth?

If it is argued that memory is the perception [of the object], would there not then be an attainment of its [the object's] state? Not so; for that final moment is not characterized by the clear persistence of the body. Indeed, this final moment intended by us is not perceived by those such as yourself. However, in that final moment—
In whatever form [an object] must exist, there is a continuity for its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), even if it is distant,
separated by birth, place, or time;
this is because memory and latent impressions possess a single, identical nature (Yogasūtra 4.9).

According to this principle, awakening must occur; by virtue of that, there is remembrance of it, and through that remembrance, the attainment of its state [of being]. However, for some, even during the healthy state of the body, that very [awakening] is manifested by the force of a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*), as described in the Purāṇas regarding deer and other animals.
But it is that [contemplation] which causes the state of being a deer. For this very reason, even in the passage beginning with "And also at the time of departure...
me," there is the inclusion of the word "also" (api ca). For those who always contemplate the Blessed One, thinking, "We shall become such as He is," for them—
According to the principle stated in *Yoga Sūtra* 1.50, "The impression (*saṃskāra*) born of that [state] obstructs other impressions," during that stainless state of dissolution (*antardaśā*),
all other impressions are cast aside; thus, through the recollection of those respective principles produced by that [specific] impression...
And because the moment of the body's existence is the cause for its recollection, immediately following that,
at the very moment the body falls away,
the latent impressions of time cease; consequently, there is no manifestation of the differentiation of objects of knowledge such as "this is that."
"It is the very nature of the Supreme Lord, whose true essence is pure consciousness alone"—this is the consensus of the venerable teachers, the Gurus Abhinavagupta; enough said.
"Without doubt" means that one should not entertain any hesitation on this point. || 7 ||
With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice and not wandering elsewhere, O Pārtha, one who meditates upon the supreme divine Person attains Him. 8.8.
"Reflecting upon it" means that, immediately after the dissolution of the body, having ceased all suffering caused by the physical form, he subsequently reflects upon the Blessed One. || 8 ||
He who remembers the ancient Seer, the Teacher, subtler than the atom,
the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who is radiant as the sun and beyond darkness—
at the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga— [he reaches that Supreme Person].
Having properly caused the vital breath to enter the space between the eyebrows, he attains that divine Supreme Person.
"One should recollect thus": the phrase "having the color of the sun" (*ādityavarṇa*) serves as the defining characteristic of the reality of Vāsudeva,
because he has transcended the darkness of delusion consisting of the errors of conceptualizing forms and so forth.
The intention is that it is the standard of comparison by virtue of being like the sun. "Between the eyebrows"—as before. || 10 ||

That imperishable syllable which those who know the Vedas declare, which the ascetics free from passion enter, and desiring which they practice the life of celibacy—that state I shall declare in brief. "Brief" (*saṃgraha*) means that by which something is correctly grasped or determined; it is the means (*upāya*). By that means—
I shall declare that state; herein, I will explain the means for its constant practice.
Having restrained all the gates of the senses and fixed the mind within the heart,
placing the vital breath in the head, he remained established in the practice of yoga-concentration.

The "doors" are the sense organs. By the word "in the heart," the absence of attachment to objects is expressed, and not the presiding over the physical seat of the excrement. "Holding the life-force of the self"—that is, the charioteer of the self—within the "self" at the crown of the head, which transcends all principles (tattvas), by means of the power of will.
The restriction of the body. || 12 ||
Uttering the single syllable "Om," which is Brahman, and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal. (8.13)
For that yogi who, with a mind focused on no other, remembers me constantly and perpetually, I am easily attained, O Pārtha, because he is ever-disciplined. (8.14)
"Reciting *om*" refers to the restraint of speech (*vāṅ-niyama*). "Remembering Me" refers to the mind's state of being directed toward nothing else.

"He who departs" means he goes day by day toward non-return. And likewise: "Leaving the body"—how [can there be] for me again this body, which is the locus of all calamities? *mā* [is used here as a prohibitive particle].

"He who remembers me constantly with undistracted mind—let it be so—he, knowing [this], attains my state. In this regard, O Sage, there is no emphasis on the departure [of the soul] that would contradict the introduction of the supreme Brahman and the state of non-duality; for it has been said thus:
In the all-pervading existence of Śiva, that which is called "departure" (utkrānti) is fruitless; in a non-pervasive Śiva, there is no departure that bestows Śiva-hood.
Thus, even for those who have not practiced constant repetition,
when such a state arises at the very last moment due to some cause— such as the independent will of the Lord— then this means characterized by the departure [of the vital breath] occurs.

It has been stated that [this] obstructs other formative impressions (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason, the formal proposition was made with the passage beginning "That which those who know the Veda speak of as the Imperishable" and ending with "I shall describe," [referring to] even a moment's meditation upon the Blessed One.
In order to demonstrate the marvelous state characterized by the total destruction of all mental formations (*saṃskāra*),
the most excellent masters have said:
"If you were to place [your] foot in the mind of one whose defects are exhausted for even a single moment, then..."

"O Śambhu, what will you not accomplish? (Stavacintāmaṇi, verse 114). For this very reason, in order to remove the doubt of those who fear that there might be a failure [of attainment] at the time of death if one lacks remembrance, it is stated elsewhere: "with a mind constantly fixed on no other."
The meaning is: for one whose mind is not fixed upon the fruits [of action] and so forth as the goal to be attained, I am easily accessible.

For such a person, there is no need to seek out the propriety of the time of departure—namely, service at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), taking refuge in a sanctuary (*āyatana*), the increase of the quality of goodness (*sattva*), or the state of being contemplative.

The meaning is that one must strive for such hardships as auspicious times beginning with the equinox (viṣuvat), the acquisition of a naturally pure ground, a body free from oil and impurities, and the wearing of clean garments and so forth.
As was stated previously: "Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste," and so forth. || 14 ||
Now, it has been stated that "he attains my own state. One might then ask: even after reaching that, is there a return once more?
Anticipating this doubt, He says:
"Having come unto Me, they do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering."
The great-souled ones have attained supreme perfection.

But from all other [paths], there is indeed a return once again; this will be demonstrated by the very next verse: "But having reached Me, the yogis do not incur the fear of birth and so forth again. (15)
All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return; but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth. (8.16)

It has been explained by all that even for those who have attained the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), there is a return once again; and if this were accepted, it would follow that liberation is merely reaching the worlds situated above that,
which is not a satisfying conclusion.
To us, whose inner state is turbid with the great delusion of doubt,
this lamp of exposition attained through the scriptures appears thus, reaching as far as the station of Brahmā until the attainment of the state of Brahman.
Because they return again from whatever world— whether horizontal, upward, or downward— revolving like a wheel, moving incessantly from one place to another. || 16 ||
But surely, who knows this—that there is a return from all the worlds?

For even Brahmā and the others are heard of as remaining for a very long time; how then could they themselves be subject to return? Indeed, if there were such a return, they too would be [subject to it].
"Those whose nature is to originate and dissolve? To this he says:
"Those people who know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas and that his night ends after a thousand yugas—they are the ones who truly know day and night. (8.17)
At the arrival of day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest; at the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very same state known as the unmanifest. (8.18)
This very same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth at the arrival of day. (8.19)

Indeed, those who are far-sighted perceive even the day and night of Brahmā in terms of dissolution and emergence. And so it is: waking up every single day, they pursue their respective activities; and every night, it is for them alone [that these cease].

Those whose activity has ceased remain as mere potentiality. Thus, there is a repeated occurrence of creation and dissolution. It is not that different [beings] are produced again and again, but rather those same individual souls (jīvas); however, there is a distinction consisting of the notions of "long" and "short" duration caused by time. And this...
Even the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) possess such limitation; therefore, it is established that they too are subject to the nature of origination and dissolution. || 19 ||
He clarifies that there is no returning again from all the worlds, but rather upon reaching Me:
"But beyond that, there is another being, distinct [from it], unmanifest, eternal;
which does not perish even when all beings perish. (8.20)
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they say he is the supreme goal, reaching which they do not return—that is my supreme abode.
That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone;
having attained Him, O Arjuna, yogis are not subject to rebirth. (8.22)
That within which all beings reside, wherein everything is established—
that reality of Vāsudeva described in the aforementioned manner, which is indeed devoid of the calculation of time—
is manifest as it pervades all, yet unmanifest even within that reality because it is difficult to attain. And that—
It was previously stated that [the Absolute] is attainable through devotion (*bhakti*). And this entire universe resides therein.

Now, regarding that which is indeed an imperishable form, eternally existing as such—what, then, is the meaning of the word *punaḥ* (again) and the word *āvṛtti* (repetition)? For that [Absolute] is in the middle.

This depends upon the exclusion of that [limited] nature. However, for the venerable Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is supreme consciousness and sovereignty— consisting of being eternally transcendent of the universe, yet non-different from the universe and established within it— there can be no attainment of such a state [of limitation], by which...
There is no severance of one's own nature at any time or in any way; therefore, it is rightly said: "But having come unto Me... (22).

Thus, having described the conduct of those who attain the Blessed One without the destruction of their afflictions through constant practice, now some specific detail is stated regarding those who, by means of the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*), desire either liberation (*apavarga*) or enjoyment (*bhoga*).
I shall now describe that time, O bull of the Bharatas, departing at which yogis go either to non-return or to return.
Non-return is liberation; return is for the sake of experience. 23.
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—departing then, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman. (8.24)
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight and the six months of the sun's southern course—attaining the lunar light there, the yogi returns. (8.25)
The northern course is the upward movement lasting for six months;
because it possesses qualities such as luminosity, it is figuratively designated by terms such as "burning" (*dahana*).
The opposite of that is the reverse. In that regard, [the course] of the moon—
The recurrence for the sake of experience occurs due to the entry of the portions to be experienced. || 25 ||
These two paths, white and black, are indeed considered eternal for the world;
by the one [the white path], one goes to non-return, while by the other, one returns.
Between these two paths, by the first there is non-return—liberation; by the other, experience.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded. Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna. (8.27)
He who knows these two paths by the internal sequence—
that is, by means of the practice of yoga— this being explained in detail would merely expand the scope of this treatise, so enough. All these internal times...

One should practice yoga having that as its object. Our teachers, however, say: because it is beneficial to all, after describing in the middle [of the work] the various types of departure (*utkrānti*) determined by internal time, the primary subject matter concerning external time—the very topic at hand—has been concluded. Therefore, in all [cases]...
By the words "at the [proper] times," and so forth. || 27 ||
Whatever fruit of merit is prescribed for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—all that he attains by knowing this; and the yogi reaches the supreme, primordial state.

It overcomes—that is, it surpasses—because all karmic formations are rendered fruitless through mindfulness of the Blessed One. And upon the complete exhaustion of all karma, he easily attains supreme auspiciousness; may there be auspiciousness! 28.
Here is a summary verse:
When the Supreme Lord is known as pervading all principles of reality, there is no state, whether internal or external, in which the All-pervasive One does not shine.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Maheśvara, the venerable Rājānaka Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall declare to you, who are free from malice, this most secret knowledge.
Having known that which is accompanied by consciousness, you shall be liberated from the unwholesome.
Freedom from envy is the primary cause for the transmission of knowledge;
as before, this applies to both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*). (1)
This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, this supreme purifier; it is directly perceivable, in accordance with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable. 9.2.

It "shines" (rājate), meaning it blazes forth in the midst of all branches of knowledge; for it is said right here that "the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā) is the foremost among sciences. It is the secret of kings such as Janaka and others, because it is extremely well-guarded and because it remains unshakable through the heroic spirit natural to Kṣatriyas.

It is very easy to perform and carry out; moreover, unlike other types of action, this practice consisting of the meditation on Brahman does not undergo depletion through such things as the experience of its fruits. || 2 ||
O scorcher of foes, those persons who have no faith in this dharma do not reach Me, but return to the path of the mortal cycle of rebirth.
They turn back; they are born again and again, and they die. || 3 ||
By me, whose form is unmanifest, this entire world is pervaded; all beings dwell in me, yet I do not abide in them. (9.4)
"All beings abide in Me"— even after traveling for a very long time, because no other locus of establishment exists;
this is preceded by the well-known inert form of His, which consists of the nature of the elements and the nature of the object of cognition.
In its manifestation, there occurs the concealment of the nature of cognition that is contrary to it. This is what he expresses by saying: "And I am not situated within them. (4)
And yet, beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga! My Self, the source of all beings, sustains beings but does not dwell within them. 9.5.

And they do not abide in Me, because those blinded by ignorance do not perceive reality. For the deluded do not conceive of the Supreme Lord—the abode that establishes the delimitation of all things—as having the nature of uninterrupted consciousness; rather, [they think of Him as] "emaciated," etc.

"Devadatta, I know this; this stands upon the earth"—thus they perceive only a limited nature as their own basis and place of support. But how is this not contradictory? To this he says: "Behold my divine yoga."

Yoga is power (śakti), because it is that which is being joined. This alone is my sovereignty—the meaning is that it is this very independence characterized by such unsurpassed and wondrous activity. || 5 ||
Just as the great wind, omnipresent and eternal, remains ever situated in space, even so, understand that all beings abide in Me. 9.6.
Thus indeed do I move among all beings unobserved, abiding in the true nature of reality, both together with them and yet apart from them. (9.7)

Just as, although there is an inseparable relationship between space and air, the touchability of the sky is never perceived, so too the reality of the Blessed One, though pervading the entire cycle of existence, is not an object for all people. || 7 ||
All beings, O son of Kuntī, go to my own nature at the end of a kalpa;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth.
Nature, whose form is unmanifest. || 8 ||
Holding fast to my own nature, I project forth this entire multitude of beings again and again, which is powerless under the sway of nature.

By the phrase "having taken hold of its own nature," it is shown that even this collection of insentient entities, though inert by itself, attains luminosity through its connection with the Supreme Nature. || 9 ||
And those actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya,
for I remain as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
Under my supervision, nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving; by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves.
And I have no bondage of karma, because I abide in equanimity;
for this very reason, I am the cause in the creation of the world, since I do not depend upon any activity. || 11 ||
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
being ignorant of my supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed nature.

Thus, I am one who dwells within all people, yet I am an object of contempt because I appear both as the self and as the other; for since no Lord distinct from the fourteenfold creation beginning with humans is perceived, how can He exist? || 12 ||
Futile their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and devoid of discernment, they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and fiendish.

And their actions, knowledge, and desires are all fruitless, because they have unreal things as their objects. "Demoniacal and rakshasa-like" refers to those whose qualities of passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas) are predominant. || 13 ||
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in my divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. 9.14
Constantly glorifying me, striving with restrained vows, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (9.15)
Others also, sacrificing by the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as one, as distinct,
and manifoldly as the one whose face is everywhere.
"Divine" means characterized by *sattva*. "Worshiping" means through sacrifices with external substances and so forth.

But others worship Me solely through the sacrifice of knowledge. Thus, some do so as one through knowledge, while others do so in many ways through the yoga of action; yet all are devoted to Me alone. 16.

Now, an objection may be raised: since action (karman) is characterized by an intensification of distinctions pervaded by a multitude of causal factors (kāraka), how can it lead to the attainment of the undivided state of the Blessed One? It is replied:
"I am the sacrifice (kratu), I am the oblation (yajña), I am the ancestral offering (svadhā), and I am the medicinal herb (auṣadha)."
I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather; I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and likewise the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas.

He is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend; He is the source of origin, the dissolution, the foundation, the treasure-house, and the imperishable seed.
I heat; I withhold the rain and I send it forth. I am both immortality and death, as well as existence and non-existence, O Arjuna. (9.20)
Furthermore, it establishes the oneness of action— which depends upon the imagined means— of the single, partless reality of Brahman; namely,
that through the action’s abiding in the direct realization of the self as all the factors of action (*kāraka*), there is the attainment of the state of the Blessed One.
Because it is not far removed [from the Self]. And it has been said:

"This power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing in bound souls (paśu), is the binder when it remains on its own path; when known, it brings about accomplishment. (Svacchandatantra, Part 3, Chapter on Powers, Verse 16)
Thus it was said; and I too have stated:
"Whatever cognition follows after existence and non-existence at the time of commencement, that same [cognition] follows after existence and non-existence at the time of conclusion."

Thus, this has been examined at length in various places; therefore, we shall desist here. This was stated in the context of the discourse on non-duality beginning with "I am that" (tat tvam asi) and so forth. || 20 ||

Now, if Brahman is attained even through external sacrifices and the like, then in the case of the *agniṣṭoma* and other such rites, who else would there be to be worshipped? If you accept this, it results in dualism (*bhedavāda*).
If you say that Vāsudeva alone is the one to be worshipped, then why is liberation (*apavarga*) not attained through those [external rites]? To address this, it is said:

Those who possess the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven; they, having reached the holy world of the Lord of the Gods, enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven. (9.21)
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and desiring objects of desire, they obtain the state of coming and going. (9.22)

Although they worship me alone, nevertheless, because their actions are limited by their prayers for heaven alone and because of the weakness of their own nature, they restrict themselves to results such as heaven alone. For this very reason, their dharma leads to rebirth. Thus they...

They attain the state of going and returning, but the nature of sacrifice does not possess the quality of producing rebirth. For it is said: "Those people who worship Me, thinking of no other... [For them... 22.
For those who are constantly devoted [to Me], I provide for their acquisition and preservation.
How do others, different from them, meditate upon Me? They are "ananya," meaning those for whom there exists nothing else—no other desirable fruit apart from Me.
Yoga is the attainment of My own nature which has not yet been attained.

The attainment and preservation of the state established in the nature of the Blessed One, which has been reached as security—meaning, that by which even the suspicion of falling away from yoga shall not arise. || 23 ||
Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.
For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize me in truth, and therefore they fall.

Those who are devoted to the gods go to the gods; those who are devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to Me also come to Me. (9.26)
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept. (9.27)

And even those who worship under other names, they too worship Me alone; for there is nothing whatsoever to be worshipped that is distinct from Brahman. However, the distinction is that it is "not according to rule. "Not according to rule" means a different rule—that is, by various kinds of rules, it is I alone [who am worshipped].

The one to be sacrificed to (*yājya*) is the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is pure existence; it is not, however, as others—stained by the great sins acquired through the refutation of other systems of philosophy—perform sacrifice with a distracted mind, according to improper rites, or by means of corrupt rituals. For if it were so, they would be sacrificing to me alone.

Furthermore, the observation that "I alone am the enjoyer of all sacrifices" would become inconsistent [if this were not the case]. Enough, then, with this conversation accompanied by the turbid mire of defilements. Our teachers, however, explain: "Other" means distinct from one's own self.

According to the perspective of the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda), they grasp that there is some deity who is devoid of the very nature of Brahman, and they worship that [deity] alone. Even they, in reality, worship Me alone—whose form is their own Self—but by an improper method, namely, through a defective procedure characterized by the grasping of duality. Therefore, He says: "But not..."

They know me—their own self—in its true essence as the form of the deity and as the enjoyer; therefore, they "move away" from my nature. What is meant by "by being devoted to the gods they go to the gods," and so forth?
This very thing is what constitutes such movement. However, those who know my true nature as non-different [from themselves]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

"Even by means of sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and so forth, they worship Me alone. And he will conclude that "those who sacrifice to Me go to Me alone. Now, it is said that a deity is designated for the purpose of relinquishing a substance; how then can the reality of one's own Self be the object of sacrifice without being so designated? [The Lord says: "The sun..."
"The *caru* is to be obtained"—this dedication (*uddeśa*) is indeed produced by another injunction consisting of the designation of a deity which serves as a supplement to that injunction;
and there is no injunction whose object is itself. With this intention, he says: "not preceded by an injunction" (*avidhipūrvakam*).

Regarding the word "me" (*mām*): with respect to a deity distinct from one's own self, there exists an injunction (*vidhi*) that is to be expected, because it consists in the attainment of what has not yet been attained. However, the Supreme Lord as one's own self is not preceded by an injunction, because He is not something to be brought about by an injunction. Indeed, [He is not attained] without aiming at Him.
Something proceeds; therefore, in all those instances where Indra and other deities are brought forth by ritual injunctions,
that very Self— whose nature is the manifestation of the universe—
acts with a sense of "I-am-ness," serving as the foundational ground for the manifestation of the deity intended by that injunction.

It is established by reasoning that [the sacrifice] is "constantly offered" because it is continuously manifest, like the thread of a garland; thus they sacrifice to Me alone, since it is not preceded by the ritual injunctions [of the Vedic rites].
For those [who perform such sacrifices], there is no "intention for the agent" (*kartṛ-abhiprāyatva*) regarding the primary fruit, which is the attainment of Me.

Moreover, the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is intended to demonstrate that these [liberated souls], like officiating priests, find their purpose fulfilled merely by attaining a status such as that of Indra and others, which corresponds to a limited sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
As I myself have said:

If one speaks of the state of Śambhu yet does not know it, he becomes despondent; seeking his own welfare, he abandons the status of the sacrificer and becomes a mere performer of sacrifice for others. All the flowing streams of consciousness, which are the currents of the essence of ritual action— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.)
They do not create this great ocean of bliss without first attaining the state of fullness.
Thus [ends the section]. || 27 ||
Thus, for one who understands according to the stated sequence— that even the sacrifice to deities such as Indra is a sacrifice to the Supreme Lord— whatever other ritual action there may be,
that too takes the form of worshiping Maheśvara as one's own Self, because He alone is the objective of all [actions]. Thus he says:
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me.
Thus you shall be freed from the bonds of action through their very fruits, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you shall come to Me. (9.29)

Since those who worship other deities have limited desires and thus diminish their fruit, you should therefore perform dedication to Me—the contemplation of being absorbed in Me—according to the sequence of instruction previously mentioned.
This indeed is the yoga of renunciation (*saṃnyāsayoga*). Thus [the teaching] has been explained in detail and for the most part with clarity.
Precisely as before. || 29 ||
I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear. But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I too am in them. (9.29)
Moreover, even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is indeed to be regarded as righteous, for he has rightly resolved. 9.31
He quickly becomes a soul of righteousness and attains eternal peace. O son of Kuntī, declare this with certainty: my devotee never perishes. (9.32)
"I affirm"—this point, being consistent with reason, becomes most excellent and firm because it has been affirmed by the Blessed One. || 32 ||
For even those who may be of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—by taking refuge in me, O Pārtha, they too attain the supreme goal. (9.33)
How much more so, then, O meritorious Brahmins, and likewise royal sages devoted to me! Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, worship me. (9.34)
Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me. Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. 9.35.
Those of evil birth are animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth; "women" refers to those lacking knowledge;

"Vaiśyas" refers to those devoted to other occupations such as agriculture; and "Śūdras" refers to those entirely ineligible for Vedic rites and those whose livelihood is dependent on others—even they, when they take refuge in Me, [attain perfection].

They worship me alone. (For the deeds of the Blessed One, who is supremely compassionate, such as the liberation of Gajendra and others, are heard of by the thousands. How much more so, then, those whose conduct is the opposite of this?
Some say that this statement is intended solely as praise for the twice-born and the kṣatriyas,

and does not have the aim of establishing the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*) for women and others; for they, by thus limiting the scope of the Blessed One’s power which favors all beings, undermine it.

Unable to endure the Supreme Lord’s extreme compassion, they contradict such statements as "To Me there is none hateful and none dear, even if one is of very wicked conduct," and other passages that clearly establish this same meaning.

If those who, while forcibly introducing the mark of difference into the reality of the Lord— which is non-dual and established through an unsurpassed proliferation of reasoning— fail to perceive other contradictions with scripture, and when questioned as to how this can be and how that can be, [should respond as follows]:
With their inner faculties possessed by the great seizure of birth and so forth that have been deeply internalized,
their faces and gazes cast downward with shame and the pretense of envy, they project upon themselves the state of being objects of ridicule for the entire populace as speakers of falsehoods.
Whatever explanation was previously given, it brings auspiciousness to all—may it be auspicious! || 35 ||
On this point, there is a summary verse:
"In non-dual Brahman, the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), which is characterized by universal grace, unfolds;
therefore, one should strive for its attainment. (9)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Maheśvara, Rājānaka Abhinavagupta. 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Whatever subject matter was indicated by the nine preceding chapters is further elaborated in this chapter through word-for-word explanations. Thus it is said: "Furthermore..."

"Thus" (*eva*) means: "Listen as this very matter already stated is being explained again for the sake of clarification. Arjuna will likewise say, "Speak further"—this is the purport of the chapter. The remainder is self-evident through its literal explanation; what more is there to say?
[This will be explained] by way of repetition. As for that which is doubtful, it shall be determined [later].
The Blessed Lord said:
"O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word, which I [shall speak] to you."
I shall speak to you, who are well-disposed, out of a desire for your welfare.
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin; for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect.
He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins. (10.3)
Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, calmness, pleasure, pain, birth, existence, fear, and even fearlessness; 10.4.
Non-delusion is enthusiasm. || 4 ||
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these various states of beings arise from Me alone. (10.5)
The seven great sages of old and likewise the four Manus were born from my mind, imbued with my own nature; from them these creatures in this world have descended.
He who knows in truth this glory and this yoga of Mine is united with unshakable yoga; of this there is no doubt. || 10.7 ||
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. Thinking thus, the wise, filled with devotion, worship me. (10.8)
With their minds fixed on Me and their lives surrendered to Me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of Me, they find contentment and rejoice. 10.9.

Through mutual awakening, by means of the expansive transmission of one another’s consciousness, all subjects indeed become the one Lord; thus, through this pervasive extension, they easily attain the state of Maheśvara by realizing the nature of their own self as omnipresent and possessing all powers.
The state of being. || 9 ||
To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love,
I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
Arjuna said:
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, the Ultimate Purifier;
the Eternal, Divine Person, the Primal God, the Unborn, and the All-pervading Lord.
"All the sages, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have told you this; and you yourself are telling it to me. (10.13)
I consider all this that you tell me, O Keśava, to be true; for neither the gods nor the great seers, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.
O Supreme Person, O Creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the world, you alone know yourself by yourself.
You should describe in their entirety your auspicious manifestations,
by which manifestations you abide pervading all these worlds.
How may I know you, O Yogi, as I contemplate you? And in what various states, O Blessed One, are you to be contemplated by me? (10.17)
O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of your own yoga and majesty;
for there is no satiety for me as I drink in this nectar.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Very well, I shall declare to you my auspicious manifestations (vibhūtis), which are my very self, according to their preeminence, O best of the Kurus; for there is no end to my expansion."
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminaries, the radiant Sun;
among the Maruts, I am Marīci; and among the stars, I am the Moon. (10.21)
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava; among the senses, I am the mind;
and among beings, I am consciousness.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
And know, O Pārtha, that Bṛhaspati is the chief among the domestic priests;
likewise, Skanda is the commander-in-chief of my armies, and among bodies of water, I am the ocean. (10.24)
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om. Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña); among immovable things, I am the Himālaya.
Among all trees, the Aśvattha; among the divine sages, Nārada;
among the Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among the Siddhas, the sage Kapila. || 10.26 ||
Know me as Ucchaiḥśravas among horses, born from the nectar; as Airāvata among lordly elephants, and as the king among men. (10.27)
Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; of cows I am the wish-fulfilling cow;
I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and of serpents I am Vāsuki.
Among the Nāgas I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa; among the ancestors I am Aryaman;
and among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama.
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon time, I am Time; among beasts I am the king of beasts; and among birds I am Vainateya. (10.30)
Among purifiers I am the wind; among weapon-bearers I am Rāma;
among fish I am the makara; and among rivers I am the Jāhnavī.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna; among sciences I am the science of the Self, and of those who debate, I am the discourse.
Among letters I am the letter *a*; among compounds I am the dual. I alone am inexhaustible time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.
I am death, the destroyer of all, and the source of those who are yet to be; I am fame, prosperity, speech among women, as well as memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.
Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters I am the Gāyatrī; among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and among seasons I am the flower-bearing spring. || 10.35 ||
I am the gambling of the deceitful; I am the splendor of the splendid; I am victory;
I am resolve; and I am the goodness of the virtuous.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among the poets, the poet Uśanas.
I am the rod for those who seek to subdue; I am the policy of those who desire victory; I am silence among secrets, and I am the knowledge of the wise. (10.38)
Moreover, O Arjuna, I am the seed of all beings; there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me. (10.39)
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
this detailed expansion of my manifestations has been declared by me only in brief.
Whatever being possesses majesty, or is endowed with beauty, or is even powerful, know that to have sprung from but a fragment of my splendor.
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge of yours, O Arjuna? Sustaining this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain.

By the phrase "I am the Self" (aham ātmā), he precludes [any] limitation; otherwise, in statements such as "Himālaya is among the immovable things," there would be a limitation implying that Himālaya alone is the Blessed One and no other,
whereby the vision of Brahman would lack indivisibility.

It would have been fragmentary. For this instructional treatise is intended for one whose mind has not yet ascended to the realization of the all-pervading non-dual form (*akhaṇḍākāra*), and who desires to know it. Thus, at the conclusion, regarding the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*): "Whatever being possesses glory... (*yadyadvibhūtimatsattvam*).
Having declared this, he subsequently concludes with non-difference itself: "Or rather, by much of this what need is there? Supporting this entire universe with a single fraction of myself, I stand."
Thus it is said:
"One foot of His is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven.
This entire world, which is the cause of the creation of living beings, is indeed the reality of the Blessed Lord alone.
Being meditated upon through those various diverse forms, it becomes the object of everything; may there be auspiciousness! || 42 ||
Regarding this, there is a summary verse:
Whatever comes within the range of the desire or even the sense organ, one should forcibly dissolve that very thing and meditate upon it as the tranquil Brahman. (10)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and royal counselor of the Great Maheśvara.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Arjuna asks in order to directly perceive that very same matter which was stated in the immediately preceding chapter. He who—
The meaning understood through the sequence of instruction becomes clarified when it is ascended by direct perceptual awareness; for that very purpose,
these questions and answers are spoken.
Arjuna said:
By that supreme secret discourse concerning the self which you have spoken for my benefit,
this delusion of mine has been dispelled.
For the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from you,
O lotus-petal-eyed one, as well as your imperishable majesty.
"It is even so as you say; you are the Supreme Lord. O Supreme Person, I desire to see Your divine form."
If you think, O Lord, that it is possible for me to see it, then, O Lord of Yoga,
show me your imperishable self.
The Blessed Lord said: Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands— divine, of various kinds, and of various colors and shapes.
Behold the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
behold, O Pāṇḍava, many wonders never seen before.
Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings gathered together here in one place within my body, and whatever else you wish to see.
But you are not able to see Me with this very eye of yours; I shall give you divine vision;
behold My sovereign form.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great lord of yogis, then revealed to Pārtha his supreme, divine form.
He possessed many mouths and eyes, a sight of many wonders, many divine ornaments,
and many uplifted divine weapons.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, that god consists of every wonder— Ananta, whose faces are everywhere.
If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky,
that might resemble the radiance of that Great-Souled One.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld the entire universe, divided into many parts, situated within the body of the God of gods.
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end,
bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Arjuna said:
O God, I see all the gods in Your body, as well as the hosts of various beings;
I see Brahmā, the Lord seated upon his lotus-throne, and all the ṛṣis and serpents.
The divine ones. || 11-15 ||

I see You with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms on all sides; O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form! I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning.
I behold You wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus—a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to gaze upon, of immeasurable radiance like a flaming fire or the sun.
You are the supreme imperishable to be known; You are the ultimate refuge of this universe.
You are the imperishable protector of the Sāttvata dharma; you are considered by me to be the eternal Puruṣa.

Regarding the term *sāttvatadharmagoptā*: those for whom there exists that reality which consists of existence (*sattā*), whose nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), and which is characterized by the non-appearance of any distinction between both being (*sat*)—meaning truth (*satya*)—and action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), are the *sāttvatas*. Of them...
Dharma—because it is intent upon the continuous process of grasping and relinquishing—is concerned with creation and dissolution;

it transcends all paths and protects that [reality]. This very secret has been revealed by me here in this chapter, for the most part, in the commentary on the *Devīstotra*. May it be understood by those who possess a refined heart (*sahṛdaya*).
Since this is understood by oneself through the very instructions, what is the use of such prolixity in repeatedly clarifying it more clearly? || 18 ||
I see You, who are without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite vigor and infinite arms, with eyes like the moon and the sun;
I see Your face like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with Your own splendor.
Indeed, this space between heaven and earth, as well as all the quarters of the sky, are pervaded by You alone.
O Great-Souled One, having seen this wondrous and fierce form of yours, these three worlds are deeply distressed.
For these hosts of gods are entering into you; some, filled with fear, praise you with joined palms;
and the hosts of great seers, saying "All hail!", extol you with abundant hymns of praise.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
and the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas—all gaze upon you, utterly amazed. (11-22)

Seeing Your form as vast, with many mouths and eyes, O mighty-armed one, with many arms, thighs, and feet, with many bellies and terrifying with many tusks, the worlds are struck with fear, and so am I.
O Viṣṇu, seeing you touching the sky, blazing, multicolored, with gaping mouths and glowing, wide eyes, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
Having seen your mouths, terrible with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, I no longer know the directions nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe!
All these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with all the hosts of kings,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karna), along with our own leading warriors as well— 11.26.
Hurrying, they enter your mouths, which are terrifying and formidable with tusks;
some are seen caught between the teeth with their heads crushed.
Oppressed by men of various forms, they enter your mouth of inconceivable appearance.
All the warriors, both the sons of Yudhiṣṭhira and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, were indeed cut down by various weapons.
"Surely these have been struck down by your splendor; for thus they have entered your body, just as the many currents of water from rivers flow toward the ocean."
Thus these heroes of the world of men enter your mouths blazing on all sides,
just as moths with full force enter a blazing fire for their destruction;
even so do these people enter your mouths for their destruction.
Possessing full force. || 11-30 ||
You lick up the entire worlds on all sides while devouring them with your flaming mouths;
having filled the whole universe with your splendors, O Viṣṇu, your fierce radiances scorch everything.
Tell me, who are you of such fierce form? Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primordial One, for I do not understand your purpose.
I do not know your motivation—by what intention is this [conduct] of yours so fierce? || 32 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown mature; I have set out here to gather in all the worlds.
Even without you, all those who stand arrayed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.
The warriors. || 11-33 ||
Therefore, arise and win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone;
be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin.
Slay Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna, and likewise other heroes of the world—all of whom have already been slain by me; do not be distressed. Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.

In this regard, the Blessed One provides the following answer: because he has swallowed up the power of consciousness—whether pure, impure, or mixed—of the world whose nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance. This is the intended meaning; the secret doctrine has been thus aphoristically indicated in this chapter.
Let it suffice for those capable of understanding through a mere brief indication;

why should we subject ourselves to the distress of the labor of writing out the entire sequence? Regarding what was said by me here—"When they are slain, you shall be the cause of their fame"—this was spoken by the Blessed One.
That which was previously stated by Arjuna—"Of these two, which is the weightier for us? and so forth—has been answered [in this verse]. (11.35)
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, trembling with joined palms,
bowed again to Kṛṣṇa and spoke with a faltering voice, utterly terrified.
Having prostrated. || 11-36 ||
Arjuna said:
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by the proclamation of Your glory the world rejoices and is filled with devotion;
the demons flee in fear to every quarter, and all pay You homage.
The assemblies of Siddhas. || 11-37 ||
By means of proclamation—that is, by not proclaiming it. || 37 ||
And why, O Great-Souled One, would these not bow before You, who are even greater than Brahmā, the original creator?
O Infinite Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe, You are the Imperishable—that which is both being (sat) and non-being (asat), and that which is beyond them.
[You are] "being" (sat) by virtue of being the ultimate reality; "non-being" (asat) because You are not an object of perception. Or alternatively—
Even non-existence (abhāva), when conjoined with its respective specific designator within the intellect and assuming the form of cognition, is not distinct from the reality of the Supreme Brahman;
for that Supreme [Reality] transcends both the forms of existence and non-existence when both those cognitions have subsided.
Because there is perception of that form. || 38 ||
You are the primordial God, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe.
You are the knower and that which is to be known, and the highest abode. By you, who possess infinite forms, the universe is pervaded.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, and Prajāpati.
And the Great-grandfather; he who is without beginning, whose nature is incomparable, the Lord of all, O you of all-great majesty.

Salutations, salutations be unto you a thousand times; again and yet once more, salutations, salutations unto you! Salutations from the front and from behind; salutations be unto you from every side, O All!

By the repetition "namo namaḥ," the intensity of his devotion is manifested; thus, Arjuna reveals through praise that very nature of the Blessed One which was previously described by the Lord in the preceding chapters, now having become an object of direct perception.
The explanation of that [point] is omitted here, as it would result in mere redundancy. || 41 ||
O Lord, no one else in these three worlds is seen here who possesses such inconceivable deeds;
you are of infinite power and immeasurable prowess, you pervade all, and therefore you are everything.
Whatever was said by me rashly, thinking "you are my friend"— 'O Kṛṣṇa', 'O Yādava', or 'O friend'— out of negligence or even out of affection, not knowing this greatness of yours;
and whatever you were treated with disrespect for the sake of jest during recreation, on the bed, on the seat, or at meals.
Or else, O Acyuta, being alone in Your presence, I beg forgiveness from You, the immeasurable one.

You are the father of this world of the moving and the unmoving; you are the most venerable teacher of this entire universe. There is no one equal to you, much less anyone superior, even throughout the three worlds, O You of incomparable power!
Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I seek to please you, the adorable Lord.
As a father bears with his son, a friend with his friend, and a lover with his beloved, O God, it behooves you to endure me.
Your divine and wondrous deeds of old are remembered by the ancient seers.
There is no other creator of the universe; you alone are the sustainer, the ordainer, and the all-pervading Lord.

What indeed could be wondrous for you? What could be impossible, or what could be possible for another that you might proclaim? Since you yourself, O All-pervading One, are truly the creator of everything, therefore [you are so].
All this is indeed you alone.
This most wonderful deed is not difficult for you; indeed, no comparison for your deed exists. There is no limit to your virtues, nor to your splendor, nor to your strength, nor to your majesty.
I am thrilled at seeing what has never been seen before, yet my mind is distressed with fear; therefore, O God, show me that very form again; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe!
"I wish to see you just as before—wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with the discus in hand. O thousand-armed one, O universal-formed one, appear in that very four-armed form!
The Blessed Lord said:
O Arjuna, being pleased with you, I have through my own yoga shown you this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primal— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.
Neither by the study of the Vedas nor by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities,
can I be seen in such a form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus;
let there be no distress and no confusion in you upon seeing this terrible and fierce form.
"This is mine. Free from fear and with a joyful mind, behold once again this very form of mine."
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed him his own form once again;
and the Great-Souled One, assuming once more his gentle form, comforted him who had been terrified.
Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, I am now restored to my senses and have returned to my natural state. (11.56)

At the conclusion of the complete withdrawal, He bestows the state of abiding in the reality of Brahman, which is of the nature of supreme tranquility—such is the Lord’s gentleness at the time of withdrawal. 56.
The Blessed Lord said:
This form of Mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold; even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner as you have seen me.
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known in truth, seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe. (11.59)
He who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme goal, who is my devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward all beings—he, O Pāṇḍava, comes to me. (11.60)
For those in whom devotion— which finds no other object of knowledge to delight in— shines forth,
Vāsudeva enters them through the wonder of the previously mentioned instruction beginning with "Vāsudeva is all," [realizing him] as the soul of the universe.
The reality of Vāsudeva descends effortlessly upon the path of awakening; may there be auspiciousness. || 60 ||
On this point, there is a summary verse:
By reflecting upon the unity of consciousness arising from the pure, the impure, and the mixed, the sage, perceiving the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar—with equanimity, becomes equal. || 11 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Arjuna said:
Those devotees who, thus constantly disciplined, worship You with devotion; those...
And among those who [seek] the imperishable and unmanifest, who are the best knowers of yoga? || 12.1 ||
In accordance with the method thus stated, a question is posed for the purpose of explaining the distinction between those who worship Brahman along with Īśvara and those who worship the Self alone.
Śrī Bhagavān said:
Those who, having fixed their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline, endowed with supreme faith—they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined. (12.2)

"Those in whom there is an immersion into the domain of Māheśvarī—an unartificial state of identification with Her—are, in my view, the most perfectly united (yuktatama); by this, a formal proposition is established. (2)
But those who worship the Imperishable, which is indefinable, unmanifest, omnipresent, unthinkable, immutable, immovable, and eternal; || 12-3 ||
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses and possessing equanimity toward all things, those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone. 12.4.
The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater; for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by those who bear a body.
Furthermore, those who worship Brahman as the Imperishable—

through such attributes as "the Self that is omnipresent"— superimpose all the qualities of the Lord upon the Self. Therefore, even though these worshippers of Brahman go to Me alone, [they do so by way of My own nature].
Nevertheless, their affliction is even greater;

for they first superimpose upon the Self the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin, and subsequently worship that very [Self], whereas [the former] [worship the Self] which possesses a natural abundance of a multitude of established qualities.
Even though the Lord is present and requires no effort to accomplish [their aims], they undergo double the labor.
But those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are intent on Me alone, and worshiping Me while meditating with an exclusive yoga— || 12.6 ||
I become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence, O Pārtha, without delay, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me. 12.7.
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me. Abiding in Me alone, you shall attain the supreme Yoga.

But for those who, by means of the instruction previously mentioned, surrender everything to Me, I am their deliverer from all afflictions such as obstacles and the like. The "entering of the mind" has been explained. And thus, this alone is the supreme yoga because it is uncontrived. And so it is said:

If my hymn should cause some awakening to arise by virtue of being contemplated as a distinguished means for the attainment of the state of meditative absorption while seated, that is not equal to Your [awakening], which is ever-arisen and flows spontaneously.
For this reason, it is clearly experienced here as well, due to the presence of the triad of consciousness.
But when, with the fuel of passion departed, he takes refuge in self-mastery—
accompanied by unfeigned, surging horripilation, trembling, and tears—
and clearly assumes an indifference toward the body, then the mind itself suddenly [awakens].
The fire of awakening awakens simultaneously; at that very moment, O Goddess,
your body perceives Maheśa— who is devoid of dependence on the gunas and who violently shatters the bonds of those who are helpless.
And so forth. || 8 ||
If you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me, then seek to reach me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of practice.

Without an exceedingly intense descent of the Lord’s power (śaktipāta) and the grace of a teacher whose feet have been propitiated for a very long time, this state of possession (āveśa) is difficult to attain; such is the practice. || 9 ||
If you are unable even to practice, be intent on performing actions for Me; by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.

Even practice cannot be maintained due to being overwhelmed by obstacles and the like; therefore, perform ritual action, worship, recitation, study, fire-offerings, and so forth, for the sake of destroying them. 10.
But if you are unable even to do this, then, taking refuge in my yoga,
renounce the fruits of all actions with a self-controlled mind.

And if you are unable to perform the work of the Blessed One due to ignorance—that is, because you do not know the sequence prescribed in the scriptures—then you should consign all of that to me by means of self-surrender; this is the intended meaning. Relying upon this very intention:
In the *Laghuprakriyā*, I myself have said:

"Whatever is deficient or excessive, whatever is not understood, whatever is devoid of proper sequence, whatever is lacking in attention, and whatever has slipped from the intellect— all that [is forgiven] by me, O Lord of All, for my devoted and suffering disciple."
O Śambhu, you who are devoted to compassion, this [act] of the evil-minded one should be forgiven out of mercy.
By means of this application of praise, I offer myself to you; yet once again, for no reason, I become a vessel for sufferings.
Thus, for indeed, this is the very intention regarding the surrender of the self in the Siddhānta scriptures of the Supreme Lord. || 11 ||
This essential meaning is now summarized:

Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation follows peace immediately. (12.12)
Knowledge consists in the nature of immersion (*āveśa*); through practice, it leads to the highest good, because that is the fruit of practice.
From that very immersion, meditation—which is absorption in the Blessed One—is distinguished;
it attains excellence through the attainment of the desired goal. When meditation, which is absorption in the Blessed One, exists, the fruits of action [no longer bind].
Renunciation is appropriate [only for one who has realized this]; otherwise, where is there renunciation for one whose form remains unknown?
And in the relinquishing of the fruits of action lies absolute peace. Therefore, because it is the root of everything, knowledge consisting of spiritual immersion (āveśa) alone is primary. || 12 ||
One who is not a hater of any beings, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and egoism, equal in pain and pleasure, and patient; 12–13.

He who possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and freedom from envy (*amatsaratā*). Likewise, he is compassionate (*karuṇaḥ*). "This is mine" and so forth is possessiveness (*mamakāra*); "I am generous, I am majestic, I am patient" and so forth is egoism (*ahaṃkāra*); he for whom these two do not exist. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is [the quality directed toward] a harmful enemy.
The state of mind characterized by the absence of aversion. || 13 ||
The yogi who is always content, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. (12.14)

Because the yogi’s internal organ is perpetually tranquil even during the state of worldly activity, he does not cause the world to tremble, nor does he himself tremble before the world; he who is free from joy, envy, fear, and agitation—he, indeed, is dear to Me. (12.15)
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, and free from distress;
who renounces the fruits of all undertakings—he who is my devotee is dear to me. (12.16)
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced the fruits of both good and evil, and who is full of devotion—he is dear to Me. 12.17
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment.
A man who is equal toward blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion— such a person is dear to Me.
But those who worship this nectar of dharma as it has been described, full of faith, regarding Me as their supreme goal— those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me.
One who is homeless— meaning one who has no vow such as "this alone must be done by me"—
and who experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth with the heedlessness that comes from whatever happens to arise,
having his heart absorbed in the Supreme Lord, attains [the goal] with ease indeed.
Supreme liberation—may there be auspiciousness. || 20 ||
Here is the summary verse:
For those who have attained the perfection of intense immersion born from the helplessness of supreme bliss, the reality of Brahman indeed manifests spontaneously in all states without effort. (12)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Maheśvara, Rājānaka Abhinavagupta. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Arjuna said:
"Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as Kṣetra and Kṣetrajña—"
I desire to know this, O Keśava: knowledge and the object of knowledge.

In certain scriptural passages, it is heard that the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field) is the object of worship. Regarding the doubt as to whether he is the Self (*ātman*), or the Lord (*īśvara*), or perhaps some other third entity altogether,
the Blessed Lord instructs:
The Blessed Lord said:
This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the "field" (kṣetra). Those who know this [reality] call him who knows it the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). (13.2)
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata;
that which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is, in My opinion, true knowledge. (13.3)

The body of transmigrating beings is the *kṣetra* (field), wherein the seeds of karma sprout. For this very reason, their self (*ātman*), when defiled by adventitious impurities, is called the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field). For those who are awakened, that same [body] is the *kṣetra*. As for the distinction based on the literal meaning of the terms, it is as follows: it "wastes away" (*kṣiṇoti*)...
It protects them from the bondage of karma through experience and from the fear of birth and death.

And with reference to them, the Supreme Self, Vāsudeva, is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). Regarding the word "knows" (*veda*) in the phrase "he who knows this field," the verbal root *vid* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it. Therefore, by whose grace this insentient [universe]...

That very *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) becomes conscious; it is nothing else whatsoever. However, the distinction is that when it assumes a form of limited pervasion, it is called the "self" (*ātman*), whereas when it pervades all fields without limitation, it is the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
In the word "mama," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object; the meaning is: "I am to be known by this knowledge. || 3 ||
Listen to me in brief concerning that field: what it is, of what nature it is, how it changes, from whence it comes, who he is, and what his essential nature is. (13.4)
It has been sung by the seers in many ways, through various distinct meters,
and it has been definitively established by means of reasoned arguments in the form of the words of the Brahma-sutras.
By means of that by which one undergoes modification and that which is subject to modification—
in short, he resolves these questions with a common answer, without any distinction. And although this has been stated in many ways by the seers and in the Vedas, nevertheless—
"I shall explain in brief," he said. || 5 ||
The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses. (13.6)
The unmanifest is primordial nature (prakṛti). The senses are eleven, including the mind.
The objects of the senses are the five, beginning with form (rūpa). 6.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the physical aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—this, in brief, is declared to be the field together with its modifications. (13.7)

The Puruṣa is the power of consciousness and vision. "Fortitude" (dhṛti) indeed means that, whether an undertaking is already begun or completed—whether it be Brahmā or a mere worm—one thinks regarding desires, anger, and so forth: "This much alone is sufficient for me; what need is there for anything else?"

And the thought, "May I always be such as this," gives rise to a firm resolve that sustains the vital breaths, consisting of consolation; in the secret teachings of others, this is designated by the term *rāga*. (7)
Thus the field has been explained, as well as the knower of the field. Now, knowledge is being described:
humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, and service to the teacher.
Purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint. || 13-8 ||
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism, and the contemplation of the defects of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. (13.9)
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (13.10)
And devotion to me through undivided yoga that is unswerving;
the habit of resorting to solitary places; and a lack of delight in the assembly of worldly people. (13.11)
Devotion to the knowledge of the Self and the perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is otherwise is ignorance. (13.12)

"By means of undivided devotion" (*ananya-yogena*) means that there is nothing else whatsoever other than the Supreme Self, Maheśvara; this very certainty that He is non-different [from all things] is itself *yoga*. Through that certainty, there is devotion (*bhakti*) toward Me. For this very reason, it is not...

It is never non-deviant, because there is an absence of those desires which are considered to be the causes of deviation; or else, because even those [desires], being of the nature of other mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), consist solely of that [knowledge].
This should be understood accordingly in all cases. Ignorance is the opposite of this.
Likewise, [the qualities] beginning with honor (mānitva). || 12 ||
By means of this knowledge, that which is to be known is now declared:
"I shall proclaim that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality.
That Brahman is without beginning, supreme; it is said to be neither being nor non-being. (13.13)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands pervading everything.
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses; it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all, devoid of qualities and yet the experiencer of qualities.
It is both outside and inside all beings; it is the unmoving as well as the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away and yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings; it is to be known as the sustainer of beings, as well as their devourer and their progenitor.
That is the light even of lights; it is said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of every being.

By means of such qualifiers as "the beginningless supreme Brahman," he declares that the nature of Brahman— which supports the implication of its own essence— is non-different from the consciousness described in all philosophical systems. And these...
Since the qualifiers have already been explained, what is the use of this fruitless repetition? || 18 ||
Thus, this field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been declared in brief. Having realized this, my devotee attains to my own state of being. (13.19)
He who knows this triad consisting of the knower of the field, knowledge, and the object of knowledge—he alone is my devotee; and he attains to my state of being. 19.
Having established this definition, the examination is conducted as follows:
"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless; know also that the modifications and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti. (13.20)
Nature (prakṛti) is also beginningless, because there is no other cause for it. Transformations (vikāras)—such as cloth and the like—are its effects.

Nature is said to be the cause in the state of being the agent of the body and the instruments [of action]. The Person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the state of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. (13–21)
Prakṛti is the cause in the relationship between cause and effect; the Puruṣa, however, is the enjoyer by virtue of its predominance. 21.
For the person, situated in material nature, experiences the qualities born of nature; attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. (13.22)
The functioning of Prakṛti and Puruṣa is indeed based on mutual dependence, like that of the lame man and the blind man. || 22 ||
The supreme Person within this body is called the witness, the permitter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also the Supreme Self. (13.23)
For this very reason, the authors of the treatises designate its nature by various names, such as "the witness" (upadraṣṭṛ) and so forth. This is the intended meaning here:
[it is distinct from] primordial nature (prakṛti), its transformations, and the fourteenfold creation, as well as—
The Puruṣa: All this is beginningless and eternal, because, while being permeated by the reality of Brahman, it is non-different from it. || 23 ||
And so it has been said:
"He who thus knows the Puruṣa and Prakṛti along with its qualities (guṇas), no matter how he may conduct himself, is not born again. (13.24)

Thus, by this vision of Brahman in its entirely non-differentiated form, the yogi who knows primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual self (puruṣa), and the qualities (guṇas) along with their transformations—whatever he may do in any manner whatsoever—he is indeed liberated; such is the meaning. || 24 ||
Some perceive the Self by means of the self through meditation; others by the yoga of Sāṅkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others; they too surely cross over death, being devoted to what they have heard.
And such knowledge as this is worshipped by some as the primary principle (pradhāna) in the form of the Self;
by others according to the previously mentioned Sāṃkhya system; by others through ritual action;
and even by others who themselves do not know such knowledge.

Those who are intent on hearing worship [the Lord] exactly as they have heard it; they too cross over death and saṃsāra. By whatever means the reality of the Blessed One is worshipped, it delivers one.
Therefore, it is said that "it was always thus. || 26 ||
Whatever being exists, whether stationary or moving—know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field. 13.27
Whatever exists, whether moving or unmoving, none of it can possibly exist apart from the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 27 ||
He who sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings,
and remaining undestroyed when they are destroyed— he truly sees.
Therefore, seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy oneself by means of the self; from that, one attains the supreme goal. (13.29)
The yogi who possesses an even mind toward all things does not harm himself; he does not cause himself to fall into the difficult-to-cross ocean of saṃsāra. || 29 ||
For he alone truly sees who perceives that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise that the Self is the non-doer. 13.30
For he whose intellect becomes as firm as this—that "it is nature alone that acts, I do nothing at all"—he does not act even while performing everything; such is non-agency.
Or rather,
when one perceives the manifold existence of beings as situated in the One, and likewise perceives their expansion from that very source,
then one attains Brahman. (13.31)
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this Supreme Self is immutable; O son of Kuntī, even though dwelling in the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.
Just as space, being all-pervasive, is not defiled because of its subtlety, so the Self, though situated everywhere within the body, is not defiled. 13.33
