When, through its vastness and all-pervasiveness, one perceives the distinctness— the separateness— of all beings within the Self alone, and considers that [distinction] as impelled by the Self alone,
even then, because it is the agent of all, one is not subject to taint; for such a person is the Supreme Self itself.
Though situated within the body, it is not tainted, like space. || 33 ||
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field.
Now, one might raise the objection: "How can the one Supreme Self pervade many fields?"—this doubt is dispelled by the well-known illustration of the sun.
"The entire field" means all fields consisting of moving and non-moving beings. || 34 ||
Thus, those who perceive with the eye of knowledge the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, as well as the liberation from the material nature of beings, they go to the Supreme.
Thus, by this chapter, that which was stated— namely, the object of knowledge (jñeya), knowledge (jñāna),

the distinction between the field and the knower of the field (kṣetra-kṣetrajña), and liberation from the material nature (bhūta-prakṛti) due to its quality of undergoing slight transformation— that has been explained through the characteristic of knowledge.
Beholding with an unimpeded, supramundane eye everywhere, they attain the state of Vāsudeva and indeed obtain supreme auspiciousness; may there be auspiciousness! 35.

On this point, there is a summary verse: "The distinction between 'the person' and 'primordial nature' belongs to those of deluded minds; but the perfected ones consider the world to consist of the stainless Self. (13)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Maheśvara, the venerable Rājānaka Abhinavagupta. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall further declare that supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge.
Knowing which, all the sages have attained supreme perfection from this state.
That very knowledge which was previously mentioned, I shall now explain again with greater detail, by defining the nature of each of its qualities individually.
By the phrase "having known which," [the Lord] indicates that this knowledge possesses empirical verification and is well-established.
And he said: || 1 ||
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained a state of similarity with me;
they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution. (14.2)

The verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in *vyathanti* is used because of Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). The same should be understood regarding other verbal (*tiṅ*) and nominal (*sup*) suffixes elsewhere as well. || 2 ||
In this regard, he first states the sequence of transmigration: "The Great Brahman is my womb; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs. (14.3)
When that which is to be abandoned and its cause are known, abandonment is indeed easy.
For me, Brahman—which is of the nature of inexpressible supreme bliss—is the power inherent to the Great Self (*mahadbrahmavṛṃhaka*), whose form is my own. Indeed, it is my very own...
Relying upon the power of discernment (vimarśa-śakti), I cause the individual souls (ātmāṇu), who are beginningless "I-sense" (aham-anādi), to transmigrate for the sake of bestowing grace. || 3 ||
Therefore:
"O son of Kuntī, whatever forms are produced in all wombs, the Great Brahman is their womb, and I am the seed-bestowing father. (14.4)

The power of the Blessed One, which expands [all things] as the primordial cause in all wombs, is the Mother, whose nature is the vomiting forth of the entire cycle of existence; whereas I am the Father, designated as the possessor of that power. (4)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of material nature, O mighty-armed one, bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body. (14.5)
And this embodied being would be bound by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as its own nature for the sake of experience until final liberation.
In that regard, O sinless one, *sattva*, being pure, luminous, and free from affliction, binds [the self] through attachment to pleasure and through attachment to knowledge.
Know that *rajas* is of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment; it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, by attachment to action. (14.7)
The nature of these is stated in sequence: Sattva is stainless, from which arises attachment and thirst. (7)
Know that darkness (tamas), born of ignorance, deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep.

Heedlessness is the vain passing away of human existence— which, though difficult to obtain and acquired through hundreds of merits accumulated over a very long time, is the sole cause for attaining liberation. For it has been said:
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for all the jewels in the world; he by whom that moment is spent in vain is a negligent man, the lowest of men.
Thus: indolence regarding virtuous deeds; "drāṇam" means completely sinking; a base state is sleep. (8)
Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bhārata; rajas to action; but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence.
It binds; it yokes. || 9 ||
Overpowering rajas and tamas, sattva prevails, O Bhārata; likewise, rajas overcomes sattva and tamas, and tamas overcomes sattva and rajas. (14.10)

Sattva increases by overpowering rajas and tamas; rajas [increases] by overpowering sattva and tamas; and tamas [increases] by overpowering sattva and rajas. For it has been said: "The increase of the qualities occurs through mutual subdual. (10)
When, through all the gates of this body, light arises as knowledge, then one should know that the *sattva* has increased. (14.11)
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and thirst—these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas. (14.12)
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—these arise when Tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus. (14.13)

"In all the gates"—that is, in all the sense organs. Greed and the other qualities arise sequentially when *rajas* is predominant; likewise, non-illumination and the others manifest sequentially as *tamas* increases. (13)
But when the embodied soul meets its dissolution while sattva is predominant, then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest.

When, throughout one's entire life, sattva has been increased through the constant practice of virtuous activities, then, upon the attainment of dissolution, there is the acquisition of an auspicious world. || 14 ||
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born among the dull-witted species.

Thus, for one who has practiced rajasic actions throughout their life, the attainment of human birth occurs after death for the sake of mixed experience. Likewise, when by that same process rajasic action is practiced throughout an entire lifetime, then one is born in the bodies of hell-beings, animals, trees, and so forth.
As for those who explain that these fruits arise only when sattva and the other qualities have increased at the very moment of death— they have not correctly entered into the experience of the body;
for in every case, at the final moment, only delusion (moha) arises.
And in our commentary, there are these other verses that corroborate this. 15.
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by sattva; the fruit of rajas is suffering, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas*, greed; from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance. (14.17)
Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas stay in the middle;
those established in the conduct of the lowest quality, the tamasic, go downward.
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities,
and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state of being.
Having transcended these three qualities that arise from the body, the embodied soul,
liberated from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, attains immortality.

In this regard, certain unrelated verses have been composed; because they are redundant, they should indeed be discarded. However, conduct that transcends these qualities leads only to liberation. (20)

"Now, if this embodied being is such, how can he transcend the qualities? For in every way he exists through some modification of the mind, and that modification must necessarily be one of the three qualities. With this intention, Arjuna asks.
Arjuna said:
By what marks, O Lord, does one transcend these three qualities? What is his conduct, and how does he go beyond these three qualities? (14.21)
To this, the Blessed One replied:
"O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion."
They have proceeded and do not turn back; he does not desire them. || 14-22 ||
Although illumination and the other qualities exist in all phenomena, nevertheless,
yogins do not become attached to those qualities such as illumination, nor do they become subject to aversion; rather, [they think],
"These exist merely as properties of the physical body (piṇḍadharma), and they are not able to disturb me."
Thinking thus, they become transcendent of the qualities. || 22 ||
Therefore, he said:
"He who remains seated like one indifferent, who is not shaken by the qualities; who, knowing that 'it is the qualities that move,' remains steady and does not waver. (14.23)

Equanimous toward pain and pleasure, sleeping in peace, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, the wise man is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and views blame and self-praise with equanimity. (14.24)
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward friend and foe,
and who renounces the fruits of all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.

He who remains ignorant and devoid of discrimination is himself the knower, by virtue of his perfect knowledge. For it is thus: he does not move—that is, he does not deviate from his true nature. And here the means is this: the very nature of the body, senses, and so forth is their engagement, but that is not the fruit.
The firm conviction that "I am intending to do something" is the intellect (buddhi). || 25 ||
And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, becomes fit for the state of Brahman.

By this, he teaches the fundamental means, namely "Me" (mām). The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, meaning "he who serves Me alone. By this, it is stated that one who desires fruits and the like resorts to Me as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), while the fruit remains the primary goal; thus, [the practice] is uninterrupted. For this very reason, there is no failure in its result.

For he is one who places his confidence in the fruit, thinking, "This is my power. But as for one who does not desire even the slightest fruit, even when questioned, "Why do you perform this which is false?"—
With his heart pierced by the continuous flow of devotion to the Lord,
his hair stood on end, his body trembled, and a stream of tears welled up and rolled from his wide-open eyes.

He gives his answer by means of silence alone; it should be understood that he alone has been purified by devotion to the supreme power of the Blessed Maheśvara—a power that is unfailing—and no other. || 26 ||
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. (14.27)
For I alone am the foundation of Brahman. When I am served, Brahman becomes manifest;
otherwise, if Brahman were worshipped as an insentient entity, it would lead to liberation that is no different from deep sleep. May there be auspiciousness! 27.
Here is a summary verse:

Free from the delusion of egoism through the immersion in the savor of radiant devotion, the ascetic remains equanimous, transcending the qualities even while they are present in their full intensity. (14)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below; [its leaves are] the Vedic hymns (*chandas*).
He whose leaves are [these], he who knows him is a knower of the Veda.

By this, it is stated that when it is said in other treatises—such as "the aśvattha tree is everything; he alone is to be worshipped"—the intended meaning is that worship is directed toward the Lord who transcends [the world].
The root is the form of supreme peace (*praśānta*). That is "upward" (*ūrdhva*), for it is entirely withdrawn from all things.
Its attainment [is as follows]: "The Vedic meters are the leaves"— just as a tree's majesty, fruitfulness, and sapidity are indicated by its leaves,
so too is the realization of the reality of Brahman described as occurring through the gateway of the scriptures characterized by the Vedas.
Its branches, nourished by the gunas and having sense objects as their sprouts, extend downward and upward; and its roots, which bind one to action, stretch out below in the world of men. (15.2)
Its form is not perceived here in that way; it has neither end, nor beginning, nor any fixed foundation.
Having cut down this deeply rooted Ashvattha tree with the sharp weapon of non-attachment, one must then seek that goal, reaching which one does not return again.
I take refuge in that very same primordial Puruṣa, from whom the ancient course of worldly activity has proceeded. (15.4)
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state. 15.5.

"By the qualities"—namely, by *sattva* and the others. "Increased"—ranging from the gods down to stationary beings (*sthāvara*). And its roots are below, consisting of actions (*karma*) that are both auspicious and inauspicious.
Regarding the phrase "having cut that": although the action is expressed with respect to the substantive (the tree), it is understood here by implication [to apply to the self].
He takes up the qualifying word, "one who possesses a staff (daṇḍī)," according to the rule: "One should cause the servants to recite.
By that [qualification], one should cut its roots that have grown downward. That very word is the tranquil, immutable state. || 5 ||
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return. (15.6)

There is no place for the sun and other luminaries therein, because they are delimited by time and so forth, because they are objects of cognition, and because they serve as instruments [of perception]. That [Self], however, is not delimited by space, time, and so forth; it is the cognizer, the activator of the instruments [of perception], and it transcends them. || 6 ||
An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living being in the world of the living, draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature. (15.7)

"This is a portion of Brahman alone. Its status as a "portion" is merely figurative, due to the non-perception and the cessation of consciousness in that which is otherwise perfect by virtue of its nature as ignorance; it does not, however, logically constitute a state of being possessed of parts in reality.

Even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its possession of all forms; for such is the Śruti, stating that it is "indeed beyond conceptualization. Furthermore, this very figurative usage should be applied as the occasion demands; one should not entertain any misconception regarding this. || 7 ||
Whatever body the Lord assumes and whatever body He departs from, He takes these [qualities] with Him as He unites [with a new body],
just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.

"Attains" means he grasps; "transmigrates" means he abandons. Together with these [elements], just as the all-pervading wind, having reached a terrestrial resting place, takes up its fragrance and moves to another location accompanied by it, so too does the individual soul (jīva) [move] with the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).

Thus, having stated his association with these [faculties] during both creation and dissolution, it is determined that even during maintenance— whether in the form of standing, sitting, or reflection, or in the nature of perceiving objects— his activity occurs only in conjunction with them. || 8 ||
Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose, as well as the mind, this [Self] experiences the objects of the senses.
Whether it is standing, departing, or eating, those possessed of qualities—the deluded do not perceive it; those with the eye of knowledge perceive it. (15.10)
By the word "mind" (manaḥ), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is indicated. Therefore,
the deluded do not perceive Him as He remains joined to the maintenance of the body, as He departs for the sake of assuming another body, or as He enjoys sense objects.

They do not see [it] because they are unawakened; however, those who are awakened, maintaining the very nature of consciousness everywhere, certainly know [it], for they possess undiminished samādhi due to their dedication to effort. || 10 ||
Striving yogis behold Him established within themselves;
yet those of unrefined self, though striving, do not behold Him, being devoid of wisdom.

But for those of unrefined self, even effort does not lead to fruit because their afflictions (*kaṣāya*) have not ripened. Indeed, even when there is a convergence of conditions such as water and so forth in autumn, seeds of grain that are sown are not capable of yielding a harvest. For this very reason, that [effort] is not even a "condition" for them; it is something else entirely.
It is said that water is merely that which is driven forth by the mass of clouds gathered in the month of Madhu;
and that earth is merely that which, when overcome by the cold, possesses luster only through contact with the rays of the sun.
Thus, for those who have not disciplined themselves, effort is in vain.
They attain the state of being complete in all their limbs; yet even after obtaining such means as the initiation of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-dīkṣā) and so forth,
there are those whose inner vision remains enveloped within the dense knot of anger, delusion, and other such afflictions.
It should be understood that among these, the means (upāya) alone does not possess completeness. As it has been said:
"For one who remains under the influence of anger and other such states, even if initiated, does not partake in liberation.
That light which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in the fire—know that light to be mine. 15.12.
And entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital power; and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all herbs.
Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire and abiding within the bodies of living beings, I— joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths— digest the four kinds of food.
Regarding the manifestation of creation, maintenance, and dissolution as indicated in the tenth chapter by way of the threefold nature of the light of the Sun and others,
the venerable Gurus have said: "Of the five elements, both collectively and individually..."
This [verse] demonstrates that the quality of being the sustainer of the world belongs solely to the Blessed Lord, which is His supreme sovereignty (*māheśvarya*).

For instance, the sun’s capacity to illuminate and its capacity to sustain are due to its non-dual identity with the sustaining fire-element (*tejodhara*). This very point has been stated in the words: "That which is in the sun... (Gītā 15.12).

And by the two half-verses beginning with "Entering the earth" (gāmāviśya ca), [it is shown that] the lunar light is both illuminating and nourishing due to its conjunction with water and light. This has been stated by the portion beginning with "That which is in the moon":
"Becoming Soma, whose essence is nectar, I nourish all herbs."

And this is stated by the half-verse: "The fiery element (vāhnaṃ tejaḥ), however, consists of illumination, drying, burning, sweating, and digestion, [arising] from the conjunction of earth, water, fire, and air. This very point is expressed here by the phrases "that which is in the fire" and "I am indeed Vaiśvānara."
But space, by virtue of its nature as the locus for consciousness, is indeed omnipresent. || 14 ||

Therefore, having described [the Self] as being of the nature of awakening (*bodhi*), one should understand oneself as having the essential nature of autonomous consciousness (*svātantryabodha*) which follows upon the very form of that which is to be awakened;
as being the supreme nature, the form of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and independent of all knowledge.
To demonstrate that He is the creator of all, He says: "And I am seated in the heart of every being; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas as well."
That which is the nature of autonomous consciousness, capable of withdrawing all that is to be known into the heart—
within that, the reflective awareness "I" is itself knowledge consisting of the manifestation of the unprecedented,
which is the form of the Great Universal Emanation (viśvamahāsṛṣṭi), such as [the thought] "this is indeed a jar."

The essence of the negation of all things as having a self-nature consists of the exclusion (*apohana*) which is of the nature of conceptual cognition; it takes the form of the fettered creation (*pāśava-sṛṣṭi*) and is appropriate for the limited subject (*pramātṛ*) composed of *māyā*. Furthermore, memory is the re-manifestation of that which has been withdrawn and reduced to a mere residual impression (*saṃskāra*).

By this much, all forms of knowledge have been withdrawn. Thus, agency in the form of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), preceded by omniscience, has been described. Regarding the word "by all": indeed, it is the very reality of the Supreme Lord (*parameśa-tattva*) that is to be established by all the scriptures acting in concert.

By virtue of being the author of the Vedas and Vedāntas, and by way of [establishing] the fruits of action and their relationship [to causes], the Lord alone possesses sovereignty in the creation of the entire universe, in its subsequent uprooting, and in re-establishing it in its true nature; thus, His status as the creator of the universe has been stated. Others, however, [argue as follows]:
Apohana is the cognition of distinction, [expressed as] "by this unmade thing, this comes to be"; he makes the Vedānta his own through the state of identification. Thus is the Veda. 15.
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (the immutable) is called the imperishable.
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self; the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. (15–17)
Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 15.18 ||
By the passage "There are these two persons in the world," this is stated: first, in the world,
even one whose nature is unawakened perceives the self— which is composed of a body made of all the elements such as earth and the rest— as conscious and of a perishable form.

Because the world is deluded, it does not cease from the perception of duality, thinking "he knows. But I, the benefactor of all, having pierced the knot of duality, am to be known as pervading the entire world.
"Transcending the perishable"—because beings are insentient.
He who has transcended the syllable (akṣara)—for if the Self were unawakened, its all-pervasiveness would be negated.
By such scriptural statements as "The Supreme Person in the world" and "In the Veda also, He is the Supreme Person," that very non-dual Supreme Self is thus described. || 18 ||
He who, undeluded, knows me thus as the Supreme Person—he, O Bhārata, knowing all, worships me with his whole being. (15.19)

Knowing thus, meditating upon Me alone—the reality of Brahman—which consists of all things, and perceiving everything as being composed of Me, he worships Me alone with his entire being—that is, with his whole nature consisting of form, action, and knowledge. Whatever he sees, he sees as the form of the Lord, and so forth. And likewise by Me alone:
In the *Śivaśaktyavinābhāvastotra*:
"O Ambikā, there can be no praise of You that does not consist of some word, for Your body is indeed composed of all words;
in all forms—whether those born of the mind or those manifesting externally—I perceive Your presence."
Having reflected thus— that in this world, where all inauspiciousness has been pacified by Śiva, everything that has arisen is under the sway of *māyā*—
not even a single fraction of time remains for me, indeed, devoid of praise, recitation, worship, or meditation.
Thus [ends the section]. 19.
Thus has this most secret teaching been spoken by me, O sinless one. By understanding this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done.

It is the most secret because it establishes all things as non-dual. This alone is true awakening, not the awakening that pertains to conventional discourse. And by knowing this very thing, one has fulfilled all duties, but not by merely performing actions.
[The goal is attained] by means of conquering enemies, acquiring wealth, enjoying women, and so forth. The word *ca* (and) indicates something marvelous (*adbhuta*).
For it is observed that the fulfillment of one's purpose (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) is achieved through action; yet here, it is achieved through mere knowledge—this is indeed wonderful.
By the word *iti*, the completion of the treatise is indicated, due to the fullness of that which was to be said.

Because it has reached its conclusion. For instance, by the sixteenth chapter, only the fitness of the disciple Arjuna is established; nothing is taught [further]. Such is the divine endowment, and such is the demonic endowment consisting of ignorance. You—
The intended meaning is simply this: he has attained the divine wealth consisting of knowledge (*vidyā*).

As he will say later: "Do not grieve; [attain] the divine wealth. For this very reason, previously, on the occasion of defining the union of knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā-saṃghaṭṭa*), [it was stated].
Under the guise of the battle between the gods and the asuras, the conflict between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) has been indicated.
Thus, while the true nature of the disciple is being primarily described, other matters have also been mentioned by way of context. In this manner, there will be two chapters.

The instruction, however, is completed by this very point. For the goal to be attained is the worship of the Supreme Lord through every aspect of one's being, which takes the form of total immersion (*āveśa*). And for that purpose, it was stated previously that "everything must be abandoned. Indeed, it is precisely the immersion into the nature of the All-Maheshvara that constitutes the goal.
The supreme auspiciousness—this is auspiciousness. || 20 ||

Regarding this, there is a summary verse: Having removed the great delusion of duality and having made his consciousness consist of Brahman, the sage should always remain absorbed [in that state], even while engaged in worldly affairs. (15)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and royal sage (*rājānaka*) of the Great Maheśvara. 15.

Now begins the sixteenth chapter. It was stated [in the previous chapter] that "having understood this. And what is called "understanding" (bodha) is the arising of knowledge consisting of reflection and meditation—namely, the thought "it is thus"—following upon the knowledge consisting of hearing (śrutamayajñāna).

When there is the attainment of a well-practiced form of consciousness consisting of the contemplation of that [reality], free from the suppression of heterogeneous elements, in the form of investigation (*vicāra*), deliberation (*vimarśa*), profound reflection (*parāmarśa*), and so forth, it occurs. As will be stated:
"Having thus reflected in its entirety, do as you wish. (18.63).

In that regard, regarding knowledge consisting of scripture (*śrutimaya-jñāna*), only the teacher and the scriptures are primarily effective; however, regarding that which consists of reasoning, reflection, and meditative cultivation (*yukticintābhāvanāmaya*), it is the capacity for discernment (*vimarśakṣamatā*) [that is primary].
The unique perfection of a disciple’s qualities is the most essential factor;

therefore, Arjuna certainly possesses this. With this intention, and having reflected upon what is about to be said, [the Lord] utters the word "thus" (*evam*) in order to establish the subject matter of the statement.
With the intention of providing a detailed exposition of the preliminary requisites, the Blessed Lord, the Teacher, said:
The Blessed Lord spoke:
"Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, and self-control..."
Sacrifice, study of the sacred texts, austerity, and uprightness. || 16.1 ||
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, non-attachment, absence of backbiting, compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (16.2)
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, contentment, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride— these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with divine fortune.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the asuric endowment. (16.4)
The divine nature leads to liberation, while the demonic is considered to lead to bondage. Do not grieve, O Pandava, for you are born with a divine nature.

Ignorance, which is indeed characterized by darkness (*tamas*), is situated in the portion belonging to the Asuras; it is suppressed by knowledge (*vidyā*), which increases and apprehends the divine portion. This is the very nature of things.
And you have attained the divine, sattvic portion, which is the essence of knowledge.

Therefore, having abandoned internal ignorance characterized by delusion (*moha*), perform the scriptural activity characterized by the slaying of the external enemy that is ignorance—thus begins the chapter. For instance, these [verses] pertain to the divine portion: [The text continues with the verses: *divyamaṅgaṃ...* etc.
Those signs are clearly perceived: self-restraint (*dama*) is the conquest of the senses;
lack of fickleness (*acāpalya*) is the absence of acting without first reflecting on what precedes and follows;
and vigor (*tejas*) is the removal of meanness by maintaining enthusiasm within oneself. This is divine.

This is prosperity; and it leads to your liberation through the abandonment of desire. Therefore, do not fall into grief, such as thinking, "How might I attain happiness by killing my brother and others? The remainder is clear. || 5 ||
There are two types of creation of beings in this world: the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described in detail;
now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic. (16.6)
This divine nature has been described by the words beginning with "fearlessness. Now he speaks of the demonic:
"The demonic persons know neither the path of action nor the path of renunciation; in them there is neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth" (16.7).
Activity: from what has this arisen? Cessation: where does it dissolve? || 7 ||
They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
it has arisen from mutual interaction, is devoid of substance, and is without cause. (16.8)
There exists no effect whatsoever other than that which is seen; thus, it is "non-existent" (akiñcitka). 8.
Holding fast to this view, those of ruined souls and small intellects, performing cruel deeds and being inauspicious, arise for the destruction of the world. (16.9)
Resorting to insatiable desire, endowed with hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, stubborn in their evil convictions, cruel, and following impure vows, they roam about. (16.10)
Resorting to immeasurable anxiety that lasts until the end of dissolution, they are intent upon the enjoyment of desires, convinced that this is all there is.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger, they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment to accumulate wealth by unjust means.
Their anxiety is endless until the dissolution [of the world], because the dissolution of the cycle of rebirth never ceases.
"This much alone"—namely, the enjoyment of desires—is their supreme duty, and following its destruction, supreme anger arises.
For this very reason, it is said: "devoted to desire and anger. (12)
"Today this has been gained by me; I shall attain this desire. This is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again. (16.13)
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well; I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (16.14)
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, and I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance. (16.15)
With many thoughts and distracted, having fallen under the very sway of delusion and being attached to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, they fall into the impure hell.
"Of manifold minds" because of the absence of certainty; [this applies] to the impure hells such as Avīci and so forth, as well as to the continuum of birth and death. || 16 ||
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride, they perform sacrifices under the guise of sacrifice, motivated by hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions.
Resorting to egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger, these envious ones hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others. (16–18)

They perform sacrifices with the name [only]; the meaning is that they are fruitless. For by anger, everything is destroyed—this is the meaning. Or else: "by name-sacrifices" means those sacrifices which exist merely as names; or else, those sacrifices performed for the sake of the name—that is, for the sake of worldly renown.

Because of this, the designation "sacrificer of sacrifice" arises; yet those [acts] are preceded by hypocrisy and do not bear fruit. Because they are defiled by anger and other such passions, hating the worlds, they hate Me alone—for I, Vāsudeva, am indeed the abode of all. (18)
Those hateful, cruel, and lowest of men in the worlds, I incessantly hurl into inauspicious,
demonic wombs alone.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth, they do not reach Me at all, O son of Kuntī; from there they go to the lowest state. (16–20)
And those who harbor hatred toward Me, practicing what is harmful to themselves—the cause for falling into hell—I hurl them into the very wombs of the asuras. (20)
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to one's own ruin—namely, lust, anger, and greed—one should therefore abandon these three. (16.21)
Since this triad beginning with desire is the very gateway to hell, one should therefore abandon it.
O son of Kuntī, a man who is free from these three gateways to darkness practices what is beneficial for his own soul and thereby attains the supreme goal. (16.21–22)
Nor should this be disregarded as merely the word of a man; rather, it is said that the beginningless scripture (*śāstra*) is the authority here:
"He who, casting aside the injunction of the scripture, acts according to his own whims—he [is not]."
One does not attain success, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.

Therefore, the scripture is your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; having understood the work prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.

For one who abandons the injunctions of the scriptures and deliberates on what ought and ought not to be done solely by their own intellect, there is, on the contrary, a fall into hell. Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Do not establish the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done by means of your own understanding. (24)
Regarding this, there is a summary verse:
"In a state of ignorance, one should not deliberate on what ought to be done by relying solely on one's own intellect;
rather, one should follow the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, for the scripture increases awakening. (16)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha*, composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Arjuna said:
Those who act transgressing the injunctions of the scriptures, yet endowed with faith—of them...
But what is its ultimate nature, O Kṛṣṇa—is it goodness (sattva), or passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)?
The question is: what is the destiny of those who conduct their worldly affairs without relying on the injunctions of the scriptures? || 1 ||
In this regard, the Blessed One provides the following answer in accordance with faith:
The Blessed One said:
"The faith of embodied beings is threefold; it arises from their own nature. It is [of] the *sāttvika* type..."
They are both rajasic and tamasic; hear about them.
And in this regard, the underlying intention is as follows: what is called a "treatise" (śāstra) is indeed devoid of being preceded by an intellect tainted by partiality;
rather, it consists of a firm reflection arising solely from the sovereignty of consciousness.
By virtue of being firmly grasped, it possesses the nature of fruits and so forth;
it has the nature of the supreme Brahman, which is the ultimate reality of the principle of speech that flows from pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
and by virtue of its independent expansion, it extends outward from the internal nature of consciousness to the furthest limit of external manifestation.

From its most subtle form as the *praṇava* and so forth, up to the traditional succession of discourse well-known in worldly practice; as it has been said: "And [the authority of] the tradition and conduct of those who know that."
Thus it is said. And that [intellect] is itself, by its own nature, the discernor of what ought and ought not to be done for the sake of instructing one in what is beneficial and harmful.
He whose heart is naturally delicate due to an abundance of *sattva* acts in accordance with the scriptures; but another is defiled by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Even while practicing what is taught in the scriptures, he does not truly practice them,
because he does not carry out the meaning of the scriptures in its entirety. For the scripture itself declares that it bears fruit only for those possessed of sattva.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and virtuous conduct, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

Thus, there is no other [result] because of a lack of self-restraint. Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is that it bears fruit only for those who have abandoned desire, anger, and delusion; this is the purport of this chapter. That very point is being elaborated here, and since its meaning is clear, it is not further explained. However, merely—
It is written precisely for the purpose of preventing errors regarding the reading of the text. || 2 ||
The faith of every being conforms to their own nature, O Bhārata.
This person is made of faith; whatever one's faith is, that very person one becomes. (17.3)

Those characterized by goodness (sāttvika) worship the gods; those characterized by passion (rājasa) worship yakṣas and rakṣasas; and those characterized by darkness (tāmasa) worship spirits, ghosts, and piśācas. (17.4)
Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures, being possessed of hypocrisy and egoism, and impelled by the force of desire and attachment; 17.5.
Those who emaciate the insentient collection of elements residing in the body, as well as Me who am situated within the body— know them to be of demonic resolve.

In the phrase "conforming to the *sattva*," the word *sattva* is a synonym for *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature). This person—the self—is necessarily bound by faith that turns away from the activities of others; and he is to be understood as being composed of that [faith] alone. It is insentient because it lacks discrimination.

And by failing to practice the meaning of the scriptures, they emaciate me; therefore, performing ascetic practices fashioned by their own intellects, they are, on the contrary, characterized by tamas.
Food also, like faith, is threefold according to the distinctions of *sattva* and the other qualities; likewise are sacrifice, austerity, and charity. Thus it is said:
"Indeed, for everyone, food is dear in three ways, as are sacrifice and austerity."
Listen now to this distinction regarding their giving. || 17-7 ||
Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy—those which are savory, unctuous, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—are dear to those of sattvic nature. (17.8)
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are desired by those of passionate nature (rājasa); they bestow suffering, grief, and disease. (17.9)
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and long kept, as well as that which is leftover or impure—such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature. (17.10)
"Yātayāma" means that whose portions (yāma) have passed away. || 10 ||

That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits, with the mind composed solely on the thought "sacrifice must be performed," is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
Having concentrated the mind—having pursued it with resolve. || 11 ||
But know that sacrifice to be rajasic—which is performed with a view toward fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation—that it is unstable and impermanent. (17.12)
"Even for the sake of ostentation": ostentation is the desire that "the world may know me to be of such a character. 12.
They declare that sacrifice to be tāmasa which is devoid of prescribed rules, where food is not distributed, which lacks mantras and sacrificial fees, and is bereft of faith. (17.13)
"Devoid of ritual" (vidhihīnam) means lacking the actions prescribed by the scriptures;
that very point is elaborated by the qualifying terms "not created," "without food," and so forth. || 13 ||
Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity. (17.14)
Straightforwardness is uprightness; it is boldness that does not conceal its object. || 14 ||
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, as well as the practice of reciting one's own sacred texts—this is called austerity of speech. (17.15)
"It is truth. The definition of its essential nature is provided by the phrase "that which is pleasant and beneficial":
that which is pleasant at the present time and beneficial at another time—such speech is called truth, and not merely the reporting of events exactly as they occurred. || 15 ||
Tranquility of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint,
and purity of being— this is called mental austerity.
Bhāva means intention; its complete purity is bhāvasaṃśuddhi (purity of intention). || 16 ||
That threefold austerity, when performed by men endowed with supreme faith, by those who are disciplined and free from desire for rewards, is declared to be of the nature of sattva.
That austerity which is performed for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, and with hypocrisy, is declared here to be rajasic; it is unstable and impermanent.
That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself,
or for the sake of destroying another, is declared to be tāmasa.

There is faith in all three kinds of austerity. For one of the nature of *sattva*, faith is indeed centered on that [austerity] itself; for one of the nature of *rajas*, however, faith is directed toward hypocrisy and the like; and for one established in *tamas*, faith is directed toward the destruction of others and so forth. Thus, austerity of all three kinds is accompanied by faith.
The Sage said: || 19 ||
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who cannot return the favor, at the right place and time, and to a worthy recipient—
that gift is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
"One should give"—this is merely an injunction that "it must be given," which is to be observed as a duty. || 20 ||

But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit, and which is given with distress—that is remembered as being of the nature of passion (rājasa). || 17-21 ||
It is afflicted by the intent toward faults, due to defects such as limitedness and so forth. || 21 ||
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
And there is the disrespecting of giving, which arises from disrespecting the recipient and so forth.
Thus, the actions of worldly people have been explained according to their threefold dispositions, such as the *sāttvika* and others. || 22 ||
Now, as for those whose intellects have crossed over the narrow straits of the three qualities (guṇas), it is stated in what manner they perform their actions:
"Oṃ tat sat—this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman. By that [designation], the Brāhmaṇas..."
And the Vedas and the Yajñas were ordained in ancient times. || 17-23 ||
Therefore, having uttered the syllable "Om," the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity, as prescribed by the rules, proceed constantly among those who discourse upon Brahman.
Without aiming for a fruit, those who desire liberation perform sacrifices, acts of austerity, and various acts of charity. (17.25)
The word "sat" is used in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness; likewise, O Pārtha, the word "sat" is uttered in reference to a praiseworthy action. (17.26)
Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "good" (sat); and action performed for their sake is likewise designated as "good. (17.27)

By these three words—*oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*—there is the designation of Brahman, that is, its manifestation before one. Among them, by the word *oṃ*, it is indicated that this meaning of the scripture should be accepted as long as there is connection with the body. By *tat*...

By means of a pronoun, which denotes only the universal and is incapable of referring to a specific particular, the absence of aiming at a fruit is predicated of Brahman; for there can be no aiming without the apprehension of a specific [object].

Even though [the Lord] favors all specific [desires], because there is no attainment of all fruits despite His being the agent of everything, this Vedic text expresses praise by saying "sat" (it exists/is good). This is because even these [acts] such as sacrifice, while being performed, are [otherwise considered] defective.

An action performed with the intellect [in this manner] attains the state of being *tāmasa*; and because it is performed with the aim of a specific fruit, it is not *sāttvika*, but rather leads only to bondage. Therefore, even those who perform sacrifices and other rites while thinking "this must be done" are not bound.
With this very intention it was said in the Ādiparvan:
"Austerity is not a taint, study is not a taint, the natural injunctions of the Veda are not a taint;
the forcible seizure of wealth is not a taint, but these very things become a taint when corrupted by one's inner disposition."
(Mahābhārata) thus: "Kalka" means a debtor. Regarding the term "natural," it is said that a Brāhmaṇa should study the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs without any external motive.

The essential meaning is this: these very actions are binding when performed with a forceful disposition—that is, with a mind characterized by the three qualities such as *sattva*—and through conduct that is contrary to what is established by the scriptures and worldly consensus; they are not otherwise. Therefore, [the performance of] sacrifices and so forth...
As long as it is conditioned by the body, it must indeed be performed; the action prescribed for that purpose consists of acquisition and so forth.

Or else, by the word *oṃ*, [it refers to] that in which the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) has been completely stilled; and by the word *tat*, [it refers to] the sovereignty of will whose nature consists solely in the mere awareness of the emerging waves of the universe.
[He] enters into His own nature.

By the word "sat" (Being), it is demonstrated that even in the state of fullness, there is a manifestation characterized by a variegated nature, wherein difference unfolds through the expansion of the weight of the sovereignty of will. And so it has been said:

Regarding the phrase "in the state of being good and in the state of excellence": having placed before him that supreme, tranquil form, and having centered within himself the surge of desires consisting of the wish to give, the wish to sacrifice, and the wish to perform austerities, he became fully engaged in the entire array of activities for giving, sacrificing, and practicing austerity.
This final form that has now manifested—these three together are indeed the unimpeded, natural state; so for whom, what, how, from where, where, and by what means could there be any fruit? || 27 ||

Now, it is said that for one who lacks faith, *tāmasa* action is entirely fruitless— it yields nothing more than the mere effort produced by the exertion of assembling the various factors of performance; therefore, one should never be devoid of faith.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit hereafter, nor does it yield any here.
"Non-existent" means "unpraiseworthy. Therefore, for those striving in praiseworthy action, auspiciousness comes about with ease; may there be auspiciousness! || 28 ||
On this point, there is a summary verse:

That very same penetration of the factors of action (kāraka) and that very same undifferentiated activity—nevertheless, for those possessed of discernment, it culminates in the goal of liberation. (17)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Maheśvara, Rājānaka Abhinavagupta. || 17 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Arjuna said:
O mighty-armed one, I wish to know the true nature of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and of relinquishment (tyāga).
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O destroyer of Keśin individually!

It was previously stated: "He is a renouncer (tyāgin) and he is wise," as well as "He is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi, not one who has merely abandoned the sacred fires," and so forth. Therefore, because both the terms "renouncer" and "renunciant" are heard [in the scriptures], this question arises from a desire to know the distinction between the two. || 1 ||
To this, the Blessed Lord replied:
"The wise know the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire as *saṃnyāsa*."
The wise declare that renunciation is the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions. || 18-2 ||

"Desirable rites" refers to the Agniṣṭoma and other such sacrifices. "All actions" means that even when all obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) duties are being performed, the renunciation is the relinquishing of their fruits. Furthermore, whatever remains to be said regarding this chapter [is as follows].
Since that has already been examined at length by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara and others, what need have we—
who are devoted solely to fulfilling our vow of merely elucidating its hidden meaning?
By the effort of demonstrating what has already been stated. || 2 ||
In this very context, for the sake of determining the specific distinction, he sets forth the various opinions:
"Some wise men have said that action should be abandoned as being defective;
others, however, say that the action consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned. (18.3)

Some, like the followers of Sāṃkhya, maintain a distinction regarding renunciation, holding that action involving defects such as violence is sinful and therefore to be abandoned— though not all [action], for some results are auspicious. Others, however, who have donned the cloak of Mīmāṃsā, argue that [it is only action] for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)...
"From the scripture" means that, according to the principle beginning with "Therefore, that Vedic violence...

and so forth, [violence] which partakes in the constituent element of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) does not constitute actual violence, because the general scriptural injunction "one shall not kill" is sublated in that case. However, [the sacrifice] such as the Śyena...
"Violence [is a factor]; and regarding the result, the cognition [of the agent] conforms to the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*)" (*Ślokavārttika*).
Thus, one should not abandon other rites such as sacrifices, even though they involve violence and the like.

Those who distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done by taking refuge solely in the scriptures are considered wise. Listen now to my definitive conclusion regarding renunciation, O best of the Bharatas; for renunciation, O tiger among men, is declared to be of three kinds.
The acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. For sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise. (18.5)
Moreover, O Pārtha, these actions must also be performed, having abandoned attachment and the fruits thereof; this is my firm and supreme conviction. (18.6)
And the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate; the abandonment of such action out of delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || 18.7 ||
He who, out of fear of physical hardship, abandons action merely because it is "suffering," performs a passionate renunciation and shall never obtain the fruit of renunciation. (18.8)

Whatever obligatory action is performed, O Arjuna, simply because it is duty— having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit— that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
He does not hate unwholesome action nor does he cling to the wholesome; he is renounced, filled with being, wise, and his doubts are severed. (18.10)
Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to renounce actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a renouncer.

In this regard, however, this is the certainty: that renunciation alone— which is characterized by the diversity of the natures of the qualities previously observed— is performed by a mental modification consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Renunciation, according to the actual state of things which manifests as having that specific nature, consists for those who know the Supreme Brahman in the performance of actions with equanimity toward success or failure and the like, through the avoidance of attachment and aversion, and by being devoid of any desire for results.

Therefore he says: "Having abandoned renunciation that is rājasic and tāmasic, there is no connection with any fruit whatsoever. But from sāttvic renunciation comes the fruit consisting of the preservation of the meaning of the scriptures for one who has abandoned the grasping of the entire collection of the guṇas.
Furthermore, the sage’s statement regarding the reality of renunciation is logically sound.
The threefold fruit of action—unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced. (18.12)
Of those who do not abandon [their attachments], consisting of fruits. || 12 ||
Now, even in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), while all five causes of action remain present,
these men blinded by ignorance forcibly project the entire burden of agency onto their own selves alone. Therefore, by their own intellect, they [attribute] the self—
They bind [the self], yet in reality there is no bondage for it—this is what is taught:
"O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes which, according to the Sāṅkhya system of definitive conclusion, are declared for the accomplishment of all actions. (18.13)
That in which a conclusion or certainty is established is "kṛtānta," meaning a final doctrine or established tenet. || 13 ||
The locus, the agent, and the various instruments, as well as the diverse individual efforts—the divine is the fifth among these. (18.14)
Whatever action one undertakes with body, speech, or mind, O Arjuna—whether it be righteous or its opposite—these five are its causes. (18.15)
This being so, he who, due to his unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the sole agent—that person of dull wit does not see. (18.16)
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—even by killing these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound. (18.17)
The locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the object (*viṣaya*). Destiny (*daiva*) is the merit and demerit accumulated in the past.

These five—the locus and the others—having attained the state of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), are the causes for all actions. Others, however, explain that "everything is governed (*adhiṣṭhīyate*) by this [locus] in every action."
The *rajas* residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), having attained its functional state, is designated by the term "karma-yoga"—

which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consisting of the fivefold transformation of fortitude (*dhṛti*), faith (*śraddhā*), pleasure (*sukha*), the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), and the desire to know through inquiry (*vividiṣārūpa*).
In some instances, it is expressed by the word "effort" (*prayatna*).

The agent is characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*) and is the reflector; the instrument consists of the internal organ, the mind (*manas*), as well as external instruments such as the eyes and the sword; effort consists of the vital breaths, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and so forth; by the word "divine" (*daiva*), merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are meant; and through these two, all states (*bhāva*) residing within the intellect [are produced].

[They] have been observed. Others, however, consider the Lord to be the substratum—due to their unrefined intellect and lack of certain wisdom. But he who, through the firmness of detachment from egoism purified by the hundreds of arguments previously stated, [performs] actions...
He who acts does not partake in bondage because of his perfected understanding; this is the intended meaning. || 17 ||
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulse to action. The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action. (18.18)

In the context of action, *codanā* is the desire for engagement. At that time, for those things which— because they consist merely of non-awakening— are expressed by the terms "knowledge," "the object of knowledge," and "the knower" according to the Veda,
it is precisely for them that there is the form of correct apprehension, characterized by the thought "this is mine" through the intention for a result.
Appropriation (*svīkaraṇa*) consists of the thought, "I shall enjoy this, because it was performed by me"— it is so called because at that time, during the moment of its accomplishment,
one is possessed of being denotable by the terms instrument, object, and agent. Therefore, it is the "descent" (*āveśa*) for yogis.
For those [who hold such a view], there is no occasion for words regarding the instruments of action and so forth;
rather, the intended meaning refers solely to cognition itself. || 18 ||
Now, in order to show the distinction among these six by way of the differentiation of their qualities in brief, he says:
"Knowledge, action, and the agent— these three indeed are declared according to the differentiation of qualities."
Listen also to those [qualities] as they are enumerated according to their true nature. || 18-19 ||

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Listen to that which is called the threefold knowledge and so forth in the Sāṃkhya system, wherein there is a determination (*niścaya*) regarding the enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*) of the qualities (*guṇas*).
By the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it is stated that the instrument (*karaṇa*) involved in both cognition and action is twofold.
In this way, it should be understood that "action" (karman) refers both to the object to be acted upon and to the knower and the agent. || 19 ||

In that regard, the threefold nature of the instrument of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*) has been stated by means of the three verses beginning with "tatra sarvabhūteṣu. For this very reason, the third case ending is used in the word "yena" (by which). By this much, the essential nature of the general category of the instrument of knowledge has been described. [This is further elaborated] by the passage beginning with "niyatam" (determined).

By means of three verses, the twofold nature of action—consisting of that which is to be known and that which is to be performed—is presented. By the three verses beginning with "free from attachment" (*muktasaṅga*), however, the essential nature of the two types of agents is briefly described.
Furthermore, the threefold nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) is taught for the purpose of establishing the distinctions in the essential nature of the specific instruments [of action].
