Since [the means] were previously mentioned, and because the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) and the state of desiring to know (*vividiṣu*) are implied by steadfastness (*dhṛti*) and happiness (*sukha*), their threefold nature was stated by the verse beginning with "by which steadfastness...
and the verse beginning with "but happiness now...". Thus he says:
That by which one perceives the one undecaying reality in all beings, undivided among the divided—know that knowledge to be *sāttvika*. (18–20)
They are differentiated according to their states as gods, humans, and so forth. || 20 ||
But that knowledge which perceives various distinct entities as separate from one another among all beings is declared to be rājasa. || 18-21 ||
By way of distinction—that is, through such cognitions as "herein is my pleasure" and "herein is my aversion," and so forth. || 21 ||
But that which is attached to a single effect as if it were the whole, which is causeless, devoid of the true meaning, and meager—that is declared to be tāmasa. (18.22)

That grasping at anger, passion, and so forth, which occurs without investigating the cause and without any basis in reason, solely through the force of obsession and attachment, is designated as tāmasa. || 22 ||
Action performed with determination, free from attachment, and devoid of passion and hatred, by one who does not desire its fruit—that is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). (18.23)
It must certainly be performed. || 23 ||
But that action which is performed by one desiring rewards, or again with egoism, and which abounds in afflictions—that is declared to be rajasic. (18.24)
It is "abundant," meaning pervaded by the afflictions, such as ignorance and the rest. || 24 ||
That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity, is said to be tāmasa.
From delusion, which consists of dogmatic attachment. || 25 ||

One who is free from attachment, devoid of egoism, endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm, and remains unchanged in success or failure—such an agent is said to be characterized by goodness (sāttvika). (18.26)

By the term *anahaṃvādī* (one who does not speak of "I"), which includes the suffix *ṇini*, it is indicated that one who does not say "I am the doer," but rather acts with that disposition, possesses those qualities, or performs those actions well— even for a yogin, speech such as "I am doing" exists only by virtue of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) as mere worldly usage.
It is forbidden. || 26 ||
One who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure, and possessed by joy and sorrow—such an agent is declared to be of the rajasic type. (18.27)
Filled with joy and sorrow regarding success and failure. || 27 ||
One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating is said to be a doer of tamasic nature. (18.28)
Deceit is cruelty. || 28 ||
Listen, O Dhanañjaya, as I describe exhaustively and individually the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to their qualities (guṇas). (18.29)

*Buddhi* is determination; *dhṛti* is contentment. For everyone, after performing either a good deed or an evil one, inevitably grasps the thought at the end: "What else remains? That which was to be done has been done. Otherwise, how could there be cessation from actions?
This would be the reason. Therefore, the intended meaning is that everything indeed possesses support (*dhṛti*).
As for the meaning of the term, it is explained precisely because it is not well-known. || 29 ||

O Pārtha, that intellect which understands engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, and bondage and liberation— that is considered to be sattvic.
O Pārtha, that intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, and what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is of the nature of passion (rājasī).
Not as it truly is; incorrect. || 31 ||
That intellect which, enveloped by darkness (tamas), perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and regards all objects in a perverted manner, is considered to be tāmasī.

That steadiness by which one, through yoga, holds fast the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses with unwavering constancy— that is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī).

He restrains the activities of the mind, vital breath, and senses through yoga, thinking: "What use have I for enjoyments and the like? May I become one who delights solely in the Self in every respect."
But that resolve by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna, while desiring their fruits through attachment—that resolve, O Pārtha, is of the nature of passion (rājasa). (18.34)
"By way of incidental discussion" means not with such dogmatic attachment. || 34 ||
That resolve by which a person of dull intellect does not abandon sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and even delusion, is considered to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
That resolve by which one binds oneself to contentment through devotion solely to sleep, quarrels, and the like—that is *tāmasī* fortitude. || 35 ||
Now hear from me, O bull among the Bharatas, about the three kinds of happiness:
that in which one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering. (18.36)
That which is like poison in its onset but comparable to nectar in its result—one should know that to be *sāttvika* happiness, born from the clarity of the self and the intellect. (18.37)
"At that time" means at the time of practice; it is "like poison" because the attachment to sense objects, cultivated over hundreds of lifetimes, is difficult to avoid. And it is said in the Śruti:
"The edge of a razor is uneven and difficult to traverse."
And so forth. From the clarity of the self (*ātman*), the clarity of the intellect (*buddhi*) arises, because there is no other thing to be depended upon. (37)
That which, at first, is like nectar due to the contact of the senses with their objects, but in its consequence is like poison—that is known as rajasic. (18.38)
The pleasure arising from the mutual conjunction of the objects and the senses is like that which occurs from the connection of the eye with a form. || 38 ||
That pleasure which, both at the beginning and in its consequence, deludes the self and arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence, is declared to be tāmasa.
That happiness which arises from sleep, laziness, and the negligence previously explained, is tāmasa. (39)
There is no being on earth, nor again in heaven among the gods, that is free from these three qualities born of nature. (18.40)

Thus, regarding the agent, the object, and the instrument, as well as the intellect (*buddhi*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and pleasure (*sukha*)— all of which are distinguished by the variations of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*—

there occurs a sequence and simultaneity of their functions through their mutual relationship as subordinate and principal factors, and through their states of being sublated or sublaters, and their conjunction.
Due to their connection with [the qualities] beginning with *sattva* and because they possess innumerable divisions, they are capable of producing various fruits.

By this, the profundity of actions previously indicated by the aphorism has been determined in detail along with its reasons. And all these [beings], from the deities down to the stationary objects, are connected to the three *guṇas*.
They do not transcend this. For it has been said:
"From Brahmā down to the smallest insect, no one is truly happy;
everyone who desires to live undergoes various transformations."
Thus, the intention is that happiness in its true nature belongs to one whose mind has transcended the *guṇas*, and not to anyone else.

In this way, it has been demonstrated that each of these six—beginning with fortitude (*dhṛti*)—possesses a threefold nature. From among those, one who abides in the *sāttvika* group [attains] the divine...

Arjuna has been encouraged with the thought, "Having attained perfection in this knowledge, you are likewise fit for it. Now, however, this is being said: if you proceed with action by means of this understanding of knowledge, then, through engagement in your own duty (*svadharma*), [you will attain the goal].

Furthermore, due to the purity of consciousness, you have no connection with karma. If you do not accept this, then you must necessarily engage in activity, because birth itself remains established as being of such a nature; for everything is determined by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Even if its true nature remains concealed for some time due to some defect, it certainly regains that manifested nature once the obscuring factor has vanished;
for such is the inherent nature of phonemes. Thus, when this [manifestation] is inevitably to occur—
From that [division of labor] follows the distribution of fruits; thus he said:
"O scorcher of the foe, the duties of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are divided according to the qualities born of their own natures. (18.41)

Tranquility, self-control, as well as purity, forbearance, and uprightness; knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith in the hereafter—this is the action pertaining to Brahman, born of one's own nature. (18.42)
Heroism, majesty, fortitude, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle, as well as generosity and lordliness—this is the duty of a kshatriya, born of his own nature. (18.43)
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature; likewise, service characterized by exertion is the duty of a Śūdra, born of his own nature. (18.44)
Devoted to his own particular duty, a man attains perfection.
Listen to how one who is intent on his own duty finds success. (18.45)
From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. (18.46)
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed.
One who performs the action prescribed by his own nature incurs no sin. (18.47)
One should not abandon one's innate duty, O son of Kuntī, even though it is flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, as fire is by smoke. (18.48)
With an intellect unattached everywhere, having conquered the self and being free from longing, he attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of actionlessness.
Learn from me, O son of Kuntī, how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman, and what, in brief,
is that supreme culmination of knowledge.
Endowed with purified intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude, one should abandon objects such as sound and cast off attachment and aversion. (18.51)
Frequenting solitary places, eating sparingly, with speech, body, and mind restrained, he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken recourse to dispassion. || 18-52 ||
Having abandoned egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, being free from the sense of "mine" and tranquil, one is fit for becoming Brahman. 18.53
Having become one with Brahman, serene in soul, he neither grieves nor rejoices; equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me. 18.54
Through devotion he comes to know Me—who I am and who I truly am in essence; then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter. (18.55)
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains through my grace the eternal, imperishable state.
Renouncing all actions with your mind in Me, O Bhārata, take refuge in the yoga of the intellect and remain constantly focused on Me. 18.57
With your mind fixed on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace;
but if you do not relinquish self-conceit, you will perish.
If, relying on your ego, you think "I will not fight," this resolve of yours is in vain;
your own nature will compel you. (18.59)
Bound by your own karma born of your very nature, O son of Kuntī, you shall do that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, even against your will. (18.60)

Since the nature of defining the specific distribution of duties for the Brāhmaṇas and others does not transcend one's own essential being, your very nature— known as *prakṛti*— which is the essence of your status as a Kṣatriya, will inevitably exercise its governing power over you, even against your will. It is solely by means of that [nature]...
There is a connection between merit and demerit for one who is so enjoined. Therefore, perform actions preceded by the authority of the knowledge declared by me;
if you do so, bondage will cease. This is the meaning of this [passage].
The purpose is the composition of the supporting elements for the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya).
The meaning of the intermediate sentences is clear. In brief—that is, in summary—of the aforementioned knowledge; [it describes] its culmination through the abandonment of the web of words.
He states the certainty with the words "by means of pure intellect," and so forth.
Since all of this has already been largely explained, no further effort is made here. || 60 ||
The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by his illusory power, as if they were mounted on a machine.
Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bhārata; by His grace you shall attain the supreme perfection and the eternal abode. (18.62)

This Lord, the Supreme Self, must necessarily be accepted as one's refuge; for when that presiding agent, the doer, the knower, who is identical with one’s own self, is realized, actions no longer persist. Indeed, not...

While the lion cub, whose majesty was revealed by the mass of pearls falling from the temples of rutting elephants split open by the tips of his exceedingly sharp claws, presided over the cave, the young deer— possessing only the strength to flee at the first sign of a restless mind— roamed about at will.

"They depend upon a state of proficiency in the cultivation of their own specific functions. Having begun with the words "Go to Him alone as your refuge," the Blessed Lord concludes with the statement "By my grace," thereby identifying the Supreme Self, the Lord, and Vāsudeva as one and the same. || 62 ||
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared by Me to you.
Having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.

This very knowledge has been declared. It is more secret than even the secret—that is, more secret than the Vedānta—because it reveals supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*). "Having reflected upon this in its entirety" means that its essential purport (*tātparya*) should be investigated here. And that purport is as follows:

Although we have already elucidated this point by way of specific illustrations on various occasions, nevertheless, a clear and exhaustive investigation is now presented, for this subject is most worthy of being adopted;
indeed, the mind is never satiated when it is either contemplated or heard. (63)
"Now hear that knowledge which is the most secret and certain among all things here," he said:
"Hear again from Me My supreme word, the most secret of all; you are dearly beloved to Me and your mind is firm, therefore I shall speak what is for your benefit. (18.64)
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me; thus you shall come to Me alone.
I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. (18.65)

By the passage beginning with "Fix your mind on Me" (Gītā 18.65), it is established that, in every respect, the offering to Brahman alone holds primacy in the scripture; it has been stated that for one who performs the offering to Brahman, this scripture is meaningful. (18.65)
And it is said:
"Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (18.66)

"Regarding 'all phenomena' (*sarvadharmān*): this refers to such things as the incidental killing of kinsmen during the act of fighting; having abandoned the notion of a self-nature (*ātma-dharmatā*)—thinking "I am the doer of all that"—likewise, [one abandons it] regarding the prohibition against the act of killing one's teacher and so forth."

Abandoning [the thought] with your mind that "it will happen," go for refuge to Me alone— the Supreme Lord, the independent creator of all— as the one who presides over the nature of everything. Therefore, I, the omniscient one, [will deliver] you from all sins.
"I shall liberate you. Do not grieve; do not fall into the delusion of not knowing what ought to be done.
(66) This [teaching] must never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who is unwilling to listen, nor to one who finds fault with Me. (18.67)
The concealment of this knowledge bestows success because it is not accessible to all people.
First, when the knot of sin has been shattered by austerity (tapas), there arises a readiness for the ripening of merit;
thus, first comes austerity, and from austerity, faith (śraddhā) is born. That very faith is what is meant here by devotion (bhakti).

Faith, even when it has arisen, sometimes does not take root, because—like a flash of lightning—it vanishes as soon as it is seen for a moment. Therefore, once that [faith] has taken root, there arises a desire to hear.
And this much [desire] occurs even in some regarding non-divine matters, such as the dry knowledge of Sāṃkhya and other systems.

Or even in the case of a theistic system, for someone who, out of a desire for a fruit, makes that very fruit the primary object and degrades the Blessed Lord by making himself the recipient of his favor,
it would be as has been said:
"Furthermore, the person exists for the sake of action, and actions exist for the sake of the fruit" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra).
Thus, in either case, the meaning is that there is only malice and disregard toward the Blessed One. || 67 ||
He who shall proclaim this supreme secret among my devotees, having established the highest devotion toward me, will undoubtedly come to me alone. (18.68)

"Devotion" (bhaktim)—this very act of generating devotion toward Me consists in this exposition [of it] for My devotees. He will state: "He shall bestow" (dhāsyati)—that is, he shall extend—[it] directly according to the method taught in the scriptures. "He attains identity with Me" (manmayatām eti)—this is indeed an injunction (vidhi).
This is not a figurative statement; so it is elsewhere as well. || 68 ||
And among humans, there shall be no one who does more for my pleasure than he; nor shall there be anyone else on earth more dear to me than he.
And whoever shall study this righteous dialogue between us, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. (18.70)
Even that man who, possessing faith and free from malice, should merely hear [this], he too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds. (18.71)
"Has this been heard by you, O Pārtha, with a one-pointed mind?
Has the delusion of ignorance been destroyed within you, O Dhanañjaya? (18.72)
Arjuna said:
My delusion is destroyed and memory has been regained by me through your grace, O Acyuta. I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do your bidding. (18.73)

By the words "Delusion is destroyed" and so forth, [the Lord] indicates that Arjuna’s engagement in battle has indeed arisen, but that perfect knowledge of Brahman has not yet been born; thus, He provides an opportunity for the future subject matter of the *Anugītā*. || 73 ||
Sañjaya said:
Thus have I heard this wonderful conversation between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha, which causes the hair to stand on end.
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this great and most secret Yoga,
as it was being taught directly by Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of Yogins.
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful and meritorious dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over again.
And as I recall again and again that most extraordinary form of Hari, O Great King, I am filled with wonder and rejoice over and over again.
Where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yogins, is, and where Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, is, there prosperity, victory, and fortune are certain; such is my conviction.
Concluding the dialogue with the words of Sañjaya, this very meaning— by means of a sequence of firm composition and through the very continuity provided by an uninterrupted stream of reflection—
is brought at the end to the state of a perfectly clear, non-conceptual experience.
It is said that mere remembrance alone bestows the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, through the attainment of reality by the mere remembrance of this dialogue between the Blessed One and Arjuna, there are the glorious splendors of victory; may there be auspiciousness. 78.
Here is a summary verse:

Having shattered the intellect— which is sluggish with the delusion of ignorance and divided by [the qualities of] *sattva* and so forth— and having attained Viṣṇu, who transcends all conceptual construction through the beauty of his own manifested self-power;
Whatever he performs even in play, while remaining solely in the natural operation of his senses arising from his own innate disposition,
all that becomes conducive to auspiciousness for him.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher and royal sage of the Great Maheśvara.
There was the illustrious Kātyāyana, who, like Vararuci, was satisfied by his radiant awakening; he was the ornament of that lineage,
the very learned and steadfast-minded one named Sauśuka, a Brāhmaṇa of great fortune.
After that, his son Bhūtirāja was born, a high-souled one by whom all these worlds, fallen into darkness, were uplifted as if by the sun. || 1 ||
Abhinavagupta, a bee at the lotus feet of that [teacher], composed this *Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* under the influence of the exhortation of Saddivajaloṭaka. (2)
Therefore, whether this is untrue or even true, it is in every way not to be resented by the wise; for this deed is indeed for the sake of a kinsman. (3)
I bow to Abhinavagupta, the auspicious one, who is the union of the ever-new Śakti and the Great Lord Maheśvara who is concealed within her; that which is the stainless form of both. || 4 ||

This *Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha* is complete; it is the work of Abhinavagupta, whose renown was attained through meditation upon the lotus-feet of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva). May there be auspiciousness!
